records.title: Why distinguishing kalām by ‘belief’ is difficult
records.arabic: قوله خاصة والمراد من اختصاص علم الكلام هو الاختصاص الإضافي على ما صرح به المصنف في شرح المقاصد
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله خاصة)» · «الاختصاص بعلم الكلام» · «الاختصاص ... على ما صرح به المصنف في شرح المقاصد» · «اعتقاد القلب».
records.english: Concerning his expression “specifically”: the particularity intended for the science of kalām is a relative particularity, as the author explicitly states in Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:8; Only the initial marginal argument is transcribed; its continuation and the second lower block are substantial. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 21. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: The marginal commentator insists that the difference between kalām and logic or law cannot simply be a difference in **subject terms**. Many theological proofs concern bodies, accidents, possibility, causality and language, all of which can also be examined in other disciplines. The relevant differentiation is through the **end for which the inquiry is undertaken**: establishing a religious belief rather than, for instance, deriving a legal action or analysing the formal structure of an inference.

records.title: Necessary judgments and practical judgments
records.arabic: لكن الغرض منها ليس مجرد ذلك الاعتقاد، بل الغرض هو الاعتقاد وكيفية العمل معاً ...
records.arabic_anchors: «الأحكام التي يتعلق الغرض بمجرد اعتقادها» · «وجوب القلب» · «الأحكام الشرعية» · «كيفية العمل».
records.english: But the aim in their case is not merely that belief; rather, the aim is both belief and how to act. […]
records.proof_note: Connected lower reading, several compact examples unverified.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: Some religious judgments call for the **assent** of the believer; others are concerned with the manner of acting. The marginal writer examines whether this separation is absolute or is better expressed by a difference in the **proximate aim** of the relevant science. An obligatory practical act may also be something one must believe is obligatory; that does not make its detailed derivation a question of kalām. Likewise, a proposition about theological doctrine may have practical consequences without ceasing to be a doctrinal proposition.
records.stage88_source_note: lower register, transition from the discussion of the legal ruling to its practical purpose; clear clause, with its unstated antecedents preserved as an open context
records.stage88_proof: direct visual reading of first-print facsimile; requires second independent proof
records.stage88_copytext: Būlāq, 1318 AH, vol. I printed p.8, combined PDF physical p.21

records.title: Remarks on the naming of the discipline
records.arabic: (قال المصنف رحمه الله الكلام هو العلم إلخ) أي علم الكلام هو
records.arabic_anchors: «(قال المصنف رحمه الله الكلام هو العلم الخ)» · «أي علم الكلام».
records.english: “The author—may God have mercy on him—said: ‘Kalām is knowledge,’ etc.” That is, the science of kalām is [the knowledge here intended].
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:8; The ruled author’s historical theories of the name kalām remain untranscribed, and no author is inferred for this note. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 21. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: On the author's words “kalām is knowledge, etc.”: the phrase is intended as **‘the science of kalām’**, not a statement that every instance of speech counts as knowledge. The gloss alludes to other historical explanations of why the discipline came to be called ‘kalām’; these alternatives do not all supply its formal definition.

records.title: The specific scope of theological science
records.arabic: كمباحث العلم والنظر والدليل لأن تحصيل العقائد بطريق النظر والاستدلال والرد على منكري حصول العلم مطلقا أو استفادته من النظر مطلقا أو في الإلهيات خاصة يتوقف على ذلك
records.arabic_anchors: «الكلام خاصة» · «كمباحث العلم والنظر والدليل» · «لا تحصل العقائد بطريق النظر والاستدلال» · «الإلهيات خاصة».
records.english: [These introductory investigations include] questions of knowledge, inquiry and proof, since acquiring doctrines through reflection and inference—and responding to those who deny the attainment of knowledge altogether, or deny that it is gained through reflection either in general or specifically in divine matters—depends upon them.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:8; Upper opening follows the I:7 division; the brief concluding transition on I:8 is not transcribed. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 21. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: The designation ‘kalām’ does not simply mean every investigation of **knowledge, inquiry, and evidence**. Those subjects also belong to logic and the theory of demonstration. Nor is its defining mark merely that doctrinal propositions are asserted. What distinguishes this science is the way its investigations are ordered toward establishing **religious convictions** through arguments. The statement therefore moves from the preparatory discussion to a definition of kalām.

records.title: Definition through doctrinal knowledge
records.arabic: (الكلام هو العلم بالعقائد) وهي الأحكام التي يتعلق الغرض بمجرد اعتقادها بالقلب
records.arabic_anchors: «(الكلام هو العلم بالعقائد)» · «وهي الأحكام التي يتعلق الغرض بمجرد اعتقادها بالقلب».
records.english: “Kalām is knowledge of doctrines”: these are judgments whose intended object is simply their being believed in the heart.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:8; Only the opening lemma and its immediate explanation are transcribed; the upper discussion continues and the different practical class is not fully entered. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 21. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: “Kalām is knowledge of the doctrines.” These are judgments for which the relevant end is **assent in the heart** as such, rather than the bodily execution of a practice. This distinction does not imply that religious practice is unimportant; rather, it determines the formal respect under which the science studies its judgments, in contrast to a discipline concerned with the practical derivation of rulings.

records.title: Why the distinction does not reduce kalām to fiqh
records.arabic: قلت يمكن أن يجاب بأن لا نسلّم أن الغرض فيها لا يتعلّق بالعمل، فإن المقصود كما تقدّم ...
records.arabic_anchors: «الفقه ذكرنا لا إجماع حيث يتعلق الغرض باعتقادها دون العمل بها» · «تدخل في التعريف» · «في أصول الفقه مقصودة لذاتها».
records.english: I say: one may answer that we do not concede that the aim in those matters is unrelated to action; for what is intended, as stated earlier, […]
records.proof_note: Lower-register source-facing explanation, several lines compressed in English.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: The marginal discussion distinguishes an act's being relevant to *belief about a ruling* from the act's *practical observance*. Some propositions examined in law or legal theory can enter theology under a different respect, namely when what matters is assent to a revealed judgment rather than deriving an action from it. That change of perspective does not turn kalām into jurisprudence: in legal theory, the principles are pursued for their role in establishing rulings; in kalām, a proposition can be discussed because of its relation to religious belief itself. The writer tests which disciplines would be improperly included if this regard were omitted from the definition.
records.stage88_source_note: lower register, reply to the example offered against the definition of kalām; clear clause, ending before the difficult subsequent qualification
records.stage88_proof: direct visual reading of first-print facsimile; requires second independent proof
records.stage88_copytext: Būlāq, 1318 AH, vol. I printed p.9, combined PDF physical p.22

records.title: The imitator, fallible assent and status of evidence
records.arabic: (قوله مطلق التصديق) أي الجازم ليخرج الظن
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله عن الأدلة اليقينية)» · «(قوله سواء طابق الواقع أو لا)» · «(قوله أي المكتسب)».
records.english: On “assent without qualification”: namely, firm assent, so as to exclude conjecture. […]
records.proof_note: Argument summary grounded in visible anchors; literal clause mapping incomplete.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: On the phrase “from certain proofs,” the gloss presses the distinction between possession of a true belief and possession of it **through an argument**. The imitator may assent to a true theological proposition without himself knowing the proof. If every correct conviction were counted as the science of kalām, its boundary would expand beyond the intellectual activity under definition. Conversely, treating any proof the speaker calls “certain” as genuinely demonstrative risks admitting erroneous arguments. The author of the gloss does not allow the subjective impression of certainty to settle this issue.

stage91_source_note.location: lower ruled commentary, short parenthesized lemma and explanatory phrase
stage91_source_note.scope: Only the Arabic words supplied above have been transcribed; all omitted printed text remains pending
stage91_source_note.limits: The longer note about the reality of assent and proof is not transcribed.

records.title: The intended scope of ‘acquired’
records.arabic: (قوله أي المكتسب) أشار بهذا التفسير رحمه الله إلى أن قوله عن الأدلة متعلق بالعلم باعتبار تضمنه معنى الاكتساب
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أي المكتسب)» · «الدليل متعلق بالعلم» · «باعتبار تضمّنه معنى الاكتساب لا ...» · «الإذعان في المقاصد».
records.english: Concerning his words “that is, acquired”: by this explanation—may God have mercy upon him—he indicates that “from proofs” is connected with “knowledge,” insofar as it involves the notion of acquisition.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:9; Initial ruled grammatical gloss only; remaining printed clause is open. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 22. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: On “that is, acquired”: the phrase about proofs is understood as relating to knowledge **insofar as it is acquired**, rather than as an independent condition attached indiscriminately to every belief. This is a grammatical and conceptual clarification: it explains why the definition appeals to proofs where the activity of the discipline is demonstrative, without implying that every occurrence of the same theological proposition must be acquired by a proof.

records.title: Religious convictions rather than juridical practice
records.arabic: (الدينية) المنسوبة إلى دين نبينا محمد صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم ⟦كلام مطبوع متروك هنا⟧ وسواء كانت من الدين في الواقع ككلام أهل الحق أم لا ككلام الفرق المبتدعة الضالة
records.arabic_anchors: «الاعتقاد، أيضاً المقصود من العلم به علم الفقه» · «(الدينية) المنسوبة إلى دين نبينا محمد صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم» · «سواء أكانت من الدين في الواقع ككلام أهل الحق أم لا ككلام الفرق المبتدعة».
records.english: “Religious”: ascribed to the religion of our Prophet Muḥammad—may God bless him and his family and grant him peace. [An intervening printed qualification has not been transcribed.] Whether they belong to the religion in reality, as in the discourse of those the writer calls the people of truth, or do not, as in the discourse of groups he calls errant innovators.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:9; Explicit middle omission; the attribution belongs to the historical discourse, not a modern editorial endorsement. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 22. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: What is at issue is **doctrinal assent**, not the objects of jurisprudential knowledge in their practical aspect. “Religious” means attributed to the religion of our Prophet Muḥammad—God bless him and his family and grant him peace. The designation can therefore include both propositions that truly belong to that religion, as the author understands the discourse of the orthodox, and propositions that are only **claimed** to belong to it, as in the discourse of groups he calls innovators. Such attribution does not imply that every proposition so named is correct. The author is defining the class of questions discussed in a discipline, not certifying every proposed answer.

records.title: Evidence that yields certainty
records.arabic: (عن الأدلة اليقينية) أي المكتسب
records.arabic_anchors: «فإذا كان المراد من العلم مطلق التصديق سواء طابق الواقع أو لا ...» · «(عن الأدلة اليقينية) أي المكتسب».
records.english: “From certain proofs”—that is, [knowledge] acquired [through those proofs].
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:9; The prior objection about mistaken assent and its final qualification are not fully transcribed; I:10 continues the argument. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 22. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: If “knowledge” is interpreted indiscriminately as any assent, whether or not it corresponds to reality, the definition would also include mistaken conviction. The qualification “from **certain proofs**” is introduced to delimit the intended sort of acquired cognition. But it raises a further question: does certainty here qualify the *proof objectively*, the *knower's state*, or the *evidence as deemed certain by the proponent*? The next page examines these readings rather than presuming their equivalence.

records.title: Error, opinion and objective conformity
records.arabic: إذا كان المراد من العلم هنا مطلق التصديق الشامل لإدراك المخطئ ...
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله العلم اليقيني)» · «المطابق للواقع في نفس الأمر» · «(قوله الدليل اليقيني)» · «لا يخرج إدراك المخطئ».
records.english: If what is intended by knowledge here is assent in general, including the apprehension of someone who is mistaken, […]
records.proof_note: Partial lower translation, no definitive transcription.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: On “certain knowledge,” the gloss asks whether *conformity to reality* is built into the notion of knowledge. If it is, a wrong judgment cannot become knowledge merely through its firmness. If the proof is “certain” only **in the disputant's opinion**, incorrect judgments may again enter through that concession. A likely intended response distinguishes correctness from the psychological condition of firmness; both must be checked. The marginal writer is investigating the **scope of the definition**, not asserting that all reported opinions have the same evidential standing.
records.stage88_source_note: lower register, objection regarding certainty and the mistaken thinker; clear conditional clause; question and answer continuing in the print not transcribed
records.stage88_proof: direct visual reading of first-print facsimile; requires second independent proof
records.stage88_copytext: Būlāq, 1318 AH, vol. I printed p.10, combined PDF physical p.23

records.title: The difficult case of the imitator
records.arabic: ويحتمل أن يكون جوابًا عما يقال: إذا كان المراد من العلم هنا مطلق التصديق الشامل لإدراك الخطأ، فلم أخذوا في أدلتها اليقين ولم يكتفوا بمطلق الأدلة؟
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله العقيدة بزعم المستدل)» · «المطابقة للواقع باعتقاده» · «التصديق الجازم سواء طابق الواقع أم لا» · «المقلد».
records.english: This may be a reply to the objection: if “knowledge” here means assent in general, including mistaken apprehension, why did they require certainty in its proofs instead of being content with proofs in general? […]
records.proof_note: Source-facing marginal account; lower proof remains open.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: A person who imitates a teacher can hold a firm conviction and even, by good fortune, a true one; but that alone does not mean he possesses the **science** characterised by justified inference. The gloss tests whether the exclusion is achieved by “certain” or only by specifying the act of acquisition from proofs. It also distinguishes an opinion which is merely *probable*, a categorical **error**, and a firmly held **true** assertion. None should be conflated with the activity of establishing religious doctrines through arguments.

stage89_source_note.limits: Bounded question only; surrounding explanation in this long lower note remains to be transcribed.

records.title: Does kalām concern only necessary propositions?
records.arabic: فلو اقتصروا بمطلق الأدلة لدخل فيها الظنية، مع أنها غير معتبرة في الاعتقادات، على خلاف في الظن الغالب القريب من اليقين. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «اليقين ...» · «هل المراد ... القطعية» · «علم الكلام».
records.english: Were they to stop at proofs in general, merely probable proofs would also be included, although these are not accepted in doctrinal matters—subject to a disagreement concerning preponderant supposition approaching certainty. […]
records.proof_note: Condensed lower text; final compact sentences still need separate Arabic extraction.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: The discussion notes that a proof of a theological claim must not be judged conclusive merely because its proponent feels no doubt. Nor does the word *certainty* mean that every theological issue is a self-evident proposition. It concerns the character of the assent appropriately established by the investigation. The closing observation returns to the stated limits of the discipline and supplies the join to I:11.

stage89_source_note.location: lower register, middle and final lines
stage89_source_note.limits: First visual rendering of the reasoning; the printed lower paragraph has additional objections and qualifications.

records.title: Is certainty in the proof or in the mind?
records.arabic: لأن الدليل اليقيني ما يفيد اليقين إلا أنهم قالوا المراد بالأدلة اليقينية المعتقدة بزعم المستدل
records.arabic_anchors: «ذلك العلم عن أدلتها» · «العلم اليقيني» · «لأن الدليل اليقيني ما يفيد اليقين» · «المراد بالأدلة العقدية المعتقدة بزعم المستدل».
records.english: For a certain proof is one that produces certainty. Yet they said that what is meant by “certain proofs” is proofs believed [to be certain] in the judgment of the one arguing.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:10; The upper response before and after this sentence is not fully transcribed; “believed” is not to be mistaken for objective certitude. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 23. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: The qualification directs one to knowledge **through its proofs**, and the evidence called certain is, strictly speaking, that which gives rise to certainty. Yet a different reading is also reported: the proofs intended might be those **believed to be conclusive by the person arguing**. These are not equivalent. In one reading the definition selects genuinely warranted cognition; in the other it describes the kind of claim put forward by practitioners, including those who dispute one another.

records.title: The boundaries of acquired religious knowledge
records.arabic: ثم إنهم اعتبروا في أدلتها اليقين، لا عبرة بالظن في الاعتقادات بخلاف العمليات، وخرج عن التعريف علم الله وعلم الرسول بالاعتقادات وكذا اعتقاد المقلد.
records.arabic_anchors: «ثم إنهم اعتبروا في أدلتها اليقين» · «لئلا عبرة بالظن في الاعتقادات» · «وعلم الرسول بالاعتقادات وكذا اعتقاد المقلد».
records.english: They then required certainty in its proofs: conjecture is of no account in matters of doctrine, unlike practical matters. Thus God’s knowledge, the Messenger’s knowledge of doctrines, and the imitator’s belief fall outside this definition. […]
records.proof_note: Upper text, joined I:10→11.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: Because these are questions of faith, some authors demand certainty rather than mere probability. But the commentary asks about exceptional forms of correct theological assent: God's knowledge, prophetic knowledge, and the conviction of a person who merely follows another. The function of the word “science” in the definition must be **acquired and disciplined doctrinal knowledge**, not the simple occurrence of a true judgment in any knower whatever. The argument is continued on I:11.

stage89_source_note.limits: The printed argument continues across the page edge; only this bounded section has been entered.

records.title: Whether imitation can count as justified knowledge
records.arabic: أن مسائل العلم يجب أن تكون نظرية؛ فلا معنى للمسألة إلا ما يُستدل عنه ويُطلب بالدليل، نعم قد يورد في المسائل الحكم البديهي. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وكذا اعتقاد المقلد)» · «أهل الكشف» · «المعتقد المقلد» · «الاعتقاد الجازم».
records.english: The questions belonging to a science are required to be matters of inquiry: a question, on this account, is something for which an argument is sought and whose resolution is pursued by proof. Yet a self-evident judgment can also be presented among its questions. […]
records.proof_note: Lower argument partly interpretative.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: The lower author tests the previous claim about imitation. An imitator's conviction may be firmly held and correspond to reality, yet lack the evidence appropriate to a demonstrative science. In contrast, the settled cognition of a competent investigator may be acquired through the orderly pursuit of proof. The gloss distinguishes the issue **whether a belief is true** from the issue **whether its possessor can establish it**. That distinction bears directly on the definition of kalām by proofs.

stage89_source_note.limits: Bounded excerpt, with a possible lexical doubt around the connective preceding this clause; not a complete lower register.

records.title: Is ‘the known’ too broad a subject?
records.arabic: اتفقت كلمة القوم على أن تغاير العلوم ... إنما هو بحسب تغاير الموضوعات، فناسب تصدير العلم ببيان الموضوع ...
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله موضوعه)» · «لفظ المعلوم» · «الموضوع عام» · «العقائد الدينية».
records.english: The scholars agree that the differentiation of the sciences […] is according to the differentiation of their subjects; hence it is fitting to open the science with an account of its subject. […]
records.proof_note: Marginal source-facing reading; line-by-line correspondence pending.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: The subject term “the known” appears excessively broad, since it can include both what exists and what does not, and things studied by many other sciences. The commentator therefore insists on the delimiting **relation to religious doctrines**. Another question arises: does the word “known” refer to the *subject term* in every theorem, to all entities in the field, or to whatever is considered for the sake of proving theological conclusions? An adequate definition must not switch silently between these senses.
records.stage88_source_note: lower register, opening discussion on the subject of the science; clear main relation, but intervening print words deliberately marked by omission
records.stage88_proof: direct visual reading of first-print facsimile; requires second independent proof
records.stage88_copytext: Būlāq, 1318 AH, vol. I printed p.11, combined PDF physical p.24

records.title: Propositions versus constituent terms
records.arabic: أعني التصديق بوجود الموضوع في نفسه، وهو الذي عدوه جزءًا من المعلوم
records.arabic_anchors: «التصديق بوجود الموضوع» · «جزء من المعلوم» · «المبادئ التصورية» · «المبادئ التصديقية».
records.english: I mean assent to the existence of the subject in itself; this is what they counted as part of the object of knowledge. […]
records.proof_note: Provisional lower explanation, ending connects to I:12.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: The margin elaborates the relation between knowing the *terms* of a proposition and assenting to the *proposition itself*. Demonstration presupposes conceptions of its terms, while the truth of a conclusion involves judgment. On that basis, subjects, predicates and first principles may all enter a discipline without each separately being the final object of its assent. This is relevant to whether the subject of kalām should be stated in terms of “the known” or in terms of the propositions it establishes.

stage91_source_note.location: lower register, discussion of the subject of science, middle lines
stage91_source_note.scope: Only the Arabic words supplied above have been transcribed; all omitted printed text remains pending
stage91_source_note.limits: The passage before and after the quoted clause still requires transcription.

records.title: The Companions and the historical term ‘kalām’
records.arabic: علم الصحابة وإن لم يسم في ذلك الزمان بالكلام كما أن علمهم بالعمليات فقه وإن لم يسم به
records.arabic_anchors: «علم الصحابة» · «وإن لم يسمَّ في ذلك الزمان بالكلام» · «كما أن علمهم بالحساب ... لم يسمَّ به».
records.english: [The doctrinal] knowledge of the Companions [was present] even if it was not called kalām in that age, just as their knowledge of practical matters was jurisprudence even if it was not called by that name.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:11; A sentence continuing from I:10; initial words depend on the preceding page. Note بالعمليات, not بالعقائد, in the second comparison. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 24. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: The knowledge possessed by the Prophet's Companions was not called “kalām” at the time, just as their knowledge of other matters was not necessarily named after the later disciplines in which those matters were organised. The historical **name** of a discipline does not determine whether earlier persons possessed the relevant knowledge. One must distinguish the activity or insight from the subsequent technical label applied to it.

records.title: Subject of the science
records.arabic: (وموضوعه المعلوم من حيث يتعلق بذلك)
records.arabic_anchors: «(وموضوعه المعلوم من حيث يتعلق بذلك)».
records.english: “Its subject is the knowable insofar as it bears upon that [doctrinal concern].”
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:11; Only the short parenthesized lemma is entered; the following explanation continues on I:12. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 24. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: “Its subject is **the known**, insofar as it is connected with that”—that is, with the establishment of religious doctrines. The restriction “insofar as” is doing essential work: kalām is not simply an inventory of all knowable things, but a study of things under the regard in which they enter demonstrations concerning belief.

records.title: The author's use of ‘connection’
records.arabic: (قوله أي بالعقائد الدينية الخ) أي الأحكام والنسب التي ذكرناها
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أي بالعقائد الدينية الخ)» · «الأحكام والنسب» · «لا يتم بيان الموضوع بدون غير الموضوع».
records.english: On “that is, religious doctrines, etc.”: namely, the judgments and relations we have mentioned. […]
records.proof_note: Connected lower source interpretation; incomplete literal transcript.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: The lower commentary objects that the phrase “insofar as it is connected with religious doctrines” requires explanation. The proof of a theological assertion may use not only doctrines but **relations, negations, and judgments** concerning items considered in other disciplines. Some things are not taken up because of their intrinsic nature, but because denying or affirming them makes a difference to an eventual conclusion. The author tests whether that consideration is sufficient to distinguish kalām from other sciences, or merely imports their questions wholesale.

stage91_source_note.scope: Only the Arabic words supplied above have been transcribed; all omitted printed text remains pending
stage91_source_note.limits: The remainder of the lower argument about subject and predicate remains omitted.

records.title: Predicates and the relation of the ‘known’
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله المتناول للموجود والمعدوم)» · «المعلوم» · «الموضوع» · «المحمول».
records.english: The breadth of the known object matters especially when a question concerns a thing **that cannot exist**. The impossible is still an object of conceptual judgment: one can affirm its impossibility without giving it external existence. The gloss turns from this to a logical objection. If the theological matter is **predicated** of a subject rather than itself functioning as the subject term, can the definition still say “the known” is the science's subject? The discussion prepares the solution on I:13, where the predicates of theological problems are explicitly mentioned.
records.proof_note: Source-facing partial translation of the long lower continuation; the opening should be checked together with I:11.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified

records.title: Does a subject have to be demonstrable in every proposition?
records.arabic: ثم موضوع العلم مرجع إليه مسائله، فيكون جهة وحدتها، إذ فيه اشتراكها وبه اتحادها. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لا تبحث الخ)» · «بموضوعية الموضوع» · «اه منه».
records.english: The subject of a science is that to which its questions refer. It therefore constitutes their unifying aspect: they share in it and are united through it. […]
records.proof_note: Middle ruled note, partial reading. A compact clause requires another image check.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: The marginal note tests the claim that inquiry must always be about the subject *as such*. It is enough in some cases to understand how the subject or a property of the subject figures in a chain of demonstration. The distinction is again a matter of how propositions are organised within the science, not a proof that the things considered are all actual existents.

stage92_source_note.witness: Būlāq 1318 AH printed Volume I (single printed copy, no manuscript collation)
stage92_source_note.scope: selected contiguous source phrases, omissions explicitly signaled
stage92_source_note.limitations: A single sustained sentence from the middle ruled note; the lemma and surrounding argument are not yet fully transcribed.

records.title: The range of auxiliary questions
records.arabic: أي بالعقائد الدينية لأنه يبحث فيه عن أحوال الصانع من القدم والوحدة وغيرهما وعن أحوال الجسم والعرض والحدوث والتركيب من الجواهر الفردة وقبول الفناء وغير ذلك
records.arabic_anchors: «أي بالعقائد الدينية» · «أحوال المانع من القدم والوحدة» · «أحوال الجسم والعرض والحدوث والتركيب» · «أحوال المحال والمعدومات».
records.english: That is, in relation to religious doctrines; for it investigates the states or attributes of the Maker, including beginninglessness and oneness, and also questions of body and accident, origination, composition from indivisible particles, susceptibility to annihilation, and other matters.
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:12; Selected contiguous opening of I:12; remainder of examples and terminological question still require complete transcription. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 25. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: The connection intended is to **religious doctrines**. The scope of inquiry therefore includes characteristics that exclude a body's beginninglessness or absolute unity, the properties of body and accident, origination and composition, and questions about substantiality, individuation and other categories. It also extends to **impossibilities** and **nonexistents**, so far as propositions about them are needed to establish the desired doctrines. The scope is not limited to propositions that themselves state an article of faith; the inquiry can examine premises and distinctions used to demonstrate such propositions.

records.title: A common subject broad enough for nonexistents
records.arabic: فالمراد بموضوعات هذه المسائل هو المعلوم المتناول للوجود والعدم وقد يقال المعلوم
records.arabic_anchors: «فالمعلوم المتناول للموجود والمعدوم» · «وقد قيل المعلوم».
records.english: Thus what is intended as the subject of these investigations is the knowable, comprising existence and nonexistence. One may also say: the knowable ... [the following qualification has not been entered].
records.proof_note: Stage 84 visually reread from printed page I:12; Opening phrase of the second upper argument only; must be joined to complete explanation of the science’s subject and include its ruled/lower glosses. Untranscribed parts remain visible in facsimile. No independent secondary proof.
records.provenance: Stage 84 direct reread of Būlāq 1318 AH printed source image, source physical PDF page 25. Previous Stage 83 overview retained separately as historical commentary.
records.stage83_historical_english_overview: Consequently the “known” can be taken broadly enough to embrace **existent and nonexistent** alike. This is why the discipline's subject cannot simply be “body,” “existent substance,” or another restricted ontological genus. Whatever is needed as a subject of intellectual judgment under the specified theological relation can enter consideration.

records.title: Is the 'known' an adequate general subject?
records.arabic: من الذهني وغيره يساوي الموجود المعدوم في العموم
records.arabic_anchors: «من الذهني وغيره يساوي الموجود المعدوم في العموم» · «إنما يحتاج إليه عند من يجعل مباحث المعدوم والمحال من مسائل علم الكلام» · «أن المراد بالعقائد الدينية المحمولات».
records.english: [The knowable], whether mental or otherwise, is as general as the existent and the nonexistent.
records.proof_note: Lower-gloss source-facing exposition, not a complete literal rendering of every line.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: The marginal writer begins by challenging how the ‘known’ is supposed to extend to what exists only in thought as well as to what exists outside thought. Making the known object of inquiry fully coextensive with existence and nonexistence may be broader than the argument warrants. The issue becomes pressing especially if one counts discussion of the nonexistent and the impossible among the questions of kalām. The writer therefore asks whether the alleged subject is being construed as the *subject term* of the propositions, their *predicates*, or the whole range of things to which theological demonstration must refer. He reports the suggestion that ‘religious doctrines’ denotes the predicates, but cautions that this may not settle the problem by itself.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «من الذهني وغيره يساوي الموجود المعدوم في العموم» · «إنما يحتاج إليه عند من يجعل مباحث المعدوم والمحال من مسائل علم الكلام» · «أن المراد بالعقائد الدينية المحمولات».
records.stage85_source_caution: Excerpt starts mid-sentence; this is not the entire lower note.

records.title: Indirect propositions and intermediate bases
records.arabic: أقول: المعلوم من حيثية التعلّق بالمحمول كما يتناول الموضوع يتناول الحكم أيضًا، فلِمَ قصر هذا الإخراج على الموضوع؟ […]
records.arabic_anchors: «من حيثية التعلق بالمحمول كما يتناول الموضوع» · «ليس هذا الإخراج من ورطة» · «قال المصنف» · «ليس تصوراً لموضوعه».
records.english: I say: the knowable, considered with respect to its relation to the predicate, embraces the judgment just as it embraces the subject. Why, then, confine this exclusion to the subject? […]
records.proof_note: Connected argumentative paraphrase; several compact expressions at the top of the lower stream remain uncertain.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: The text develops a difficulty in restricting the discipline to its directly professed conclusions. It is not enough simply to say that what enters a proof as a premise is itself a credal conclusion: a science often studies conditions of its own arguments without taking each such condition as its final object. A predicate may be introduced under the respect in which it relates to an ultimate doctrinal result, just as a subject can be. The commentator uses this to question whether the proposed escape from the difficulty is genuine, rather than a shift between two ways of describing the same material.

stage89_source_note.limits: The last interrogative is a bounded contextual rendering; all following argumentation remains unchecked.

records.title: ‘Ultimate’ and ‘proximate’ ends of the discipline
records.arabic: وذكروا أن الفائدة والغاية والمنفعة أمور لا تختلف إلا بالحيثية والاعتبار. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله الفوز بسعادة الدارين)» · «ذكروا أن الفائدة والغاية والمنفعة أمور لا تختلف إلا بالحيثية والاعتبار» · «بالأحكام الشرعية اعتقاداً حقاً» · «لا يؤدي إلى الفساد في الآخرة».
records.english: They have stated that benefit, end, and advantage are things that differ only according to aspect and consideration. […]
records.proof_note: Lower text partly normalized in English; the precise wording of the final lines joins I:14.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: On “attaining felicity in the two abodes”: benefit, end, and utility are not always three distinct realities; they may describe one result under different **considerations**. The nearer end of kalām is to establish firmly and correctly the doctrines that belong to religion, removing uncertainty and error. Its more remote end is a right faith that prevents misdirection in this life and leads toward deliverance in the next. The marginal writer objects to confusing this final good with the particular cognitive act that defines the science; something may be sought through the science without thereby becoming the science's own formal subject.

stage89_source_note.limits: Clear source clause; this is not a translation of the full surrounding discussion of ends.

records.title: Sufficiency of the subject-based distinction
records.arabic: مع أن المقصود من ذلك تمييز العلم من سائر العلوم باعتبار الموضوع
records.arabic_anchors: «المعلوم المذكور لا يعتبر من المحمول» · «المقصود من ذلك تمييز العلم من سائر العلوم باعتبار الموضوع» · «والبيان المذكور كاف فيه» · «اه منه».
records.english: Moreover, what is intended is to distinguish this science from the other sciences by reference to its subject. […]
records.proof_note: Separately ruled text; source-located reading.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: The ‘known’ that was mentioned is not itself treated here as one of the predicates. The purpose is to distinguish this science from other sciences **by reference to its subject**, and the explanation given is sufficient for that. Allowing the discussion also to range over predicates does not destroy the proposed distinction. [The closing «منه» denotes a source or speaker, but does not independently identify a named glossator.]

stage91_source_note.location: middle ruled stream, last portion of brief notice
stage91_source_note.scope: Only the Arabic words supplied above have been transcribed; all omitted printed text remains pending
stage91_source_note.limits: The incoming and concluding sentences of the ruled passage require checking.

records.title: Predicates of theological questions
records.arabic: ويمكن أن يقال المراد بالعقائد الدينية المحمولات المنسوبة إليها
records.arabic_anchors: «من الحيثية المذكورة يتناول محمولات مسائله» · «العقائد الدينية» · «المحمولات ...» · «فلا إشكال».
records.english: It may be said that what is meant by religious doctrines is the predicates attributed to them.
records.proof_note: Source-facing, interpretative at one indistinct phrase; no independent second proof.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: Under the respect already specified, the expression also embraces the **predicates** in the propositions that constitute its questions. One may therefore say that the religious doctrines intended here are the things predicated within the discipline, and what serves as the means of reaching those doctrines. On that understanding, the objection—that not every matter investigated is itself one of the credal conclusions—does not arise. [The precise intervening formulation after *al-maḥmūlāt* is difficult in this impression; the paraphrase is explicitly provisional.]
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «من الحيثية المذكورة يتناول محمولات مسائله» · «العقائد الدينية» · «المحمولات ...» · «فلا إشكال».
records.stage85_source_caution: The sentence has material on either side; no claim of exhaustive transcription.

records.title: Benefit and ultimate end
records.arabic: وكأن المصنف رأى أنه من العلوم التي غايتها أنفسها فاكتفى ببيان حده
records.arabic_anchors: «وفائدته أمور وغاية الكل الفوز بسعادة الدارين» · «وكان المصنف يرى أنه من العلوم التي غايتها أنفسها فاكتفى ببيان ...».
records.english: It seems that the author regarded this as one of the sciences whose ends reside in themselves, and so contented himself with stating its definition.
records.proof_note: Connected upper-text reading; final word of the last clause requires a high-resolution recheck.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: The discipline has several benefits, while their ultimate end is **attaining felicity in the two abodes**. The commentator suggests that the author regarded this as one of the sciences whose immediate aim is, in one respect, its own knowledge. That helps explain why he was satisfied with specifying the discipline itself rather than treating every benefit or remoter aim as its defining subject.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «وفائدته أمور وغاية الكل الفوز بسعادة الدارين» · «وكان المصنف يرى أنه من العلوم التي غايتها أنفسها فاكتفى ببيان ...».
records.stage85_source_caution: The opening of the sentence and intervening argument are not completely transcribed.

records.title: The two possible senses of an end
records.arabic: العلم غاية لنفسه بمعنى أنه مقصود في ذاته وليس آلة لعلم آخر […] الإتيان بفاء التفريع صريح في أن المراد بما ذكر هو الأمور التي غايتها الفوز لا الفوز نفسه.
records.arabic_anchors: «العلم غاية لنفسه» · «لا تكون غاية الغاية» · «أن الأمور التي غايتها الفوز لا الفوز نفسه».
records.english: Knowledge is an end in itself: it is sought for its own sake, and is not an instrument for some other discipline. […] The use of the consequential particle *fāʾ* makes clear that the earlier expression concerns matters whose end is attaining success, not success itself.
records.proof_note: Lower-register source-based reading, selected clauses; not all words diplomatically transcribed.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: The marginal writer asks what the earlier reference to the end intends. If knowing itself is the immediate aim, a further end such as felicity can only be called the ‘end of the end’ under a particular ordering of aims. Not every benefit produced by a discipline is part of its essence or immediate purpose. The criticism is directed against sliding between the **knowledge sought**, the **good achieved through possessing it**, and the **farther religious outcome** of such possession.

stage90_source_note.scope: First three lines of the lower stream; two source stretches with an intervening omission. The term الفوز requires surrounding context before fixing its referent.

records.title: Does knowledge of one's existence require prior knowledge of knowledge?
records.arabic: أوردهما المصنف في شرح المقاصد لإثبات كون العلم واضحًا ضروريًّا عنده، حيث قال: ذهب الإمام إلى أن تصور العلم بديهي لوجهين […]
records.arabic_anchors: «تصور العلم بديهي» · «لوجهين الأول أنه معلوم» · «اكتساب الماهوية» · «فحكم الوجدان» · «إما ضرورة ... أو اكتساب».
records.english: The author included both arguments in *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid* to establish that, in his view, knowledge is evident and necessary. He says: “The Imām held that the conception of knowledge is self-evident for two reasons.” […]
records.proof_note: Partly interpretative lower reading; this distinction is explicit in the print, but the full argument is lengthy.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: The margin distinguishes knowing that one exists from possessing a definition of what ‘knowledge’ means. One may immediately have a cognition without being able to analyse its nature. The fact that something is given in awareness is not in itself a proof that its **quiddity**, as an object of reflective analysis, is also immediately apprehended. If one says that the conception of knowledge is acquired, a question remains: what knowledge must be present for the acquisition to take place? The argument is delicate because it can use *knowledge* for the act of apprehension in one premise and for the concept being studied in another.

stage90_source_note.scope: Middle lower stream; the two proofs and subsequent counter-arguments are not transcribed here.

records.title: Circularity, ‘beginning’ and the limits of the proof
records.arabic: والثاني علم كل أحد بوجوده ضروري، أي حاصل بلا نظر، وهذا علم خاص مسبوق بمطلق العلم لتركيبه منه ومن الخصوصية. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «يلزم الدور» · «بداهته مستلزمة لعدم تجدد» · «مستلزم للمطلوب المذكور» · «معلوم لا بالضرورة بل بالاكتساب».
records.english: Second: each person’s knowledge that he exists is necessary—that is, attained without reflection. This is a particular act of knowledge, which presupposes knowledge in general, because it comprises that general notion and a particular qualification. […]
records.proof_note: Close source-guided synthesis. The sentence continues onto I:15.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: The critic tests the regress argument by distinguishing an unqualified prior act of knowing from a reflexive act in which knowledge becomes its own object. If every act of knowing presupposed a previously **defined** notion of knowledge, a circle would indeed appear; but if an initial act can occur without reflective grasp of its nature, the inference requires another premise. Conversely, declaring that all cognition must be obtained through acquisition raises the question of its beginning. The marginal discussion does not treat these alternatives as automatically equivalent.

stage90_source_note.scope: Lower final portion; the ensuing objection and response are not yet translated.

records.title: A further end and the inadequacy of a strict definition
records.arabic: والعلم لا يحد لوضوحه واختاره الإمام الرازي لوجهين: الأول أن علم كل أحد بأنه موجود ضروري
records.arabic_anchors: «فيكون هذا كذا غاية الغاية» · «والعلم لا حدّ له بوجهه» · «واختاره الإمام الرازي لوجهين».
records.english: Knowledge is not strictly defined because of its evidentness. Imām al-Rāzī chose this view for two reasons. First, every person’s knowledge that he exists is immediate.
records.proof_note: Upper text, first-pass connected translation.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: In that case, this is the **end of the end**: a remoter result beyond the more immediate purpose of the science. The discussion then turns to *knowledge*. One position holds that it cannot be defined by a strict essential definition and instead must be made known in another way. The commentator reports that Imām Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī preferred this view and adduces two arguments for it.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «فيكون هذا كذا غاية الغاية» · «والعلم لا حدّ له بوجهه» · «واختاره الإمام الرازي لوجهين».
records.stage85_source_caution: Selected first reason; remainder and ensuing dispute omitted.

records.title: Two arguments for immediacy
records.arabic: والثاني أن غير العلم يعلم بالعلم فلو لم يعلم العلم لزم الدور
records.arabic_anchors: «الأول أن علم كل أحد بأنه موجود ضروري» · «وهذا أعم خاص والمطلق جزء منه» · «والثاني أن غير العلم يعلم بالعلم فلو علم العلم بغير العلم لزم الدور».
records.english: Second, things other than knowledge are known by means of knowledge. If knowledge itself were not known, a circle would result.
records.proof_note: Upper text close reading. The inferential move from particular to general is an **argument being reported**, not endorsed by the editor.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: First, everyone’s knowledge that **he himself exists** is necessary or immediate; this is a determinate case of knowing, and knowledge considered without that determination is more general. It is argued that, if the particular is immediate, then the more general conception should be no less so. Second, other things are known **by means of knowledge**; if knowledge itself could be known only by way of a further act of knowledge, a vicious circle or regress appears to threaten. The text specifies that the second objection bears against one who says that knowledge is known but **not** necessarily or immediately.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «الأول أن علم كل أحد بأنه موجود ضروري» · «وهذا أعم خاص والمطلق جزء منه» · «والثاني أن غير العلم يعلم بالعلم فلو علم العلم بغير العلم لزم الدور».
records.stage85_source_caution: The printed qualifying reply is still outstanding.

records.title: Knowledge as an actuality of the knower
records.arabic: فإن قيل: لا يتعيّن لحصول العلم إلا وصول النفس إلى المعنى وحصوله فيها، والعلم لما كان من المعاني النفسانية يكون حصوله في النفس تصوّرًا وإحاطة. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «حصول العلم» · «الضروري ... حصول علم جزئي بوجوده وهو غير تصوره» · «لم يصح وجهها إلا على عدم التحديد فقط».
records.english: If it is said: for knowledge to occur, nothing more is required than the soul’s attaining the meaning and that meaning’s presence within it; and since knowledge belongs among psychic meanings, its presence in the soul would be a conception and an encompassing apprehension. […]
records.proof_note: Source-facing lower reading, not a literal complete mapping.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: The marginal commentator explains that the occurrence of a particular knowledge is not the same as an explicit, reflexive conception of the nature of knowledge. A person can be aware of his existence without arranging a definition of cognition. If one uses such awareness to argue that knowledge resists **essential definition**, that is a more modest conclusion than showing that no explanatory account of knowledge can be given. The second proposition needs a separate proof.

stage89_source_note.limits: Source-based bounded argument; the subsequent objection and answer remain outside this span.

records.title: Whether self-consciousness is unavoidable
records.arabic: فإذا كان حصول العلم ووجوده بديهيًّا كان تصوره بديهيًّا وهو المطلوب. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «أن حصول العلم العلم لا يعني حصول النفس إلى الذي وحصوله فيها» · «يكون حصوله في النفس تصوراً وحكاية» · «بالدليل الثاني».
records.english: If the occurrence and existence of knowledge are self-evident, then its conception would likewise be self-evident—and that is precisely what was to be established. […]
records.proof_note: Several tightly printed clauses are insecure, especially the lead-in to I:16; the Arabic anchor is deliberately fragmentary.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: The margin considers whether every occurrence of a cognitive state includes awareness of that occurrence. It distinguishes the presence of the knowing **act** in the soul from a subsequent representation or conception **of that act**. If the two are identified, the claim that self-awareness is necessary may appear plausible; if distinguished, the claim needs qualification. The discussion leads to the second proposed route for making knowledge understood, namely division and example rather than a strict definition.

stage90_source_note.scope: Middle lower portion; this is the conclusion of an objection, not an endorsement by the editor. The response remains untranslated.

records.title: Conception of the acquired cognition
records.arabic: هذا إن كان تصوره لازم حصوله كما في سائر الوجدانيات
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وهو غير تصوره)» · «لكن تصوره لازم لحصوله كما في سائر الوجدانيات» · «اه منه».
records.english: That is so only if conceiving it necessarily accompanies its occurrence, as with other immediate experiences.
records.proof_note: Short separately ruled note, provisional source reading.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: On “and it is not its conception”: nevertheless, one might contend that some conception is required for its occurrence, as with other objects of inner experience. Thus the distinction, while real, does not by itself establish that the cognition can occur without any accompanying apprehension of what is taking place. [Closing annotation has no positively established personal author.]
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(قوله وهو غير تصوره)» · «لكن تصوره لازم لحصوله كما في سائر الوجدانيات» · «اه منه».
records.stage85_source_caution: Very short bounded ruled gloss; remainder not read as a continuous span.

records.title: Resolving the first argument's equivocation
records.arabic: وغير العلم إنما يعلم بحصول علم جزئي لا بتصور العلم على تقدير اكتسابه
records.arabic_anchors: «على عدم التفرقة بين تصور العلم وحصوله» · «والضروري حصول علم جزئي بوجوده» · «وهو غير تصوره وغير العلم».
records.english: Things other than knowledge are known through the occurrence of a particular act of knowing, not by forming a conception of knowledge, even if such a conception has to be acquired.
records.proof_note: Upper text connected translation, with opening join from I:14.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: The objection rests on a **failure to distinguish between conceiving knowledge and its occurrence**. What is necessary here is the occurrence of a particular cognition of one’s own existence. That cognition's occurrence is not the same as the conception of the cognition, still less a universal definition of knowledge. Hence the first argument cannot simply carry the immediacy of one cognitive event over to the concept of knowledge as such.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «على عدم التفرقة بين تصور العلم وحصوله» · «والضروري حصول علم جزئي بوجوده» · «وهو غير تصوره وغير العلم».
records.stage85_source_caution: Part of the reply to the second reason on previous leaf.

records.title: The objection from acquired conceptions
records.arabic_anchors: «أما ... حصول علم جزئي ... يتوقف تصوره على تصوره» · «وقيل لا يجدي ...» · «وإليه ذهب الغزالي».
records.english: If the concept of knowledge is acquired, it is argued that some prior grasp of what one is acquiring may be required. Yet that cannot be established merely from the fact that a particular act of knowing has occurred. The discussion reports a further objection to the proposed distinction and associates a position in this dispute with al-Ghazālī. The crucial point is whether what requires a prior conception is **the acquired representation of knowledge**, or every instance of knowledge occurring in a knower.
records.proof_note: Upper passage partly compressed; attribution and precise final words should be rechecked before citation.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified

records.title: Is the knowledge of a division itself known through knowledge?
records.arabic: وحصول العلم به يستلزم إمكان العلم بأنه عالم بذلك العلم، وعلى تقدير وقوع ذلك الإمكان يلزم حصول العلم بالعلم الخاص قبل حصول العلم بمطلق العلم، وهو محال. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «وحصول العلم به يستلزم إمكان العلم بأنه عالم» · «فيلزم حصول العلم بالعلم الخاص قبل حصول العلم بمطلق العلم» · «مفهوماً مطلق العلم».
records.english: Having knowledge of it entails the possibility of knowing that one knows by means of that knowledge. If that possibility is realized, knowledge of the particular act of knowing would have to occur before knowledge of knowing in general—and that is impossible. […]
records.proof_note: Connected reading of a major lower-register objection; unverified compressed subclauses remain.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: The lower commentator contests the logic of the proposed division. Knowing by an act may permit one to know that one is a knower, but this does not mean the **unrestricted concept of knowledge** must have been defined before the particular act occurred. Conversely, if the mind has to grasp the general category before any example becomes intelligible, the explanatory procedure may tacitly presuppose what it was intended to provide. The point hinges on keeping distinct a concrete cognitive act, reflective awareness of that act, and the general concept of knowledge.

stage89_source_note.limits: Bounded statement of the regress objection; the subsequent reply and its distinctions remain to be translated.

records.title: The particular and the general
records.arabic_anchors: «حصول العلم بالعلم الخاص» · «حصول العلم بالعلم الغير» · «مطلق العلم» · «ليس فقط».
records.english: The marginal reasoning also asks how an item can be recognised as a **particular kind of knowledge** without prior conception of the general description. The author considers the contrary order as well: one might have a specific cognition and acquire a generic concept through subsequent comparison or reflection. That opposition is not resolved by simply calling either a particular or a general concept ‘necessary’; the alleged priority must itself be clarified.
records.proof_note: Source-facing exposition, not all lower lines supplied in literal English; the final marginal clause continues to I:17.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified

records.title: Why an example is not a definition
records.arabic: (قوله وأما المثال) المثال يطلق على المشابه وعلى الجزئي، فالأول للأول والثاني للثاني. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وأما المثال)» · «يطلق على المشابه وعلى الجزئي» · «فالأول ... والثاني ...».
records.english: On “as for the example”: the word “example” is used both for what resembles [something] and for a particular instance. The first [kind of example] pertains to the former, the second to the latter. [A short interposed gloss, with its own ending “from him.”]
records.proof_note: Short ruled note, first visual reading; precise ending requires recheck.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage87_previous_english: On “as for the example”: *mithāl* can refer to something **similar** or to a **particular instance**. The text assigns the two examples their different roles accordingly. An illustrative instance can make a state recognisable without supplying the essential features demanded of a strict definition.
records.stage87_source_note: Direct reading of the short middle-ruled entry on I:16, separate from both the upper discourse and the lower commentary.
records.stage87_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, Vol. I printed p.16, original combined PDF physical p.29

records.title: Four divisions of assent
records.arabic: بالدليل الثاني، وطريق معرفته عنده القسمة والمثال، أما القسمة فنقول: الاعتقاد إما جازم أو غير جازم، والجازم إما مطابق للواقع أو غير مطابق، والمطابق إما ثابت أو غير ثابت.
records.arabic_anchors: «بالدليل الثاني وطريق معرفته عنده القسمة والمثال» · «الاعتقاد إما جازم أو غير جازم» · «والجازم إما مطابق للواقع أو غير مطابق» · «والمطابق إما ثابت أو غير ثابت».
records.english: [Continuing from] the second proof: according to him, the way of making knowledge known is division and example. As for division, we say: assent is either firm or not firm; firm assent either accords with reality or does not; and what accords with reality is either stable or unstable. [The reason this classifies rather than strictly defines knowledge is discussed further on the printed page.]
records.proof_note: Upper source text; each ternary split visually checked.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage87_previous_english: The second route consists in making knowledge known through **division and example**. Under division: an assent is either firm or not firm; a firm assent is either in accordance with reality or not; and an assent in accordance with reality is either stable or unstable. In this way, one distinguishes certain knowledge from mere non-firm opinion, firm error, and even a correct belief that is not settled or secure. The divisions are supplied **to identify** knowledge, not as a strict definition giving its genus and essential differentia.
records.stage87_source_note: Continuous first four upper lines on p.I:16 (physical PDF 29). The initial words continue an argument begun on I:15.
records.stage87_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, Vol. I printed p.16, original combined PDF physical p.29

records.title: Example and the limits of an essential definition
records.arabic: وأما المثال فكأن يقال: العلم إدراك البصيرة الشبيه بإدراك الباصرة، أو يقال هو كاعتقادنا أن الواحد نصف الاثنين.
records.arabic_anchors: «وأما المثال فكأن يقال العلم إدراك البصيرة» · «كاعتقادنا أن الواحد نصف الاثنين» · «لا يحدّ بعبارة جامعة للجنس والفصل الذاتي» · «والإحساس به معروف».
records.english: As for illustration, one might say: knowledge is the perception of inner sight, resembling perception by the seeing eye; or that it is like our belief that one is half of two. [The following argument concerning genus and essential differentia has not yet been transcribed in this record.]
records.proof_note: Upper source-facing reading; punctuation and the exact phrase concerning insight need verification against a second impression.
records.provenance: source reread + inherited previous English + explanatory restatement; not certified
records.stage85_prior_overview: Under example, one might speak of knowledge as the insight of the inner faculty, or point to our certain conviction that **one is half of two**. The intention of the thinker cited is not that the word can never be explained, but that a definition collecting an essential genus and difference is difficult or impossible in the present case. Many things are recognised perfectly well through experience or example without an analysis that displays their ultimate essence. The example helps a reader identify the intended state even where a genus-and-difference definition cannot be supplied.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «وأما المثال فكأن يقال العلم إدراك البصيرة» · «كاعتقادنا أن الواحد نصف الاثنين» · «لا يحدّ بعبارة جامعة للجنس والفصل الذاتي» · «والإحساس به معروف».
records.stage85_source_caution: This is an illustrative verbal approach, not an essential definition; subsequent comparisons are not exhaustively transcribed.
records.stage87_previous_arabic: وأما المثال فكأن يقال العلم إدراك البصيرة
records.stage87_previous_english: As for explanation by example, one might say that knowledge is the apprehension of the inner faculty of insight.
records.stage87_source_note: Continuous example from the third and fourth upper lines, I:16.
records.stage87_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, Vol. I printed p.16, original combined PDF physical p.29

records.title: What is excluded by “complete disclosure”?
records.arabic_anchors: «المعلوم»؛ «صفة العلم»؛ «التصور المطابق والتصديق اليقيني»؛ «ليس الفصل ...»؛ «الظن».
records.english: The lower commentary tests the verbal definition of knowledge. If complete disclosure is taken to mean a **conception that correctly represents its object**, then a different condition must distinguish that from **certain assent** to a proposition. Otherwise a definition that works for knowledge by assent may be wrongly extended to every form of conception. Conversely, excluding opinion and uncertain supposition should not be construed as excluding every legitimate apprehension that is not accompanied by a proposition of assent. The author of the gloss cautions that defining a notion by its contrast with error can be useful in disputation but does not automatically explain the **nature of the cognitive act**. This portion is a source-facing English reading, not a word-for-word verified rendering of each compressed marginal line.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Why the inquiry analogy matters
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وحقيقة النظر)»؛ «التصور والتصديق»؛ «لا تنحصر ...»؛ «الاستحضار»؛ «الانتقال».
records.english: What matters in the definition of inquiry is that an investigator already possesses some terms, propositions, or general descriptions yet lacks the desired conclusion. Intellectual reflection arranges those items so that what was previously absent as a determinate cognition becomes present. “Movement” is not predicated equally of every case of perception, sensation, recall, or attention: it marks the **ordered search and transition** by which the intellect reaches a conclusion. The marginal writer asks whether this is truly a definition of every inquiry or a description of the **usual process**. The detailed dispute continues on I:18.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: The meaning of the movement of the soul
records.arabic: (قوله حركة النفس) إطلاق الحركة على الانتقالات الواقعة للنفس من معقول إلى آخر دفعة إنما هو على سبيل التشبيه لعدم وجود المسافة اللازمة في الحركة. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله حركة النفس) إطلاقاً للحركة على الانتقالات الواقعة للنفس من معقول إلى آخر»؛ «على سبيل التشبيه».
records.english: On “the movement of the soul”: calling the soul’s transitions from one intelligible object to another “movement” is only by way of likeness, because the distance required for [literal spatial] movement does not exist here. [End of the short ruled annotation.]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage87_previous_english: On “movement of the soul”: motion is used **by analogy** for the transitions occurring in the mind from one intelligible object to another. The usual term for spatial movement is here applied to the intellect's passage through the stages of reasoning. The absence of physical distance does not eliminate the ordered differences between the starting question, premises, arrangement, and conclusion.
records.stage87_source_note: Directly read two-line ruled annotation in I:17; it concerns metaphorical intellectual motion, not physical locomotion.
records.stage87_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, Vol. I printed p.17, original combined PDF physical p.30

records.title: Knowledge, disclosure, and recognition
records.arabic: وإنما فسرنا التجلي بالانكشاف التام الذي لا يشمل الظن لأن العلم عند القائلين بهذا التعريف مقابل الظن
records.arabic_anchors: «أو صفة يتجلى بها»؛ «أي ينكشف انكشافاً تاماً بذلك الصفة»؛ «(المذكور) كما من شأنه أن ينذكر ويلتفت إليه»؛ «إخراج الظن».
records.english: We explained “disclosure” as complete unveiling, which does not include conjectural belief, because those who give this definition contrast knowledge with conjecture.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: Another formula describes knowledge as “an attribute by which [the object] becomes disclosed”: through the attribute, the knowable is disclosed to the knower **completely**, so that the uncertain assent belonging to **opinion** (*ẓann*) is excluded. The thing known is called the “mentioned” or “recalled” object insofar as it can be brought into attention. These formulations are meant to mark the scope of the technical word *knowledge*, not to settle through a verbal substitution every philosophical dispute about what knowledge is. An imperfect apprehension, a complete assent, and a nonassertoric conception must remain distinguishable.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «أو صفة يتجلى بها»؛ «أي ينكشف انكشافاً تاماً بذلك الصفة»؛ «(المذكور) كما من شأنه أن ينذكر ويلتفت إليه»؛ «إخراج الظن».
records.stage85_source_caution: The definition’s preceding terms are treated elsewhere; not a whole leaf.

records.title: Conception, apprehension, and terminological convention
records.arabic_anchors: «(إن فهمت) أي تلك المفردة»؛ «الإدراك المركب والكلي»؛ «يسمى إدراك البسيط أو الجزئي معرفة»؛ «(تنبيه على اختلاف الاصطلاحات)».
records.english: If the object apprehended is simple or particular, a writer may call its apprehension **recognition** (*maʿrifa*); in other terminological arrangements the names “perception,” “conception,” and “knowledge” are distributed differently between simple and composite objects and between particulars and universals. Such a change in usage is a **difference of technical convention**, not proof that the object itself has changed. The author alerts the reader to the disagreements in terminology before defining deliberate inquiry (*naẓar*).
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: The motion of the soul in inquiry
records.arabic: (وحقيقة النظر حركة النفس) من المطلوب المشعور به بوجهه ...
records.arabic_anchors: «(وحقيقة النظر حركة النفس) من المطلوب المشعور به بوجهه ...».
records.english: “The reality of inquiry is the movement of the soul” from the object sought, which is apprehended in some respect. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: “The reality of inquiry is **a movement of the soul**” from a sought object which is known in some respect, or whose relevant question is already apprehended, toward matters by which it may be known. This movement is not a displacement of the soul through **physical space** but a transition between intellectual states. It begins with a question and proceeds toward the arrangement of what is known so as to reach what is not yet known. The sentence continues into I:18.
records.stage88_source_note: upper register, discussion of the two movements of the mind; short, clear printed lemma and gloss; full sentence crosses into following context
records.stage88_proof: direct visual reading of first-print facsimile; requires second independent proof
records.stage88_copytext: Būlāq, 1318 AH, vol. I printed p.17, combined PDF physical p.30

records.title: On the stages of the mind's movement
records.arabic: أي حقيقة النظر مجموع الحركتين المذكورتين وهما من جنس الحركة في الكيف ...
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله في المعقولات المحققة الخ)»؛ «الحركة الأولى والثانية»؛ «الترتيب المخصوص»؛ «المجهول».
records.english: That is, the reality of inquiry comprises the two movements already mentioned, both being of the kind of movement in quality. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: The marginal author considers which mental transitions are counted as the first movement and which as the return. It is possible to describe the investigator as turning from a general awareness of a problem toward its potentially relevant premises, and then directing the intellect from those premises, placed in a fitting **order**, to the desired conclusion. Some formulations count the acquisition of the conclusion as a further stage, while others treat it as the **terminus** of the second movement. These differences should not be conflated with the question whether the result itself follows by **custom**, by **generation**, or by a necessity of inference. That distinct issue is developed on I:24–26.

records.title: If a proof that inquiry works itself requires inquiry
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لكون النظر مفيداً للعلم)»؛ «دور»؛ «الضرورة»؛ «النظر الصحيح»؛ «التصورات والتصديقات».
records.english: The margin records the objection that to prove inquiry effective through inquiry seems to assume the effectiveness it aims to establish. One reply says the general relation can be **known necessarily** or from an undeniable particular instance of valid reasoning. The critic responds that a particular act of obtaining knowledge may not of itself warrant the universal claim about all possible forms of inquiry. The difference between **actual valid reasoning** and any arrangement of statements matters: not everything that someone calls reflection succeeds in yielding an insight. The discussion thereby prepares the requirement that correct inquiry employ suitable premises and their appropriate order. A few closing lines on the form of a syllogism remain to be individually transcribed.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Forward and returning intellectual movements
records.arabic: وأما الترتيب الذي ذكروه في تعريفه فهو لازم من لوازمه
records.arabic_anchors: «في المعقولات ... (حركة أولى)»؛ «(عوداً)»؛ «(التحصيل) المطلوب (المجهول)»؛ «وأما الترتيب ...».
records.english: As for the ordering mentioned in their definition of inquiry, it is one of the things necessarily attendant upon it.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: Inquiry occurs among **intelligible objects**. In one account it comprises an initial movement from the as-yet-unknown conclusion toward known matters that might establish it, and then a return, from the arranged premises toward **obtaining the conclusion**. The stages are counted differently depending on whether one includes the question's initial emergence, the collection of suitable premises, their arrangement, and the final apprehension. The cognitive movement is not a succession of physical events in spatial directions; it is a *methodological sequence* which renders a formerly unknown judgment knowable.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «في المعقولات ... (حركة أولى)»؛ «(عوداً)»؛ «(التحصيل) المطلوب (المجهول)»؛ «وأما الترتيب ...».
