records.title: Whether deliberate inquiry itself is theoretical knowledge
records.arabic: (وكونه) أي النظر (مفيداً للعلم في الجملة) خلافاً لمن قال إنه لا يفيد أصلاً ...
records.arabic_anchors: «(وكونه) أي النظر (مفيداً للعلم)»؛ «قال إنه لا يفيد أصلاً»؛ «لأن كون النظر مفيداً ...».
records.english: “That it”—that is, inquiry—“yields knowledge in some measure,” contrary to those who say that it yields none at all. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: “And whether it”—that is, inquiry—“produces knowledge”: this itself became a disputed proposition. Some deny that inquiry yields knowledge at all; others say that an inference from premises to a conclusion provides knowledge but disagree about **the mode of that provision**. Since proving that inquiry yields knowledge may itself require an act of inquiry, the sceptic threatens to make the proof circular. The text introduces the response that one must distinguish an immediately evident instance from an overarching inference concerning all inquiries, and an act's being a **means** from its being a **productive cause**.

records.title: Whether knowledge of inquiry's usefulness is circular
records.arabic: أما الأول فلكونه وسيلة، وأما الثاني فلكونه مطلوبًا، وقد يقال: لا استلزام للدور إلا إذا أُريد أن العلم بفائدة النظر يتوقف على العلم بفائدة النظر. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله كون الواحد نصف الاثنين الخ)»؛ «(قوله يلزم إثبات إفادة النظر الخ)»؛ «دور»؛ «المقدمات»؛ «التصور والتصديق».
records.english: As for the first, it is because it is a means; as for the second, because it is what is sought. It may be said that no circularity follows unless one means that knowledge of the benefit of reasoning depends on knowledge of that very benefit. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: The marginal commentator contrasts the proposition “one is half of two” with acquired conclusions that require an arrangement of premises. If the proposition is **necessary**, it cannot serve without qualification as the example of a result acquired by investigative inference. If it is called *theoretical* in this context, one must specify how that description is being used. The objection about circularity likewise requires care: employing an inference to reach the proposition “some inference produces knowledge” may be circular if the inference's **trustworthiness** already depends upon that proposition as its premise. It does not automatically follow that a particular correct inference is invalid. To show why the form of the proof yields a conclusion, we need the premises, their connection, and the status of the result; a mere label “inquiry” does not suffice.

stage89_source_note.limits: Only a bounded reply on the means/end and alleged circularity; the lower passage continues.

records.title: Necessary premises, acquired conclusions, and the false regress
records.arabic: وقد يُجاب بأن مبنى كلام المخالف على أن التصديق بالنتيجة، أي العلم بحقيقتها، إنما يلزم من التصديق بالمقدمات وكونها مستلزمة للمطلوب. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «العلم بكون المقدمات مستلزمة للنتيجة»؛ «التركيب»؛ «التصديق»؛ «الضرورة».
records.english: One may reply that the opponent’s argument rests on the assumption that assent to the conclusion—that is, knowing its truth—follows only from assent to the premises and from their entailing what is sought. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage89_prior_working_overview: The margin further distinguishes **knowing the premises**, **knowing that they entail the conclusion**, and **knowing the conclusion**. The last can be novel even where the first two are already possessed, and in some cases awareness of the entailment becomes manifest in the very act of attending to the premises. The threat of an endless regress of proofs arises only if we demand a further inference to establish **each** relation in every case. The writer reports a contrary view that some such relations must be understood without further demonstration. These are disputes about the foundations of demonstration, not a dismissal of the value of reasoned inquiry.

stage89_source_note.limits: Bounded report of the reply; the subsequent qualification about theoretical assent remains.

records.title: Disputed inference and the sphere of theology
records.arabic: (ولو في الإلهيات) خلافا للقائل بأنه لا يفيد العلم فيها لأن الحقائق الإلهية من ذاته وصفاته لا تتصور والتصديق بها فرع التصور
records.arabic_anchors: «كون الواحد نصف الاثنين»؛ «وإن كان نظرياً لزم إثبات إفادة النظر بإفادة النظر»؛ «(وفي الإلهيات)»؛ «خلافاً للقائل بأنه لا يفيد العلم»؛ «(وبدون العلم)».
records.english: “Even in theology”: contrary to the person who says that inquiry produces no knowledge there, since the divine realities—His essence and attributes—cannot be conceived, whereas assent about them depends upon conception.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: Consider the judgment that **one is half of two**. A necessity of this kind may be apprehended directly, but merely placing it in an argument does not establish that every formal reflection produces a new cognition. Where the effectiveness of inquiry is said to be theoretical, the sceptic alleges that it must itself be established by an inference—thus assuming the disputed effectiveness. The dispute is especially sharp “in matters divine,” where some thinkers deny that reasoning can provide knowledge of the objects at issue. The author distinguishes those divine truths which are understood by necessary cognition from those for which a proof can be offered. Denying the effectiveness of every inference merely because some truths are immediately evident would exceed what these examples establish.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «كون الواحد نصف الاثنين»؛ «وإن كان نظرياً لزم إثبات إفادة النظر بإفادة النظر»؛ «(وفي الإلهيات)»؛ «خلافاً للقائل بأنه لا يفيد العلم»؛ «(وبدون العلم)».
records.stage85_source_caution: Historical objection being reported, not an editorial assertion.

records.title: The sceptic's no-progress conclusion
records.arabic: (وفي الإلهيات) خلافاً للقائل بأنه لا يفيد العلم فيها ...
records.arabic_anchors: «الحقائق الإلهية من ذاته وصفاته»؛ «التصور والتصديق»؛ «(وبدون العلم)»؛ «(ضروري) لا يحتاج إلى بيان».
records.english: “And in divine matters,” contrary to the person who maintains that [inquiry] does not yield knowledge in them. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: Concerning divine things, it is argued that the essence and attributes of God do not fall under ordinary modes of conception and assent in the way everyday objects do. The reply is that one must not confuse **comprehending the divine essence** with **knowing propositions concerning God**. The latter may be accessible through demonstrative or inferential routes even if the former is beyond human comprehension. A further allegation—that proof must always presuppose the very conclusion sought—has to be stated precisely. Valid inquiry starts from something already known, not necessarily from the precise **conclusion** it is intended to establish.

records.title: The syllogism about an originated world
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فإن الضروري قد يقع الخ)»؛ «العالم متغير وكل متغير حادث»؛ «العلم بأن العالم حادث»؛ «النظر مفيد للعلم».
records.english: On “a necessary matter may be disputed, etc.” The writer suggests that we can know the usefulness of valid reasoning through a **particular correct instance** without descending into an endless series of justifications. The example is: **“The world is subject to change; everything subject to change is originated.”** From these premises comes knowledge that the world is originated. This furnishes an instance in which an inquiry leads to a conclusion. The argument should not be represented as if the word “inquiry” were itself a proof: the evidential force arises from the relevant premises and their proper relation.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: What is meant by knowing the effectiveness of inquiry?
records.arabic_anchors: «فالأثر المطلوب»؛ «هذه القضية»؛ «الموقف عليها»؛ «التصور والتصديق»؛ «الحكم على العام».
records.english: The margin examines what the general statement “inquiry produces knowledge” actually claims. Does it require knowing **every conceivable kind of inquiry**, or may the intellect reach a general recognition of a suitably specified kind from an evident example? If one must already know the general proposition in order to appreciate the example, the proposed demonstration begs the question; if one can recognize the effect in a clear instance and then identify the common features of the case, the threat of circularity is weakened. Yet the generalisation must not include **defective forms of reasoning** which do not satisfy the conditions for producing knowledge. The marginal author therefore distinguishes the **universal concept** of inquiry from its instances and asks what makes a premise-conclusion structure a proof.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Why the teacher's authority does not replace proof
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لا يستلزم أن الحقائق الإلهية الخ)»؛ «المعلم»؛ «الاستدلال»؛ «المعرفة».
records.english: The concluding note turns toward the question of instruction. If someone says that divine knowledge cannot be obtained by inquiry and must depend on a **teacher**, then the teacher's authority must itself be evaluated. A hearer cannot establish the teacher's veracity simply by accepting that teacher's own claim to be truthful; nor will invoking one more teacher avoid the question. The argument is not that no one can **learn** from a teacher, but that independent **warrant** for believing the teacher cannot be replaced by an indefinite succession of unexamined reports. The main text pursues that objection on I:21.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Disagreement over necessary matters
records.arabic: فإن الأمر ضروري قد يقع فيه خلاف
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن الضروري قد يقع فيه خلاف ...»؛ «والإلهيات ...».
records.english: For disagreement can occur even about something known immediately.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: Even a matter called **necessary** may be disputed, whether because a participant does not fully apprehend what is being asserted or because the disputant resists assent through obstinacy. The existence of disagreement does not by itself demonstrate that the matter lacks an evident foundation. The sentence then introduces the special case of divine realities and continues into I:21.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «فإن الضروري قد يقع فيه خلاف ...»؛ «والإلهيات ...».
records.stage85_source_caution: Only short continuation of the proof that reasoning can yield knowledge.

records.title: Does learning require prior proof of the teacher's truth?
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لا يفيد إلا بعد العلم بصدقه الخ)»؛ «لا تحصل لنا فائدة العلم استقلالاً»؛ «صدق نسبة ...»؛ «خبر»؛ «النظر».
records.english: On “it is of no benefit until his truthfulness is known”: the marginal writer objects to saying that a student's attainment of **any knowledge** requires a prior, independent demonstration that the teacher is trustworthy. What the principal argument needs is more exact: if a teacher's **report** is invoked as the decisive warrant for a disputed conclusion, the report's force rests on knowledge of its truthfulness. A learner may acquire or notice a true proposition on hearing the report without first articulating a proof of the speaker's character. The issue is not psychological occurrence but **epistemic warrant**. One should therefore not use the objection to deny the possibility of knowledge acquired from instruction; it attacks only the attempt to make unsupported teacher-authority foundational.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Sense, experience, and the denial of common judgments
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله اسم طائفة من الحكماء الخ)»؛ «من الشكوك»؛ «السوفسطائي»؛ «الحق ...».
records.english: The margin distinguishes a sincere **doubt** concerning a particular subject from a blanket denial of sensibles and first principles. It reports polemics against disputants who reject their own sensible experience or the axioms that make dispute meaningful. An asserted doubt is not answered simply by displaying additional testimony whose certainty the doubter has already rejected. The author suggests examining the exact **scope** of each denial: some reject the reports of particular senses, others accept ordinary appearances but deny the warrant of conclusions drawn from them, and still others claim to reject intellectual first principles. The ensuing I:22–23 debate concerns the latter distinction; no entire historical philosophical school can be inferred solely from this polemical name.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: A teacher's veracity cannot be warranted by that teacher alone
records.arabic: وأن إرشاد المعلم لا يفيد إلا بعد العلم بصدقه
records.arabic_anchors: «لا يتصور بكلاهما ...»؛ «وأن إرشاد المعلم لا يفيد إلا بعد العلم بصدقه»؛ «فأما أن يعلم بالنظر فيكون النظر كافياً»؛ «وإلا لزم التسلسل».
records.english: A teacher’s guidance is of no benefit until his truthfulness has been established.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: —the conceptions are not secured in the way demanded by the opponent. Even granting that they can be apprehended, we must ask what makes the instruction of a **teacher** a source of knowledge. That teacher's guidance yields no warranted result until his **truthfulness** has been known. If we know his truthfulness by examination, the necessity of a teacher is undermined, for the relevant investigation is already a possible path to knowledge. If we know it solely because he says that he is truthful, the explanation is circular: his testimony is authoritative only after the very truthfulness in question has been established. If a second teacher assures us of the first, then the second teacher's truthfulness must be known as well, threatening an indefinite regress. This is a proof against an **exclusive teacher-dependent epistemology**, not against the ordinary usefulness of teaching.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «لا يتصور بكلاهما ...»؛ «وأن إرشاد المعلم لا يفيد إلا بعد العلم بصدقه»؛ «فأما أن يعلم بالنظر فيكون النظر كافياً»؛ «وإلا لزم التسلسل».
records.stage85_source_caution: Small grammatical passage; read with surrounding argument on the authority of informants.

records.title: Sophists, obstinacy, and the reported etymology
records.arabic_anchors: «(والمنكر) ... (معاند) لا يسمع دعواه»؛ «(السفسطائي) المنكر للحسيات أو الأوليات أو كليهما»؛ «السوف ... اللفظ اسم لطائفة من الحكماء».
records.english: “The denier” of evident truths, insofar as he denies through obstinacy, is a **wilfully resisting opponent**, whose mere assertion does not overturn the original judgment. The name “Sophist” is applied in the text to one who denies sensible propositions, primary intellectual propositions, or both. The book reports an etymology from a word for **knowledge** and another for **error**, producing a characterization of a group said to misuse philosophical reasoning. This etymology is **reported from the historical author**, not endorsed by the translator as a modern linguistic finding.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Reports of extreme scepticism and the senses
records.arabic: ليس في العالم قوم ينتحل هذا المذهب، بل كل غالط سوفسطائي في موضع غلطه. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «والمحققون ... في العالم قوم ينتحل هذا المذهب»؛ «السوفسطائي»؛ «قوله قدح في الحسيات»؛ «البداهة».
records.english: There is no group among people that professes this position; rather, everyone who errs is a sophist at the point of his particular error. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: The lower commentator reports that it is doubtful whether knowledgeable people consistently maintained a wholesale denial of sensibles and evident first principles; the group described in polemical accounts may instead have relied on exaggerated cases of illusion. In addressing the attack on perception, the relevant distinction is between **the sensation's occurring** and **an intellectual judgment about what the sensation shows**. Deceptive appearances may be corrected by another examination of the circumstances without granting that all judgments from the senses are suspect. The source compares several reported examples of sensory error, insisting that an error which arises from an **inference attached to perception** should not be described as a failure of all immediate cognition.

stage90_source_note.scope: First lower paragraph; source words preceding the claim and later objections remain untranscribed.

records.title: The force of the example of noncontradiction
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله من قدح في الأوليات الخ)»؛ «النفي والإثبات»؛ «إما أن يكون أو لا يكون»؛ «العلم بهذه القضية يتوقف على تصور الوجود والعدم».
records.english: The marginals then turn to the proposition that a thing cannot both exist and not exist in the same respect. The sceptic is right in a limited sense that one must understand the constituent terms to assent to the proposition. But that observation does not provide an independent **argument against its evident character**. A distinction must be made between **knowing the proposition itself** and **giving an explanatory proof of why the proposition is certain**. To demand a further proof that already assumes the proposition would be circular, but it does not follow that the immediate intellectual judgment is invalid. The lower discussion joins the fuller argument on I:23.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: “Immediate” refers to the intellect's immediate recognition
records.arabic: (قوله والجواب أن البديهة) أي بداهة العقل لا الحس حتى يرد أنه إثبات حكم الحس بنفسه. (قوله إلى غير ذلك) أي من القطعيات العادية، اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله والجواب أن البداهة) أي بداهة العقل لا الحس»؛ «(قوله إلى غير ذلك) أي من الطبعات العادية».
records.english: On “The answer is that the self-evidence”: this means the intellect’s self-evidence, not that of sense-perception; otherwise the objection would arise that a judgment of the senses was being established by the senses themselves. On “and other such things”: that is, habitual or customary certainties. [End of the cited gloss.]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: “The answer is that immediate evidentness ...” means **the intellect's** immediate apprehension, not an attempt to prove the trustworthiness of a sense by appealing to that same sense. “And other cases” means other examples of customary or evident judgments. The second phrase is shortened in the print, so its ending is preserved here only as a locating anchor, not an authenticated full transcript.

records.title: Why some perceptual errors cannot refute all sensible judgments
records.arabic: قدح في الحسيات بأن حكم الحس قد يغلط
records.arabic_anchors: «قدح في الحسيات بأن حكم الحس قد يغلط»؛ «كما ترى الساكن متحركاً والمتحرك ساكناً»؛ «في بعض المحسوسات»؛ «الشمس مضيئة والنار محرقة».
records.english: He cast doubt on sense perceptions on the ground that the judgment of the senses may be mistaken.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: Some attack **sensible judgments** by observing that the senses sometimes make mistakes. The observer may regard a stationary thing as moving or a moving thing as stationary: a person aboard a moving vessel may take it to be still and see the shore as moving. From cases like these the sceptic alleges that any judgment of sense is liable to error. The response is that an error in **some** instances does not establish that all perceptual judgments fail. There are cases, such as the recognition that the sun illuminates and fire burns, in which a properly formed judgment may be evident. The lesson is **not** that the senses are infallible, but that the transition from “some perceptual judgments are mistaken” to “none can constitute knowledge” lacks justification.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «قدح في الحسيات بأن حكم الحس قد يغلط»؛ «كما ترى الساكن متحركاً والمتحرك ساكناً»؛ «في بعض المحسوسات»؛ «الشمس مضيئة والنار محرقة».

records.title: The sceptic's challenge to excluded middle and contradiction
records.arabic: ... بأن أجلّ البديهيات قولنا: النفي والإثبات لا يجتمعان ولا يرتفعان ...
records.arabic_anchors: «قدح في الأوليات بأن أجل البديهيات قولنا النفي والإثبات لا يجتمعان ولا يرتفعان»؛ «ما أن يكون أو لا يكون»؛ «توقف تصور الوجود والعدم».
records.english: […] [The objection is] that the foremost of self-evident propositions is our statement that negation and affirmation neither coincide nor can both be absent. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage88_prior_working_overview: Others attack intellectual first principles. The most evident is said to be that **affirmation and denial cannot both obtain nor both fail to obtain** in the same respect: a proposition holds or it does not. The sceptic claims that even this judgment relies on the prior conceptions of **being and nonbeing**, and perhaps on our notion of predication itself. If those notions must first be reached through proofs relying on the very judgment being defended, the proof turns in a circle. The issue passes into I:23, where the main text and commentary distinguish the **judgment's being immediate** from a purported demonstration of its necessity.

records.title: Parsing the circularity argument correctly
records.arabic: الشرطية لا صفة للأنظار لئلا يوهم أن لنا أنظارًا لا تنتهي إليها. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله ... نظراً إلى ذاته)»؛ «(قوله توقف لا محالة الخ)»؛ «الانظار المتقدمة»؛ «المقدمة»؛ «الدور».
records.english: The conditional qualification does not characterize the acts of reasoning themselves, lest it suggest that there are instances of reasoning which do not terminate in it. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: The margin considers the grammar of “it depends inevitably.” It ought to be construed as the **consequence of the stated supposition**, rather than as an incidental description of a class of investigations. Otherwise one could mistakenly infer that the author assumes certain forms of inquiry escape the very principle under examination. The consequence is that **a circle follows** when the proof of a basic proposition is made dependent on a reasoning process that already needs it. The note distinguishes the **antecedent of a conditional objection** from the **asserted conclusion**, and warns against treating a hypothetical assumption as the author's own positive position.

stage90_source_note.scope: Opening lower paragraph; referent of إليها must be resolved from the preceding upper text and continuation.

records.title: Conception before assent does not imply inferential proof
records.arabic: ويمكن أن يقال إن الأنظار المنتهية إلى هذه القضية هي الأنظار التصديقية، لأن التصورية إنما تنتهي إلى التصور البديهي. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لازمة بها)»؛ «(قوله من غير نظر واستدلال الخ)»؛ «التصورات البديهية»؛ «أطرافها»؛ «دلالة المعجزة».
records.english: It may be said that the inquiries terminating in this proposition are inquiries concerned with assent; those concerned with conception terminate instead in an immediately evident conception. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: Assent to a proposition requires **grasping its terms**, but that does not entail that the proposition's certainty must arise from a discursive syllogism. The marginal writer compares immediate conception of terms, the immediate **judgment** relating them, and the separate process of **inferring** a conclusion. Confusing these yields a fallacy: a proposition may be known after its terms are understood without having been *proved* by a prior inference. The note also asks how an obvious proposition could be defended to someone who refuses the status of all obvious judgments, and why a verbal appeal to a teacher would merely reinstate the earlier dependence problem. The final lower clauses point toward the question whether correct reflection leads to knowledge by necessity, custom, or generated action.

stage90_source_note.scope: Lower middle: selected contrast of inferential assent with conception; rest of lower argument remains.

records.title: Subject, predicate, and the danger of a circle
records.arabic_anchors: «وعلى تحقيق معنى كون الشيء موضوعاً وما يكون محمولاً»؛ «توقف لا محالة على حقيقة هذه القضية»؛ «الكل أعظم من الجزء»؛ «فلزم الدور».
records.english: The challenge asks for a conception of what it means for something to be **subject** and for another thing to be **predicated** of it. But if the very idea of predication presupposes the actuality of the law concerning affirmation and denial, our attempt to demonstrate that law from something prior will be circular. For example, a proof about the proposition **“the whole is greater than the part”** may already rely on excluding its contradictory alternative. If such a proof is required before the intellect can assent to the fundamental proposition, the proof has presupposed the principle it was meant to establish. The source states this as an objection to the **order of demonstration**, not to ordinary use of true judgments.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Certain intellectual assent as the terminus
records.arabic: والجواب أن بديهة العقل جازمة بها من غير نظر واستدلال
records.arabic_anchors: «العقل جازمة بها من غير نظر واستدلال»؛ «ومنهم من قدح فيها جميعاً»؛ «وهو معلوم».
records.english: The answer is that the intellect directly and decisively affirms it, without reflection or inference.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The reply is that the intellect's judgment in this case is **decisive without inquiry or inference**. A person may nevertheless dispute it verbally or construct a conditional argument that seems to undermine it. The existence of that dispute does not show that a first principle **must** be proved through another first principle before it can be known. If every fundamental judgment had to be derived from something yet more fundamental, demonstrations could never begin. The relevant discussion now turns from the reality of evident knowledge to its occurrence after **deliberate investigation**.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «العقل جازمة بها من غير نظر واستدلال»؛ «ومنهم من قدح فيها جميعاً»؛ «وهو معلوم».
records.stage85_source_caution: Immediate judgment and the discussion of the terms of the proposition must not be conflated.

records.title: Distinguishing custom, necessity, and generation
records.arabic: (قوله بطريق العادة) أي تكرر ذلك دائمًا مع جواز أن يتخلف خرقًا للعادة. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله بطريق العادة) أي تكرر ذلك دائماً مع جواز أن يتخلف ...»؛ «(قوله فاعل مختار)»؛ «(قوله أو التوليد الخ)»؛ «لو كان مولداً للعلم ...».
records.english: On “by way of custom”: that is, the occurrence recurs habitually, while it remains possible that it fail to occur through a breach of the customary order. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: On “by way of custom”: the regularity is said to recur while an exception remains **possible**; if an exception occurs, the regular sequence has not thereby been shown to be metaphysically necessary. On the phrase “a choosing agent”: God's freedom is intended, in contrast with the philosophers' overflowing cause. On “or generation”: the marginal writer tests what the phrase actually entails. If reflection **generated** knowledge, the actor's performance of the reflection would have to supply more than the mere temporal antecedent of the result. The first act and the purportedly generated second act must be distinguished. The opponent may ask what prevents reflection from taking place without the knowledge, and whether the claim that such failure is impossible is itself a claim about **productive necessity** rather than generation. This prepares the objection at I:25 that knowledge is not in the category of action. **Reading caution:** The printed lower annotation contains one additional tightly compressed argument around the first act's capacity; this English follows the argument's order but remains below whole-page literal certification.

stage90_source_note.scope: First opening phrase of lower paragraph, not the complete argument comparing custom with generation.

records.title: The Ashʿarite theologians' principle
records.arabic: هذا مذهب الأشعري
records.arabic_anchors: «(قال المصنف رحمه الله بطريق العادة) هذا مذهب الأشعري»؛ «الممكنات بأسرها مستندة إلى الله تعالى ابتداء»؛ «عقيب النظر الصحيح بإجراء العادة».
records.english: This is the Ashʿarī position.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The author, may God have mercy on him, said: “by way of custom.” This is the Ashʿarī position. They hold that all possible things are attributed to God **in the first instance**, and that one possible event does not independently produce another. Instead, God brings one thing into being after another in a customary order. When that order recurs, it is called **custom**; when it differs from the ordinary order, one speaks of an exception to custom. The knowledge arising after sound investigation is an originated contingent event regularly accompanying the investigation, so it is accounted for through God's customary action. This note treats **succession without independent necessitation**, not a denial that inquiry has practical epistemic significance.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(قال المصنف رحمه الله بطريق العادة) هذا مذهب الأشعري»؛ «الممكنات بأسرها مستندة إلى الله تعالى ابتداء»؛ «عقيب النظر الصحيح بإجراء العادة».
records.stage85_source_caution: The long ruled explanation that follows is not translated here.

records.title: The Muʿtazilite principle
records.arabic: (قال رحمه الله أو التوليد) هذا مذهب المعتزلة، وهو مبني على أصلهم من أن أفعالنا الاختيارية صادرة عنا إما مباشرة إن لم يكن صدورها عنا بتوسط فعل آخر منا، وإما توليدًا إن كان بتوسط فعل آخر. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قال رحمه الله أو التوليد) هذا ما ذهب إليه المعتزلة»؛ «الأفعال الاختيارية صادرة عنا»؛ «فإما أن تكون صادرة عنا بالمباشرة ...»؛ «بواسطة فعل آخر منا».
records.english: On his saying “or by generation”: this is the Muʿtazilite position, resting on their principle that our voluntary acts issue from us either directly, when they are not brought about through another act of ours, or by generation, when they arise through the mediation of another act. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage90_prior_working_overview: He said, God have mercy on him: “or generation.” This is the position attributed to the Muʿtazilites. On their account, our **voluntary acts** issue from us. They occur either by **immediate performance**, when no other action of ours mediates them, or by **generation**, when one of our acts produces another through an intermediate act of ours. They say that the knowledge that arises after rational examination is produced through the examination and thus is an instance of generation. The source's next page defines the two modes more precisely.

stage90_source_note.scope: Beginning of second note in the middle ruled stream; subsequent application to knowledge following inquiry is left open.

records.title: The Ashʿarite account of customary conjunction
records.arabic: أن جميع الممكنات مستندة إليه تعالى وأنه تعالى قادر مختار
records.arabic_anchors: «مما سبق رداً واستدلالاً (وهل هو) أي كون النظر مفيداً للعلم (بطريق العادة)»؛ «بناء على أن جميع الممكنات مستندة إليه تعالى عندنا ابتداء»؛ «وأنه تعالى قادر مختار».
records.english: All contingent things depend upon Him, exalted is He, and He is an agent possessed of power and choice.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: After the preceding argument and reply the text asks: **How does investigation bring about knowledge?** “Is it by way of **custom** (*ʿāda*)?” This follows the doctrine that every possible event depends directly, in its origination, on God, exalted is He, and that He is **able to choose**. Nothing among possible events therefore proceeds from Him with the necessity of a self-sufficient cause. Knowledge may regularly follow correct inquiry because God creates it in that order, without the inquiry's being a productive cause by its own inherent power.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «مما سبق رداً واستدلالاً (وهل هو) أي كون النظر مفيداً للعلم (بطريق العادة)»؛ «بناء على أن جميع الممكنات مستندة إليه تعالى عندنا ابتداء»؛ «وأنه تعالى قادر مختار».
records.stage85_source_caution: Direct-source clause on the Ashʿarī customary-sequence position; the causal exposition is longer.

records.title: The Muʿtazilite alternative of generation
records.arabic_anchors: «(أو) بطريق (التوليد)»؛ «بناء على أن ليس الكل مستنداً ...»؛ «يجب عنه صدور شيء ...».
records.english: “Or [is it] by way of **generation** (*tawlīd*)?” This follows the account under which the acts of a voluntary creature can give rise, through the mediation of one of its own acts, to further effects. Correct reflection, on that account, can be an agent's act through which knowledge is generated. The definition and the hand–key example appear at the beginning of I:25; the source must be read **continuously**, not as an isolated assertion that knowledge is just another bodily act.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: “Acting” and the hand–key example do not classify knowledge as physical motion
records.arabic: (قوله واعترض بأن العلم إلخ) قال في شرح المقاصد ما حاصله أن النظر على أكثر تفاسيره أيضاً ليس من مقولة الفعل، لكن أرادوا بالفعل هنا الأمر الحاصل بالفاعل لا نفس التأثير. كيف وقد اتفقوا على أن حركة اليد وحركة المفتاح فعلان لفاعل واحد، مع أن الحركة ليست فعلاً حقيقة. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله واعترض بأن العلم الخ)»؛ «النظر على أكثر تقديراته أيضاً ليس من مقولة الفعل»؛ «أرادوا بالفعل هذا الأمر الحاصل بالفاعل لا نفس التأثير»؛ «حركة اليد وحركة المفتاح»؛ «فعل واحد».
records.english: On the objection that knowledge is not an action: In Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid it is said, in substance, that inquiry too, under most of its interpretations, is not of the category of action. But what they mean by “action” here is the thing produced by an agent, not the very exercise of causal influence. After all, they agree that the movement of the hand and the movement of the key are two acts of a single agent, even though motion itself is not, strictly speaking, an act. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On the objection “knowledge is not [of the category of] acting”: the commentator observes that even investigation itself, in its most carefully qualified sense, does not simply belong to the category of action. What those employing the analogy intended by an “act” was **something obtained through an agent**, not necessarily the metaphysical category of action as a separate accident inhering in the agent. The disputants agree that the hand's movement and the key's movement may be attributed to an agent, though the movement, considered in its own category, is not strictly an instance of the category *acting*. There is therefore no warrant to force the knowledge–investigation relation into the taxonomy of bodily movements.

stage92_source_note.witness: Būlāq 1318 AH printed Volume I (single printed copy, no manuscript collation)
stage92_source_note.scope: selected contiguous source phrases, omissions explicitly signaled
stage92_source_note.limitations: Opening of lower gloss; attribution to source quoted Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid is reported, not independently verified against that book; remainder omitted.

records.title: The act, the intermediary, and the voluntary origin of inquiry
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله الفعل الآخر ... الخ)»؛ «فإن الفعل الآخر في التوليد لا بد أن يكون فعلاً واحداً»؛ «(قوله من المبدأ الفياض الخ)»؛ «الروح والكتاب المبين»؛ «سلب الاختيار منه تعالى».
records.english: In the expression “the other act” it is necessary to specify what is meant by the intermediary in a generated action. If the first action occurs through a person's own capacity and choice, that is not yet sufficient to show that every subsequent outcome belongs to the same act of choice **without a further question about causality**. The margin presses the distinction between the first voluntary act and its purportedly generated effect. The language of an overflowing principle, on the other hand, was introduced to explain a supposed necessary emergence from a cause prepared to give an effect. In the theologians' criticism, however, making the relationship simply necessary would compromise the divine **freedom of choice**. The marginal discussion closes by moving toward the contrast stated at the top of I:26. **Proof limitation:** The compact lines connecting these arguments contain quotations and allusions that require full typed Arabic collation; the current English follows the sequence but does not claim word-for-word certainty.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: The philosophers' overflowing cause and a fourth position
records.arabic: (قال قدس سره أو الوجوب) هذا ما قاله الحكماء، وهو مبني على أصلهم من أن المبدأ الفياض لوجود الحوادث موجب بالذات
records.arabic_anchors: «(قال قدس سره أو الوجوب) هذا ما قاله الحكماء»؛ «المبدأ الفياض لوجود الحوادث موجب بالذات»؛ «العلم الحاصل عقيب النظر أمر حادث»؛ «مذهب آخر اختاره الإمام الرازي والغزالي وإمام الحرمين»؛ «حصول العلم عن النظر الصحيح لازم له لزوماً عقلياً غير متولد منه».
records.english: On “or necessity”: this is what the philosophers maintain. It rests on their principle that the effusive source of originated things is a necessitating cause by its very essence. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: He said, may his spirit be sanctified, “or necessity.” This is what the philosophers maintain, building on the principle that the overflowing source entails the occurrence of originated effects **by its essence**, while their issuance from it depends on the receiver's complete preparedness. Since knowledge that follows inquiry is originated, it falls under that general rule. But another opinion—reported as the choice of Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, al-Ghazālī and Imām al-Ḥaramayn—has not been included in the main enumeration: knowledge follows **sound investigation** by a **rational entailment**, without being generated by it as the Muʿtazilites suppose. The note's final personal formula is not sufficient by itself to identify the glossator.

stage91_source_note.location: middle ruled register, opening of the philosophers’ account
stage91_source_note.scope: Only the Arabic words supplied above have been transcribed; all omitted printed text remains pending
stage91_source_note.limits: The rest of the philosophers’ explanation and objections remains untranscribed.

records.title: Generation is action mediated through another act
records.arabic: واعترض بأن العلم ليس من مقولة الفعل
records.arabic_anchors: «ومعنى التوليد هو أن يصدر من الفاعل فعل بواسطة فعل آخر صادر منه»؛ «كحركة اليد للمفتاح»؛ «وبقباله المباشرة وهي أن يصدر منه فعل بلا واسطة».
records.english: It was objected that knowledge does not belong to the category of action.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: [The Ashʿarite account holds that] God, exalted is He, brings the effect about **directly**. The meaning of “generation” (*tawlīd*) is that one act proceeds from an agent **by means of another act which also proceeds from that agent**. An example is the movement of the hand and of a key: the movement of the key takes place through the movement of the hand. Opposed to such generation is **immediate agency** (*mubāshara*), namely the production of an act without an intervening act. These definitions explain the parties' different analyses of how knowledge follows examination; the hand–key analogy is not a proof that knowledge literally is a movement.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «ومعنى التوليد هو أن يصدر من الفاعل فعل بواسطة فعل آخر صادر منه»؛ «كحركة اليد للمفتاح»؛ «وبقباله المباشرة وهي أن يصدر منه فعل بلا واسطة».
records.stage85_source_caution: The rebuttal by analogy with action and generation is still open.

records.title: Is knowledge in the category of action? The alternative of necessity
records.arabic_anchors: «واعترض بأن العلم ليس من مقولة الفعل»؛ «وأجيب بأن الفعل الآخر هنا إفادة العلم وهي فعل»؛ «(أو الوجوب)»؛ «فيضان الحوادث من المبدأ الفياض عند الاستعداد التام القابل واجب».
records.english: It was objected that **knowledge is not an instance of the category of acting**. The reply is that what is being called the additional “act” here is **imparting knowledge** (*ifādat al-ʿilm*), which can be described as acting. “Or by necessity”: this is the third explanation, according to which the issuance of originated things from the overflowing principle is **necessary** upon the complete preparation of what is to receive them. The expression concerns the **mode of dependence of the effect on its principle**, not a claim that the act of inquiry is itself the substance of knowledge.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: The fourth position chosen by al-Rāzī and reported by al-Ghazālī
records.arabic: (قوله فيه خلاف بين الأشاعرة إلخ) ذكر أن ههنا مذهباً آخر اختاره الإمام الرازي، وذكر حجة الإسلام أنه المذهب عند أكثر أصحابنا، وهو أن النظر يستلزم العلم بالنتيجة بطريق الوجوب من غير أن يكون النظر علة كمذهب الحكماء أو مولّداً كمذهب المعتزلة. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فيه خلاف بين الأشاعرة الخ)»؛ «الإمام الرازي»؛ «حجة الإسلام ... مذهب أكثر أصحابنا»؛ «النظر يستلزم العلم بالنتيجة بطريق الوجوب»؛ «من غير أن يكون النظر علة ... أو مولداً».
records.english: On his statement that the Ashʿarites differ about it: He reports another position chosen by Imām al-Rāzī; Ḥujjat al-Islām also says that it is the position held by most of our school. According to it, inquiry necessarily entails knowledge of the conclusion, without inquiry being a cause in the philosophers’ sense or producing an effect through generation in the Muʿtazilite sense. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On the phrase “there is disagreement among the Ashʿarites”: the writer recalls a further opinion selected by Imām al-Rāzī; al-Ghazālī reports it as that of many among “our associates.” It holds that investigation **entails** knowledge of its conclusion by way of necessity, **without** investigation being the productive cause posited by the philosophers or the generating act posited by the Muʿtazilites. It is not enough to say merely that the knowledge **usually** follows the inquiry; that would return us to the position of customary association. The intended entailment is logical or rational: when the investigator has actually grasped the relevant premises and their implication, the conclusion cannot fail to follow as an item of knowledge. This necessity must not be equated automatically with a necessitating agent's independently producing an effect.

records.title: Does that necessary entailment conflict with divine agency?
records.arabic_anchors: «لو امتنع أن لا يقع بأن لا تتعلق به قدرته واختياره»؛ «كون العلم أثر القادر المختار وجائز الفعل والترك»؛ «جواز الترك بمعنى امتناع ...»؛ «العلم ضروري عند ...».
records.english: The margin tests whether the position can preserve God's being a **powerful agent who chooses**. If saying that the result of sound investigation is necessary means that God could not refrain from granting knowledge even where His power and will did not attach to it, it would not describe the theological position as intended. Yet it is also possible to say that the effect is brought about by a voluntary agent and nevertheless follows necessarily **given the complete supposition under which that agent actually brings it about**. The possibility of refraining must not be understood as the simultaneous occurrence of two contradictory outcomes under precisely the same total conditions. The dispute is therefore over what remains fixed when a speaker asserts the possibility of an act and of its omission. Necessity of **inference** need not abolish divine choice; nor may freedom of choice erase the necessity by which the investigator recognises a valid consequence. **Proof limitation:** The final compact qualifications of “possible omission” are paraphrased and require another Arabic/English line comparison.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Knowledge as certain assent
records.arabic: (قوله لأجل حصول اليقين) إشارة إلى أن في التعليل والمعرفة يعني التصديق اليقيني؛ لأن المعرفة المتعلقة بالجزئي تحصل بإحساسه المستلزم للتصديق اليقيني بوجوده. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لأجل حصول اليقين) إشارة إلى أن في التعليل والمعرفة بمعنى التصديق اليقيني»؛ «المعرفة المتعلقة بالجزئي ... بالإحساس».
records.english: On “for the attainment of certainty”: This indicates that “knowledge” and “recognition” in the explanation here mean certain assent. For recognition concerned with a particular is obtained by sensing it, which entails certain assent to its existence. [End of the printed ruled note.]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On “for obtaining certainty”: the gloss indicates that “knowledge” and “recognition” here mean **certain assent**. Knowledge concerning a particular may be attained through sensation; that is not the debated inferential recognition of God. A predication of certainty and the means by which an object is apprehended must be distinguished.

stage92_source_note.witness: Būlāq 1318 AH printed Volume I (single printed copy, no manuscript collation)

records.title: The theological disagreement
records.arabic: (والنظر في معرفة الله تعالى) أي لأجل حصول اليقين
records.arabic_anchors: «وهذا مبني على سلب الاختيار عنه تعالى علوّاً كبيراً»؛ «(فيه خلاف) بين الأشاعرة والمعتزلة والفلاسفة»؛ «(والنظر في معرفة الله تعالى) أي لأجل حصول اليقين».
records.english: “And investigation with regard to knowing God, exalted is He”: that is, for the sake of obtaining certainty.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: This last position rests on denying freedom of choice to God—exalted is He far above that. “Concerning this there is disagreement” among the Ashʿarites, Muʿtazilites, and philosophers, in the order stated. “Investigation into the knowledge of God, exalted is He” means inquiry **for obtaining certainty**. The predication “is obligatory” follows at the top of I:27; it must not be attributed to the margin on this leaf.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «وهذا مبني على سلب الاختيار عنه تعالى علوّاً كبيراً»؛ «(فيه خلاف) بين الأشاعرة والمعتزلة والفلاسفة»؛ «(والنظر في معرفة الله تعالى) أي لأجل حصول اليقين».
records.stage85_source_caution: Short opening/close of the discussion; other upper clauses remain untranslated.

records.title: Obligatory according to what gives rise to the obligation
records.arabic: أي شرعا إن كان وجوب الواجب المطلق شرعيا وعقلا إن كان عقليا
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله واجب الخ) أي شرعاً إن كان وجوب الواجب المطلق شرعياً وعقلاً إن كان عقلياً»؛ «في شرح المقاصد».
records.english: That is, obligatory under revealed law if the unconditioned duty is itself legally obligatory, and obligatory by reason if that duty is rationally obligatory.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: On “obligatory”: that means **obligatory by revealed law**, if the unconditional obligation whose means are at issue is itself established by law; and **obligatory by reason**, if the principal obligation is rational, as stated in *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid*. Merely saying “obligatory” without identifying the source of the principal duty leaves the point ambiguous.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(قوله واجب الخ) أي شرعاً إن كان وجوب الواجب المطلق شرعياً وعقلاً إن كان عقلياً»؛ «في شرح المقاصد».
records.stage85_source_caution: Lower note on the word “obligatory”; source-register attribution not established.

records.title: The celebrated premise and the cause/condition disagreement
records.arabic: أن إيجاب الواجب المطلق يقتضي وجوب مقدمته المقدورة
records.arabic_anchors: «واعلم أن في هذه المقدمة المشهورة اختلافاً وفي بيانها اضطراباً»؛ «أن المقدور الذي يتوقف عليه الواجب المطلق واجب بوجوبه مطلقاً»؛ «سواء كان سبباً له أو شرطاً»؛ «لو لم يجب لجاز ترك الواجب المتوقف عليه»؛ «مع بقاء التكليف».
records.english: That making an unconditional duty obligatory entails the obligation of its prerequisite insofar as the latter lies within the agent’s power. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: Know that the well-known premise is disputed, and its exposition has been unsettled. Most writers say that what is **within the agent's power**, and upon which an unconditioned duty depends, is itself obligatory **by virtue of that duty**—whether it is called a **cause** or a **condition**. They argue: if the prerequisite were not obligatory, leaving it undone would be permitted. Yet leaving it undone necessarily prevents performance of the commanded act. The agent would then be allowed to omit the very thing he is supposedly commanded to do. Another formulation argues that, if the prerequisite were not obligatory while the duty continued to bind, the commanded act would be demanded in the absence of a necessary condition and thus would be **impossible to perform**. Both forms of the proof assume that the agent can obtain the missing prerequisite; one must not silently carry the claim over to what lies wholly outside his power.

stage91_source_note.location: lower register, centre of discussion of the well-known premise concerning prerequisites
stage91_source_note.scope: Only the Arabic words supplied above have been transcribed; all omitted printed text remains pending
stage91_source_note.limits: The comparative arguments for the competing legal-logical positions are not yet transcribed.

records.title: Disagreement over whether a condition is itself commanded
records.arabic: إن كان شرطاً شرعياً ... لأنه لولا اعتبار الشرع له لوجد مشروطه بدونه، لا عقلياً أو عادياً، إذ لا وجود لمشروطه عقلاً أو عادةً بدونه، فلا يقصده الشارع بالطلب. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «وذهب قوم إلى عدم وجوب مقدمته مطلقاً»؛ «واختاره قوم إذا كان سبباً لا شرطاً»؛ «أما السبب ...»؛ «فكا الشرط»؛ «ليس مقصود الشارع بالطلب».
records.english: If it is a condition established by revealed law ... For, were it not for the Lawgiver’s taking account of it, the thing conditioned by it could occur without it. This is not so for a rational or customary condition, since the thing conditioned does not occur without that condition, whether rationally or according to custom; thus the Lawgiver does not seek that condition by a separate demand. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: Others deny that an indispensable prerequisite acquires a **separate obligation** simply because the principal act is commanded. Some distinguish the **cause** from a **condition**, alleging that a cause is closely connected with producing the effect, whereas a condition only removes an impediment to the act's becoming performable. But the margin replies that the proximity of a cause to its effect, by itself, does not establish that the lawgiver has made that cause a separate object of command. A condition may be indispensable while its attainment remains a distinct question. The parties must distinguish the **legal object commanded** from the **means through which it can be performed** and from the circumstances under which the obligation is first activated.

stage93_source_note.limitation: Selection from the discussion of a legal condition versus a rational or customary condition; intervening words omitted.

records.title: Conditional obligation, absolute obligation, and permission to omit the means
records.arabic_anchors: «فالأشهر جواز الترك»؛ «الوجوب بالشرط»؛ «أمر الأصل»؛ «استلزام إيجاب الذي يجب بمقدمته ... وجوب مقدمته»؛ «كما هو الظاهر».
records.english: If a duty is itself **conditional**, absence of the condition may mean that no present obligation arises; that cannot be treated as identical to leaving undone a necessary means **after** an unconditional duty is already binding. The marginals test a formulation that says the lawgiver's demand for an end indirectly requires the indispensable means, without specifying those means as separate ends of worship. On another formulation, absence of an explicit command concerning the means allows the actor to leave them aside, which would undermine the effect of the principal obligation. Whether that conclusion follows depends on what “permitted to omit” means. If omission of the means is permitted **as a means of omitting the commanded end**, the position is inconsistent with the end remaining obligatory. If, instead, the text is silent regarding a **second independent command**, there is no contradiction merely on that account. The argument continues on I:28, and its full proof turns on the scopes of **obligation**, **condition**, and **permission**. The margins are **not** silently assigned to Muḥammad Wasīm.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Conclusion of the main-text sentence
records.arabic_anchors: «لوجوده (واجب)».
records.english: “... [investigation for establishing] His existence **is obligatory**.” The text closes the sentence started on I:26. **No further principal commentary is printed on I:27**: the rest of the page is the separately printed marginal debate.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Distinguishing non-obligation from the permitted omission of a prerequisite
records.arabic: فلا يكون قول القائل بعدم الوجوب واقعاً على طرف النقيض، مع أنهم اعتبروهما نقيضين. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «التعليلات»؛ «فلا يكون قول القائل بعدم الوجوب واقعاً على طرف النقيض»؛ «إمام الحرمين»؛ «وجوب مقدمة ... بتحصيل ذلك الذي بدونها أولاً».
records.english: Thus the assertion of the person denying obligation would not stand on the opposite side of a contradiction, although they have treated the two assertions as contradictories. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: These explanations do not show that everyone who denies a **separate obligation for the prerequisite** contradicts everyone who says the prerequisite must be procured. Much of the dispute turns on a change in the proposition's subject. The attributed explanation of the position of Imām al-Ḥaramayn concerns the duty of acquiring **an indispensable condition that the lawgiver requires the agent to bring about**, not the wholly general assertion that every condition on which a command depends must always be under a prior independent command. If the condition is not within the agent's control, or if the end has not yet become binding, the earlier proof cannot be applied without qualification. This is why the marginal writer resists treating the different formulas as a simple pair of contradictories.

stage93_source_note.limitation: Opening of a paragraph criticizing equivocation over what is claimed to be obligatory.

records.title: No contradiction between an unconditional duty and the need for means
records.arabic_anchors: «لا يلزم أن يكون الوجوب مشروطاً بالمقدمة»؛ «عدم الوجوب للمقدمة»؛ «التكليف بما لا يطاق»؛ «التكليف بالواجب الذي بدون وجود المقدمة»؛ «إطلاق الواجب المطلق».
records.english: The fact that the commanded action cannot occur **without** its prerequisite must be distinguished from saying that its **being obligatory** depends on the prior attainment of that prerequisite. To command the act **without allowing the existence of its indispensable means** would indeed be to demand what cannot be done. But commanding the act while not separately declaring the prerequisite obligatory is another proposition. Silence about a separate command does not establish that the means may be left unprocured; likewise, the general command does not by itself specify each candidate means and whether it is necessary in the relevant case. The margin criticizes arguments that alternate between these senses of a “conditional” or “unconditional” duty without notice.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: What the expression “the capable prerequisite” excludes
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أمر مقدور الخ)»؛ «يتعلق به القدرة أو غير فعل»؛ «(قوله المعرفة الواجبة الخ)»؛ «العلم بالقادر»؛ «متعلق الخطاب».
records.english: The qualification “a matter within one's power” is not idle. An indispensable background circumstance which the agent cannot bring about is not commanded in the same manner as an accessible act of preparation. In certain examples, an agent's power is related to an actual performance rather than to every antecedent condition of that performance; the terminology must follow the thing that the command **addresses**. Likewise, in the phrase “obligatory knowledge,” the obligation concerns the attainment of recognition of God. When examination is the available means for a legally accountable person to reach it, the dispute is whether that available means is itself commanded **as a means** and whether its necessity can be inferred from the obligation of the end. The closing marginal clause introduces the qualifications to “unconditional obligation” taken up in I:29. **Reading caution:** Compact source expressions regarding capability and addressee remain to be individually transcribed and proofed.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Proof from texts, consensus, and the agent's power
records.arabic: (والإجماع) واتفاق الأمة
records.arabic_anchors: «(بالنص) أي الكتاب والسنة (والإجماع) واتفاق الأمة على وجوبه»؛ «(ولكونه) أي النظر أمراً مقدوراً»؛ «(مقدمة للمعرفة الواجبة عند ذلك)».
records.english: “And consensus”: the agreement of the community.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: Investigation is obligatory “by the [revealed] text”—that is, scripture and the Sunna—“and by consensus,” meaning the community's agreement on the obligation, “and because it”—investigation—“is a matter within one's power, and a prerequisite of the knowledge that is obligatory.” The last clause presupposes the argument over **obligatory means**, developed throughout the extensive marginal commentary on I:27–29. The sentence at the bottom of the upper register continues immediately into the top of I:29.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(بالنص) أي الكتاب والسنة (والإجماع) واتفاق الأمة على وجوبه»؛ «(ولكونه) أي النظر أمراً مقدوراً»؛ «(مقدمة للمعرفة الواجبة عند ذلك)».
records.stage85_source_caution: Only the clause introducing the consensus proof; the rest of the printed argument is not transcribed.

records.title: Objections to an obligation established by text and consensus
records.arabic: (قوله أي بالنص والإجماع إلخ) قد منع قيام الدليل على وجوب المعرفة بالنظر. أما النص فلا، فمثل قوله تعالى: «فاعلم أنه لا إله إلا الله» ليس بقطعي الدلالة، إذ الأمر قد يكون لغير الوجوب. وأما الإجماع فلأنه ليس بقطعي السند، إذ لم ينقل تواتراً. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أي بالنص والإجماع الخ)»؛ «فاعلم أنه لا إله إلا الله»؛ «ليس بقطعي الدلالة»؛ «بل يدعي الخصم الاكتفاء بالتقليد»؛ «وأجيب بأن الظن كاف في الوجوب الشرعي»؛ «دليل إجمالي»؛ «فرض عين ... فرض كفاية».
records.english: On his words “that is, by scriptural text and consensus”: the establishment of proof that knowledge must be acquired by inquiry has been denied. As for the scriptural text, an expression such as the Exalted One’s “Know that there is no deity but God” is not decisive in signification, since an imperative may be employed for something other than obligation. As for consensus, its transmission is not definitive, since it has not been conveyed through mass transmission (tawātur). […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: On “that is, by scripture and consensus”: it has been denied that proof has been established that **knowledge must be obtained by investigation**. As to the scriptural text, the Almighty's saying, “Know that there is no deity but God,” is not decisive as a proof of obligation: the imperative is not invariably employed for obligation. As to consensus, the objection is that its transmission in this particular matter is not decisive. The opponent claims that **uncritical reliance on authority** suffices, pointing out that the Companions accepted professions of faith from common people without demanding the procedures of learned disputation, verification, and demonstration. The answer is that a **probable indication** may suffice to establish an obligation of religious law, and the Companions' acceptance of ordinary believers does not show that those believers lacked every proof. They could possess recognition resting on **general indications**. The margin therefore distinguishes two demands: possessing an elementary indication that raises one above mere imitation is an **individual duty**; possessing sufficiently detailed argumentation to remove sophistical doubts is a **collective duty**. The source signals that a related question returns towards the close of the book. This is a *reported dialectic*, not an editorial declaration that all Muslims actually carried out formal demonstrations.

stage93_source_note.scope: bounded printed span; all untranscribed passages signalled by ellipses
stage93_source_note.limitation: The opening objection to scriptural and consensus-based evidence; the remaining arguments about the Companions are not entered.

records.title: The disputed extension of “unconditional”
records.arabic: (قوله للواجب المطلق إلخ) ليس معنى الواجب المطلق ما يكون وجوبه على جميع التقادير والأحوال، وإلا لم يكن شيء من الواجبات واجباً مطلقاً، فإنه ما من واجب إلا وهو مقيد ببعض التقادير. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «ليس معنى الواجب المطلق ما يكون وجوبه على جميع التقادير والأحوال»؛ «ما من واجب إلا وهو مقيد ببعض التقادير»؛ «تحصيل الحاصل»؛ «لو نظر وجبت المعرفة وإلا فلا»؛ «مقيد بوجود مقدمتها ... لا بوجوب مقدمتها».
records.english: On his words “for the unconditional obligation”: “unconditional obligation” does not mean an act whose obligatoriness holds under every supposition and circumstance. If it did, nothing would be unconditionally obligatory, for there is no duty that is not qualified by some conditions. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: On the expression “the unconditionally obligatory”: it does **not** mean an act obligatory under every conceivable supposition and circumstance. That would leave nothing whatsoever unconditionally obligatory. Every duty is subject to some qualifications; at the least, a duty is not imposed anew under the supposition that precisely what is demanded has already been performed, since this would amount to **acquiring what has already been acquired**. Rather, the relevant point is that a duty is not conditioned, *as regards its becoming binding*, upon independently requiring the agent first to acquire the prerequisite. The disputed analysis can be expressed by saying that the knowledge whose obligatory character is being discussed may be obligatory whether the person has investigated or has not yet investigated, while **the emergence of the knowledge** still depends on the investigation in its proper order. The margin disputes a formula that makes the main duty obligatory only if its prerequisite has already occurred; in that formula, the prerequisite's **existence** is treated as a condition for the obligation, which is the reverse of the unrestricted duty being analysed. **Reading caution:** The dense final lines distinguish several scopes of “conditioned on a prerequisite,” and their pronoun references require a final Arabic transcription before this can be classed as literal complete.

records.title: What an unconditional obligation means
records.arabic: المراد بالواجب المطلق أن لا يكون وجوبه مقيدا بما يتوقف عليه
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله الواجب المطلق) المراد بالواجب المطلق أن لا يكون وجوبه مقيداً بما يتوقف عليه، كتوقف الزكاة على حصول النصاب منه».
records.english: What is meant by an unconditional obligation is that its becoming binding is not conditioned upon what its performance requires.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: On his words “the unconditional obligation”: what is intended is an obligation **whose binding force is not conditioned upon a prerequisite required for its performance**, unlike the obligation of the alms-tax, which is conditioned upon the attainment of the legally specified minimum holding (*niṣāb*). The note concerns the **condition for a duty's becoming binding**, not the claim that duties can be performed without their means.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(قوله الواجب المطلق) المراد بالواجب المطلق أن لا يكون وجوبه مقيداً بما يتوقف عليه، كتوقف الزكاة على حصول النصاب منه».
records.stage85_source_caution: The ruled note goes on to compare this with the threshold condition for obligatory alms; attribution remains unassigned.

records.title: Closing the proof from the obligatory means
records.arabic_anchors: «أي بالنص والإجماع والمقدور الذي كان مقدمة وهو قوله فالواجب المطلق».
records.english: —that is, **by scriptural text and consensus**, and with respect to the prerequisite **within one's power**, which was the earlier premise of the argument, namely the statement: “Therefore the unconditional obligation …” The sentence is continued from I:28 and the following upper argument begins on I:30. One must not make this isolated upper line into a separate complete proof.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: What is presupposed in demanding inquiry into a miracle
records.arabic: (قوله وفي جميع ما يتوقف ثبوته على ثبوته إلخ) أي جميع ما يتوقف ثبوت الشرع على ثبوته، والحاصل أن الشرع موقوف على ثبوت الصانع وإرساله الرسول والتصديق له بالمعجزات الباهرة التي تتوقف على صفاته تعالى، وثبوت كل ذلك نظري موقوف على النظر. فلو قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: انظر في هذه الأمور التي من جملتها المعجزات ليثبت عندك الأحكام الشرعية التي منها وجوب النظر في معرفته تعالى، فله أن يقول: لا أنظر، إلخ. إن قيل: هذه المقدمة غير صحيحة لأن النظر لا يتوقف على وجوبه إذ النظر يمكن الحصول وإن لم يجب؛ قلنا: نعم، لكن الكلام في إلزام النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم النظر، وإلزامه إنما يصح إذا كان واجباً، ضرورة أنه لا إلزام على غير الواجب. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وفي جميع ما يتوقف ثبوته على ثبوته الخ)»؛ «إن الشرع موقوف على ثبوت الصانع وإرساله الرسول والتصديق له بالمعجزات الباهرة»؛ «فلو قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم انظر في هذه الأمور ...»؛ «النظر يمكن الحصول وإن لم يجب»؛ «إلزام النبي ... على غير الواجب».
records.english: On his words “and in everything whose establishment depends on its establishment”: that is, everything upon which the establishment of revealed law depends. In sum, revealed law depends upon establishing the Creator, His sending of the Messenger, and confirming his truthfulness by manifest miracles, which in turn depend upon the divine attributes. Establishing all this is a matter of inference and depends upon inquiry. If the Prophet—God bless him and grant him peace—were to say, “Examine these matters, among them the miracles, so that legal rulings are established for you, including the obligation to inquire into knowledge of the Exalted One,” the addressee could reply, “I shall not inquire,” and so on. If someone objects that this premise is unsound because inquiry does not depend upon its being obligatory—one can inquire even when it is not obligatory—we answer: Yes, but the discussion concerns the Prophet’s binding demand that inquiry be undertaken. Such a demand is valid only if it is obligatory, since there is no binding imposition of what is not obligatory. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: On his words “and in everything whose establishment depends upon its establishment”: the establishment of the law is dependent on establishing the Creator, His sending a messenger, and the messenger's truthfulness through manifest miracles. The proofs of those matters involve inquiry. If the Prophet tells someone to examine the matters—including the miracle—upon which the authority of religious prescriptions depends, that person might object: “I shall not investigate until this religious obligation is proved to me.” But the authority claimed for that obligation is itself among the things that require inquiry. The reply acknowledges that **inquiry can take place without its having first been commanded**: what is possible to perform need not already be obligatory. Yet the point at issue is the Prophet's **binding demand** for inquiry; an obligation to comply does not follow from mere feasibility. The marginal argument therefore separates a person's ability to investigate from the authority to **compel** him to investigate. It concludes by returning to the danger of making the sending of prophets ineffective under the proposed circular dependency. **Reading caution:** The closing phrase about the mission's futility is compressed in the printed line and should be rechecked before publication as a verbatim quotation.

records.title: Why fear has an obligatory force on the opponent's account
records.arabic: (قوله خوف العقاب) يعني أن الخوف من العقاب على ترك معرفة الله ضرر ... وبوجود المعرفة ينتفي ذلك الخوف فكانت واجبة
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله خوف العقاب) يعني أن الخوف من العقاب على ترك معرفة الله ضرر ... فكانت واجبة».
records.english: On “fear of punishment”: fear of punishment for failing to know God is a harm. […] When that knowledge is attained, the fear is removed; hence such knowledge is obligatory. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: On “fear of punishment”: the feared punishment for abandoning recognition of God constitutes the apprehension of harm. Because obtaining knowledge removes that fear, the Muʿtazilite argument treats knowledge, and what is needed to obtain it, as obligatory. The note explains the **rational avoidance-of-harm inference**; it does not independently establish that this particular danger is actual.
