records.title: Positions concerning the source of obligation
records.arabic: (وعند المعتزلة) النظر في معرفة الله تعالى واجب
records.arabic_anchors: «(وعند المعتزلة) النظر في معرفة الله تعالى واجب لكَوْنِه مقدمة للمعرفة الواجبة»؛ «(لكونها دافعة لضرر) مظنون وهو (خوف العقاب)»؛ «فالوجوب عندنا شرعي وعندهم عقلي».
records.english: “For the Muʿtazilites,” inquiry concerning knowledge of God, exalted is He, is obligatory.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: “According to the Muʿtazilites,” examination directed toward knowledge of God, exalted is He, is obligatory, since it is a prerequisite for the knowledge that is obligatory. That knowledge wards off a harm which is thought possible, namely **fear of punishment**. Thus for us the obligation is **legal/revelatory**, whereas for them it is **rational**. The parenthesized phrases belong to the quoted matn, while the explanatory connectives belong to the sharḥ.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(وعند المعتزلة) النظر في معرفة الله تعالى واجب لكَوْنِه مقدمة للمعرفة الواجبة»؛ «(لكونها دافعة لضرر) مظنون وهو (خوف العقاب)»؛ «فالوجوب عندنا شرعي وعندهم عقلي».
records.stage85_source_caution: This introduces rather than exhausts their argument about rational obligation.

records.title: Their circularity objection against a revealed command to inquire
records.arabic: (خوف العقاب) فالوجوب عندهم عقلي
records.arabic_anchors: «(قالوا لو لم يجب) النظر (بالشرع لما صح)»؛ «(النظر في المعجزة)»؛ «وفي جميع ما يتوقف ثبوته على ثبوته»؛ «(قبل ثبوت الشرع)».
records.english: “Fear of punishment”: on their view, obligation is established by reason.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: They argue: if inquiry were not already obligatory before appeal to revelation, what would justify the demand that one investigate the Prophet's miracle and the other indications on which the establishment of revelation's authority depends? A command of religious law to perform the very inquiry by which the truth of that law is to be established cannot, without circularity, be the **first ground** of the inquiry's obligatoriness. More particularly, the Prophet, blessings and peace be upon him, directs a hearer to the miracle; the hearer might say that he is not obliged to investigate until the obligation has been established by the law, while the authority of that law depends on the examination of the miracle. The opponent thus attempts to derive a **rationally prior** obligation.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(قالوا لو لم يجب) النظر (بالشرع لما صح)»؛ «(النظر في المعجزة)»؛ «وفي جميع ما يتوقف ثبوته على ثبوته»؛ «(قبل ثبوت الشرع)».
records.stage85_source_caution: The printed conclusion contains additional qualifications about punishment and obligation.

records.title: The investigation/obligation regress and competing first duties
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله ولا يثبت الشرع عندي ما لم أنظر الخ)»؛ «(قوله وثانياً الخ)»؛ «الجواب بأن عدم الإلزام ...»؛ «وجوب النظر في نفس الأمر»؛ «وجوب العلم»؛ «فأول الواجبات هو النظر والمعرفة لفظاً ...».
records.english: The gloss reconstructs the opponent's refusal to investigate: if the religious law cannot be established without an inquiry into its proofs, then telling him that he is legally obligated to inquire seems to presuppose what the inquiry is meant to establish. The marginal author replies that the threatened regress depends on conflating the **objective bindingness** of a duty with the person's **awareness of that bindingness**. If what is at issue is knowledge of the legal command, further examination may be needed before one knows it, but it does not follow that there is no duty in the order of things. The margin separately distinguishes rationally knowing that one must investigate, actually investigating, and acquiring the knowledge sought. Since these are not one and the same act, asking which is “first” without indicating the ordering relation produces a verbal dispute. Some schools make **knowledge** first as the end; others **investigation** first as the means; still others the **intention** to investigate, because a deliberate act involves a prior determination. **Reading caution:** The bottom line of the marginal text continues the debate; this paragraph is a connected first-pass reading, not a line-exhaustive verified transcription.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: What exactly depends on proving the law?
records.arabic: (قوله بأن التوقف على ثبوت إلخ) وفي نسخة: «فإن التوقف على النظر»، فلا يحتاج إلى تقدير الثبوت عند المكلف. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله بأن المتوقف على ثبوته الخ)»؛ «وفي نسخة بأن المتوقف على النظر ...»؛ «فلا يحتاج إلى تقدير الثبوت عند المكلف».
records.english: On “because it depends on its establishment, etc.”: In one copy the wording is “for the dependence is upon inquiry,” in which case there is no need to supply “establishment for the legally responsible person.” [End of the printed ruled note.]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On “what depends on its establishment”: a separate note refers to a **different printed wording** in another copy: “what depends on investigation.” On that reading, the sentence requires no supplementary insertion of “the law's establishment *for the legally responsible person*.” This is a reported reading, **not a manuscript variant verified in Stage 76**. The note should remain distinct from the principal commentary.

stage92_source_note.witness: Būlāq 1318 AH printed Volume I (single printed copy, no manuscript collation)
stage92_source_note.scope: entire visually bounded ruled note, first transcription pass
stage92_source_note.limitations: A PRINTED statement “in one copy”; we have not inspected that second copy, so this is not a collated manuscript variant.

records.title: Can someone refuse inquiry until inquiry has been proved obligatory?
records.arabic: ولا يثبت الشرع عندي ما لم أنظر لأن ثبوته نظري
records.arabic_anchors: «ولا يثبت الشرع عندي ما لم أنظر لأن ثبوته نظري»؛ «(ورد) أولا ...»؛ «لأن النظر وإن كان واجباً عقلاً لكن وجوبه ليس ضرورياً بل كان نظرياً»؛ «لا أنظر ما لم يجب ولا يجب ما لم أنظر».
records.english: The revealed law is not established for me unless I investigate, for its establishment rests on inquiry.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The interlocutor says: “Religious law is not established for me until I investigate, for establishing its authority is itself a matter of inference.” The answer begins by challenging the alleged priority. Even if inquiry is deemed obligatory by reason, the **judgment that it is obligatory** need not be a primitive self-evident judgment; it can itself be established inferentially. The sceptical hearer could then say, even to the Muʿtazilite: “I shall not investigate until doing so is proved obligatory, and it cannot be proved obligatory until I investigate.” Merely moving the duty from revelation to reason does not automatically remove the threatened circle. The lower notes take up the force of this counter-objection.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «ولا يثبت الشرع عندي ما لم أنظر لأن ثبوته نظري»؛ «(ورد) أولا ...»؛ «لأن النظر وإن كان واجباً عقلاً لكن وجوبه ليس ضرورياً بل كان نظرياً»؛ «لا أنظر ما لم يجب ولا يجب ما لم أنظر».
records.stage85_source_caution: This is part of a reported objection about whether investigation can be legally obligatory prior to establishing the law.

records.title: Does inquiry or knowledge come first among the obligations?
records.arabic_anchors: «(الشرع) عند المكلف»؛ «(هو العلم بالوجوب) أي وجوب النظر»؛ «(لا نفس الوجوب)»؛ «(ثم إنها) أي المعرفة (أول) الواجبات المقصودة»؛ «(والنظر فيها) ... (وسيلة إليها)»؛ «فإن أراد أول المعرفة ...».
records.english: The author distinguishes the **obligation itself** from **knowledge of the obligation**. A requirement can be binding without the agent's already having arrived at an explicit demonstration that it is binding; otherwise each needed act would presuppose a prior complete knowledge of its own duty. The inquiry then turns to the expression “the **first duty**”: some mean the first **object intended**, namely recognition of God; others mean the earliest **means to the object**, namely rational examination. Yet a third formulation says that the **first intention to investigate** precedes the actual investigation. The conclusion depends on whether “first” refers to priority **as an aim** or priority **in the process of bringing about the aim**. The last upper clauses continue into I:32.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: What rests on the prior establishment of duty?
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله بل القصد الخ)»؛ «على ما لم يثبت الشرع ...»؛ «(قوله بل يلزم الدور الخ)»؛ «المعرفة بمعنى الجهل بالمطلوب»؛ «القدرة والإرادة»؛ «النظر في نفس الأمر».
records.english: The gloss returns to the concern that, if the authority of law has not been established, the attempt to derive an **obligation to investigate** from a legal command threatens circularity. But it is not necessary that **the agent know the duty's proof** before the duty be binding in itself. Some writers instead take the lack of prior knowledge of the **sought object** to be the motive for investigation: inquiry ordinarily begins with not yet knowing the conclusion, not with a demonstration of the very duty to inquire. The marginal writer distinguishes that epistemic condition from the **power and will** needed to undertake the inquiry. If one calls the earlier conditions “the first obligations,” a further specification of what “first” means is needed; otherwise a disputed logical ordering is merely restated as a practical command.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: Is transmitted certainty dependent on rational preliminaries?
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لأن يلزم الدور الخ)»؛ «ثبوت النقل من العلم بصدق الناقل المبني على ثبوت الصانع وبعثة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ودلالة المعجزة»؛ «بطريق إثباته في العقل دون ...».
records.english: The argument concerning revelation is sharpened: certainty that a report is authoritative rests on knowledge that the reporter is truthful; in the prophetic case this includes the existence of the Creator, the sending of the Messenger, and the evidentiary significance of miracles. These are not established merely by repeating the report whose authority is under examination. Thus the **reliability of transmission**, as used in theological proof, presupposes some prior rational considerations. The note ends with a transition to the general philosophical topics opened on I:33. **Reading caution:** The final lower words run into a heavily crowded line; the summary here does not claim a complete diplomatic extraction or conclusive wording.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.

records.title: The sense of a “prior intention”
records.arabic: (قوله بل القصد إلخ) وربما يظهر للنفس ما يصير سبباً باعثاً على القصد، أي العزم المصمم، وربما يكون ذلك بالكسب، فيجوز أن يكون واجباً على المكلف. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله بل القصد الخ)»؛ «وربما يظهر للنفس ما يصير مبدأ باعثاً على القصد»؛ «القصد أعم ...».
records.english: On “rather, the intention, etc.”: Something may appear to the soul which becomes a cause prompting intention—that is, a settled resolve. That may itself be acquired through effort, and hence may be obligatory for the legally responsible person. [End of the printed ruled note.]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On “rather, the intention”: a preliminary apprehension can arise in the soul and become the motive that prompts intention. This should not be made into an infinite series of **deliberate intentions before every intention**; the earlier occurrence is not necessarily an act of intending in the same sense as the later one. The note therefore distinguishes a first prompting apprehension from the deliberate intention to proceed with rational inquiry.

stage92_source_note.witness: Būlāq 1318 AH printed Volume I (single printed copy, no manuscript collation)
stage92_source_note.scope: entire visually bounded ruled note, first transcription pass
stage92_source_note.limitations: Entire short ruled band, visually proofed once against the Būlāq facsimile only.

records.title: Differing accounts of the first obligation
records.arabic: وإلا فلا نزاع في أن أول الواجبات النظر لتوقف المعرفة عليه
records.arabic_anchors: «الواجبات مطلقاً وإلا فلا نزاع في أن أول الواجبات النظر لتوقف المعرفة عليه»؛ «(والدليل) هو ما يمكن أن يتوصل بالنظر فيه إلى حكم»؛ «(جازم أو غير جازم)»؛ «(وقد خص) بالحكم (الجازم في مقابلة الأمارة)».
records.english: Otherwise there is no dispute that inquiry is the first among the obligations, because knowledge depends upon it.
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage85_prior_overview: —[if one speaks of the first of] the obligations **without further qualification**; otherwise there is no disagreement that investigation precedes knowledge in the order of **the means required for obtaining it**. “Proof” is then defined as that by the consideration of which one may reach a judgment—whether a **decisive** or a **nondecisive** judgment, according to the broader usage. The expression “proof” is also employed more strictly for what brings about a **decisive judgment**, in contrast with an *amāra*—an indication that yields probability. The notes explain why the broader and narrower uses should not be silently collapsed.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «الواجبات مطلقاً وإلا فلا نزاع في أن أول الواجبات النظر لتوقف المعرفة عليه»؛ «(والدليل) هو ما يمكن أن يتوصل بالنظر فيه إلى حكم»؛ «(جازم أو غير جازم)»؛ «(وقد خص) بالحكم (الجازم في مقابلة الأمارة)».
records.stage85_source_caution: The passage qualifies a distinction among kinds of obligation; preceding provisos are not translated here.

records.title: Rational proof and reliable report
records.arabic: (والدليل) هو (ما يمكن أن يتوصل بالنظر فيه إلى حكم) جازم أو غير جازم. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(على عقل) وسماع من الخبر الصادق»؛ «(والا) يتوقف شيء منه عليه»؛ «(عمومة القرآن القطع)»؛ «(ولازم بالحكم)»؛ «(لا يثبت إلا بالعقل)».
records.english: “Proof/evidence” is “that by examining which it is possible to arrive at a judgment,” whether decisive or not decisive. […]
notes: Source image examined, selected anchors checked where legible. Long Arabic gloss not fully transcribed. No independent second source proof.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: A proof is divided into **rational evidence** and evidence transmitted from **truthful report**. The text invokes the Qurʾān and transmitted reports and distinguishes the grounds on which their evidentiary force is established. An argument from report cannot simply bypass reason altogether: the conditions that make an utterance *reliable evidence* must themselves be known, while some of those conditions are established through rational investigation. Conversely, the fact that reason supplies indispensable premises does not erase the distinct evidentiary role of transmission. **Reading caution:** Several short connectors in the crowded upper printing need a second exact transcription; these English clauses preserve the argumentative order, not an independently certified Arabic critical text.

stage93_source_note.scope: bounded printed span; all untranscribed passages signalled by ellipses
stage93_source_note.limitation: Definition in the printed upper text. The subsequent discussion of transmitted evidence and levels of certainty remains untranslated.

records.title: The possibility of demonstrations in this general science
records.arabic_anchors: «التعقل والتوقف الشيء على نفسه»؛ «لكن ينبغي أن يعلم أن ذلك إنما هو فيما يقصد منه حصول القطع»؛ «بمجرد إفادة الظن»؛ «التواتر نظرياً واستدلالياً»؛ «(قوله من الواجب والجوهر والعرض الخ)».
records.english: The margin returns to a methodological warning: if the act of arriving at knowledge required, as a necessary prior condition, the very knowledge to be acquired, the inquiry would be circular. But the objection must be qualified by the **epistemic aim** of a proof. An argument intended to produce certainty is not the same as an indication that yields only probability. Some scholars regard the cognition established by recurring reports or testimony as depending on intellectual attention to particular conditions, while others take its force more immediately. The writer cautions against using the uncertainty of a particular example to reject the whole field of demonstrations. In the ensuing discussion of existents, the categories “Necessary,” “substance” and “accident” serve as a survey of what can be considered; they do not imply that every shared predicate is an independently existing universal.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Why these matters precede the special inquiries
records.arabic: (قال رحمه الله الباب الثاني في الأمور العامة) لما أورد كلامًا مختصًّا بواحد من الواجب والجوهر والعرض في باب احتاج إلى باب لمعرفة الأحوال المشتركة
records.arabic_anchors: «(قال رحمه الله الباب الثاني في الأمور العامة)»؛ «لما أن فيما يختص بواحد من الواجب والجوهر والعرض ما يحتاج إلى باب معرفة الأحوال المشتركة»؛ «الوجود والعلية أو بين الاثنين».
records.english: On “Chapter Two: General Matters”: having set out in separate chapters discussions specific to the Necessary, substance, or accident, he required a chapter for knowing the states they have in common. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage91_prior_working_overview: On the author's heading “General Matters”: the reason for examining them here is that the discussions specific to the Necessary, substances or accidents depend upon an earlier investigation of concepts common among different kinds of existent. Existence and causality are obvious examples, while other concepts apply to two of those kinds or concern the contrast between them. The note is a justification of **the sequence of inquiry**, not another independent proof of the particular theses to follow.

stage91_source_note.scope: Only the Arabic words supplied above have been transcribed; all omitted printed text remains pending
stage91_source_note.limits: The printed examples of conditions shared by all three or pairs are not yet transcribed.

records.title: Transition from logic to general metaphysics
records.arabic: العقائد وإثبات مباحث أخرى تتوقف عليها العقائد فهذا أوان الشروع في المقاصد
records.arabic_anchors: «العقائد وإثبات مباحث أخرى تتوقف عليها العقائد فهذا أوان الشروع في المقاصد فنقول»؛ «(الباب الثاني في الأمور العامة)».
records.english: [Having set out] doctrines and the establishment of other investigations upon which doctrines depend, it is now time to begin the principal objectives.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The discussion has established [the preliminary instruments for examining] articles of belief and other matters upon which such articles depend. It is now time to turn to the principal objectives. The text therefore announces **Book Two: General Matters** (*al-umūr al-ʿāmma*), that is, questions which recur in the investigation of existence and do not belong exclusively to one special kind of thing.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «العقائد وإثبات مباحث أخرى تتوقف عليها العقائد فهذا أوان الشروع في المقاصد فنقول»؛ «(الباب الثاني في الأمور العامة)».
records.stage85_source_caution: The quoted text begins in mid-sentence from the previous printed page.

records.title: The scope and divisions of *al-umūr al-ʿāmma*
records.arabic: الباب الثاني في الأمور العامة
records.arabic_anchors: «الشاملة للموجودات بأسرها من الواجب والجوهر والعرض كالوجود والوحدة»؛ «فإن كل موجود وإن كان كثيراً له وحدة ما باعتبار»؛ «وكثرة الموجودات»؛ «كالإمكان الخاص والحدوث والوجوب بالقيد والكسرة والعلية والمعلولية»؛ «(تصور الوجود)».
records.english: Chapter Two: On General Matters.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: These general matters include those applicable across what exists—Necessary Being, substance and accident—such as **existence and unity**. Even a many-sided existent has some unity under an appropriate consideration. Other general matters include plurality, possibility in the restricted sense, origination, necessity, and the relationships of cause and effect, though some do not belong to all existents in precisely the same manner. The discussion follows an established pedagogical order and begins with the **conception of existence** (*taṣawwur al-wujūd*). [The main paragraph continues on I:34.]
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «الشاملة للموجودات بأسرها من الواجب والجوهر والعرض كالوجود والوحدة»؛ «فإن كل موجود وإن كان كثيراً له وحدة ما باعتبار»؛ «وكثرة الموجودات»؛ «كالإمكان الخاص والحدوث والوجوب بالقيد والكسرة والعلية والمعلولية»؛ «(تصور الوجود)».
records.stage85_source_caution: Structural chapter title from printed upper frame.

records.title: The scope of general notions
records.arabic: فإن قيل: قد بحث في الباب عما لا يشمل الموجود أصلاً كالامتناع، وما يخص الواجب كالقدم والوجوب، أجيب بأن البحث عن الأول بالعرض لكونه في مقابلة الإمكان، وعن الأخيرين لكونهما من أقسام مطلقهما. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «لا يشمل الموجود أصلاً كالامتناع»؛ «وما يخص الواجب كالقدم والوجوب»؛ «وما يخص الممكن في مقابلة الإمكان»؛ «أما العدم فكذلك عند المتكلمين»؛ «(قوله إنه يتوقف على تصور الوجود الخ)».
records.english: If it is said, “The chapter discusses what does not apply to an existent at all, such as impossibility, and what concerns the Necessary in particular, such as pre-eternity and necessity,” the reply is that the first is discussed incidentally, because it stands opposite possibility, while the latter two are treated because they are divisions of the corresponding unrestricted notions. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: The gloss first considers what qualifies as a **general matter**. Not everything discussed under this heading applies positively to every actual existent; for example, impossibility is a concept concerning what is not actual, while eternity and certain kinds of necessity are specific to the Necessary, and contingency pertains to possible beings. Nonexistence too is a general contrast, but it is not an existent thing of the same order. Philosophers and theologians differ in how they classify such topics. Thus “general” concerns the scope and utility of the inquiry, not the claim that all its subjects are actual substances. On the evidence from the self-evident judgement, the gloss asks whether one means immediate conception or merely a certain affirmation once the terms have been understood.

stage93_source_note.scope: bounded printed span; all untranscribed passages signalled by ellipses
stage93_source_note.limitation: Bounded objection and response on what makes a matter “general”; later examples omitted.

records.title: The logical difference between *badāha* and *muṣādara*
records.arabic: (قوله وأنه يتوقف على تصور الوجود إلخ) فيه أنه إن أريد التوقف على التصور بالحقيقة فممنوع، وإن أريد مطلقاً فلا يفيد المدعى، أعني بداهة تصور الوجود بالحقيقة. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «بديهة تصور الموجود بالضرورة»؛ «(قوله فصادرة)»؛ «إن أراد بديهة الحكم»؛ «بداهة جميع أجزائه»؛ «العلم بالمركب»؛ «جميع أجزائه».
records.english: On “that it depends upon conceiving existence”: if dependence upon conceiving its real nature is meant, this is denied; but if dependence in an unrestricted sense is meant, it does not establish the claim, namely that the conception of existence in its real nature is self-evident. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: A judgement may be self-evident *once its terms are understood*, while understanding those terms can require earlier attention. The objection therefore rejects an **equivocation** between an evident proposition and an evident conception. If the original argument assumes that the constituent notions are already self-evident, it has assumed what it seeks to prove; if it means only that the combination yields an immediate assent, the proof is insufficient. The marginal author also asks about the difference between grasping the **whole proposition** and grasping each of its **parts**, and why certainty of the former should be thought to entail separate certainty concerning each part. The beginning of the next page continues this line of criticism.

records.title: Existence and nonexistence must already be conceived
records.arabic: فإن قولنا الشيء إما موجود أو معدوم تصديق بديهي
records.arabic_anchors: «ضروري»؛ «فإن قولنا الشيء إما موجود أو معدوم تصديق بديهي»؛ «وأنه يتوقف على تصور الوجود والعدم فيكون بديهياً»؛ «فإن قلت إن توقفت بديهة جميع أجزائه ...»؛ «وإن زعمت أن الحكم ... بعد تصور الطرفين بديهي».
records.english: For our statement that a thing is either existent or nonexistent is an immediately evident judgment.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The notion of **existence** is immediately intelligible. One argument appeals to the evident truth that “a thing is either existent or nonexistent.” That judgement must involve a conception of existence and nonexistence. But the critic objects: from the evident character of the judgement it does not follow without further qualification that all its constituent conceptions are themselves primitive and immediate. Perhaps the judgement becomes evident only **after** the two sides have been conceived; its being self-evident under that condition would not prove that the conception of either side has no dependence on earlier cognition. The main text records this objection rather than silently treating the initial argument as conclusive.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «ضروري»؛ «فإن قولنا الشيء إما موجود أو معدوم تصديق بديهي»؛ «وأنه يتوقف على تصور الوجود والعدم فيكون بديهياً»؛ «فإن قلت إن توقفت بديهة جميع أجزائه ...»؛ «وإن زعمت أن الحكم ... بعد تصور الطرفين بديهي».
records.stage85_source_caution: The argument distinguishes the immediate judgment from the conception of its component terms.

records.title: Does knowing a composite entail knowing each part?
records.arabic: (قوله هذا التصديق بديهي مطلقاً إلخ) أي بجميع أجزائه كما قرر في شرح المقاصد. (قوله ولا مصادرة إلخ) حاصله أنا نختار أن هذا الحكم بجميع متعلقاته بديهي ولا مصادرة، لأن بداهة المجموع وإن كان متوقفاً على بداهة كل جزء جزء مفصلاً ... […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله هذا التصديق بديهي مطلقاً الخ) أي بجميع أجزائه»؛ «بداهة المجموع»؛ «بداهة كل جزء مفصلاً»؛ «الاستدلال ببداهة العلم ببداهة المجموع».
records.english: On “this assent is absolutely self-evident”: that is, in all its parts, as established in Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid. On “there is no begging of the question”: the gist is that we choose the position that this judgment, together with all its constituents, is self-evident, and there is no begging of the question; for the self-evidence of the whole, even though it depends on the self-evidence of each part taken distinctly ... […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: “This judgement is self-evident without qualification” may be understood as saying that the whole composite judgement, including its constituent terms, is immediately known. The gloss denies that this is simply established: **the immediacy of the whole** cannot automatically serve as evidence for **the immediacy of each constituent part**. One can know an ordered composite under a general description without separately articulating each element's nature. Conversely, awareness of each element does not by itself yield awareness of the full arrangement. So the argument needs to specify whether the parts are taken distributively or under a collective consideration.

records.title: Avoiding a circular proof of the primitive concept
records.arabic: لكن المقصود هنا ليس الاستدلال بتلك البداهة على هذه ... بل المقصود الاستدلال بالعلم ببداهة المجموع على العلم ببداهة الجزء. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «بديهة العلم بجهة المجموع»؛ «الجزء الأول»؛ «يلزم المصادرة»؛ «لا يستلزم المدعى»؛ «بداهة تصوّر الوجود».
records.english: But the intention here is not to argue from that self-evidence to this one ... Rather, the intention is to infer from knowing the self-evidence of the whole to knowing the self-evidence of the part. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: The note tests alternatives: if the self-evidence of the whole is inferred from the self-evidence of its pieces, the conclusion about one such piece is being **assumed**. If the self-evidence of each piece is inferred from that of the whole, a further rule is needed to licence the inference, and that rule has not been established merely by citing the whole. A person may possess an immediate conception of existence, but the proposed proof may fail to demonstrate that fact. The writer distinguishes the truth of the underlying claim from the sufficiency of this particular argument. [The densely printed closing comparison to the conceptual composition of a judgement still requires a line-by-line reinspection.]

stage93_source_note.limitation: Bounded methodological distinction between self-evidence itself and knowledge that something is self-evident.

records.title: The limit of the argument from immediate assent
records.arabic: فلهذا التصديق بديهي مطلقا ولا مصادرة
records.arabic_anchors: «كسبياً فلهذا التصديق بديهي مطلقاً ولا مصادرة»؛ «لأن بديهة مطلقاً في نفس الأمر».
records.english: Accordingly, this judgment is immediately evident without qualification; this is no begging of the question.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The text distinguishes a judgement which is evident without inference from a knowledge which has been acquired. If the judgement is evident *in itself*, the description “self-evident” belongs to its manner of assent; it still does not follow that every preparatory conception has been established without a distinct process. The response to the charge of circularity thus depends on exactly what is being claimed as immediately known.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «كسبياً فلهذا التصديق بديهي مطلقاً ولا مصادرة»؛ «لأن بديهة مطلقاً في نفس الأمر».
records.stage85_source_caution: Selected closing response only; not the whole upper register.

records.title: The cost of inferring existence from existence
records.arabic_anchors: «وجود ضروري وهذا تصوّر وجود خاص فبداهته تستلزم بديهة العام»؛ «لكن أظهر من هذا الاستدلال ... الاستدلال على بديهة تصور العلم»؛ «(قوله ما يتصور منه كسب ... الخ)».
records.english: The marginal commentator observes that a particular case of *existing* may be grasped immediately. Whether that establishes the immediate conception of existence **as a general notion** is another matter. He compares this argument with attempts to demonstrate the primitive intelligibility of **knowledge itself**, and argues that such demonstrations risk presupposing the conception they are meant to establish. Even when a proposition involving existence appears evident, its proof cannot be improved by confusing the immediate recognition of an instance with the logical analysis of a universal.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The relation between primitive conception and demonstrations
records.arabic_anchors: «أن حصول العلم بالوجود ... بديهة تصوّر العلم»؛ «الوجود»؛ «بديهي التصديق»؛ «استدلال»؛ «لا يترتب إلا بأحد الأوجه».
records.english:
An argument which says “I know that something exists” already employs both **knowledge** and **existence**; if the point is to explain how either term is acquired, it must avoid covertly using that very acquisition as a premise. The author accordingly distinguishes a *dialectical illustration* of an immediate concept from a *demonstrative derivation* of it. What can be shown is how the terms behave when used in evident judgements; one should not claim thereby to have proved every part of their intelligibility from something more primitive. The marginal note ends by bringing the discussion toward the common concept of existence on I:37. [The last line of the lower gloss is compressed and remains unverified.]

# Sanandajī, *Taqrīb al-Marām* — Volume I:37–40
## Stage 75 connected first-pass reading: common existence and the Necessary's being

records.title: On “knowledge is not stopped”
records.arabic: (قوله لا يتوقف العلم إلخ) بناءً على أن العلم قد يكون إجمالاً وقد يكون تفصيلاً، وحصول الأول لا يتوقف على حصول الثاني، فيجوز أن يحصل حصول الأول هنا بداهة أجزائه التي منها تصور الوجود. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لا يتوقف العلم الخ) بناء على أن العلم قد يكون إجمالاً وقد يكون تفصيلاً»؛ «حصول الأول لا يتوقف على حصول الثاني»؛ «يجوز أن يجعل حصول الأول هنا ... بديهية أجزائه».
records.english: On “knowledge does not depend, etc.”: This is based on the fact that knowledge may be summary or detailed. Acquiring the former does not depend on acquiring the latter; so here the former may be obtained through the self-evidence of its constituent parts, one of which is the conception of existence. [End of the printed ruled note.]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On “Knowledge is not dependent, etc.”: knowledge may be **summary or general** (*ijmālī*), and it may be **detailed** (*tafṣīlī*). Possession of the former need not depend on prior possession of the latter. The author of this separate small note proposes that an immediate grasp of the whole can coexist with a later detailed apprehension of its parts, and therefore resists moving without qualification from one form of knowledge to the other. The formula at the end is an abbreviated source note, not evidence of a named writer.

records.title: Why understanding a whole does not automatically provide every part
records.arabic_anchors: «الأمر يتوقف على بديهة أجزائه في نفس الأمر»؛ «لكن لا يتوقف العلم ببداهته مطلقاً على العلم ببداهة أجزائه أي كل واحد منها مفصلاً»؛ «لا يتصور منه كسب ...».
records.english: A judgement may depend, in the order of reality, on the intelligibility of its constituents; however, knowledge that the judgement itself is self-evident does **not** necessarily depend on explicitly knowing, one by one, that each constituent is self-evident. The interlocutors dispute whether this rescues the original argument or simply changes its subject. The question is a logical one about the scope of self-evidence and the status of an inferred explanation of what is evident.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The interpretation of definition
records.arabic: والتعريف له بالكون والتحقق والشيئية
records.arabic_anchors: «(والتعريف له) بالكون والتحقق والشيئية»؛ «قصده تفسير مدلول اللفظ»؛ «والبداهة إنما تمنع عن التعريف الحقيقي».
records.english: Its explanation by “being,” “realization,” and “thinghood” …
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The text next discusses “defining” existence through terms such as **being**, **realization**, or **thinghood**. Such words may explain what a speaker means by the word “existence,” but they do not supply an **essential real definition** proving that existence is constituted by prior components. The fact that a concept is immediate rules out a real definitional analysis of that kind; it does not prevent a **lexical clarification** or an explanation of how an unfamiliar expression is used. This point introduces the dispute over whether existence has one common meaning.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(والتعريف له) بالكون والتحقق والشيئية»؛ «قصده تفسير مدلول اللفظ»؛ «والبداهة إنما تمنع عن التعريف الحقيقي».
records.stage85_source_caution: These are lexical glosses rather than a real definition of existence; continuation not entered here.

records.title: Three kinds of commonality
records.arabic: (قوله إلى وجود الواجب) حاصل ما ذكره المصنف على وجه أوضح هو أن الوجود مفهوم واحد مشترك بين جميع الموجودات بوجوه ثلاثة: أحدها أنا نجزم بوجود أمر مع التردد في كل من الخصوصيات. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «الموجودات وجوه ثلاثة أحدها أن يلزم وجود أمر مشترك مع التردد في كل من الخصوصيات»؛ «فإذا نظرنا إلى وجود الممكن ... ممكناً»؛ «المعدوم»؛ «التقسيم إلى الوجود الواجب ووجود الممكن».
records.english: On “to the existence of the Necessary”: stated more clearly, the gist of the author’s argument is that existence is one concept shared by all existents, in three ways. The first is that we can be certain something exists while remaining undecided as to each of its particular determinations. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: The marginal author says the argument from division may be understood in more than one way. When one attends to a possible thing, one can consider its particular manner of being, and also what it shares with others; when one attends to the Necessary, its being has a different determination. The fact that we can divide both under the expression “existence” requires a common *meaning*, not necessarily a common existent genus. Moreover, the distinction between existence and nonexistence must not itself be described as another division into independently existing species of a thing. The different logical statuses of the members must be retained.

stage93_source_note.limitation: Opening of the threefold argument for the conceptual commonality of existence; the remaining two arguments are not included.

records.title: True shared meaning and verbal equivocation
records.arabic: (قوله معنوي) كما عليه الجمهور، إلا أن الوجود عند المتكلمين حقيقة واحدة تختلف بالإضافات إلى الماهيات المختلفة، وعند الفلاسفة حقيقة مختلفة بالذات. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله معنى)»؛ «أن الوجود عند المتكلمين حقيقة واحدة تختلف بالإضافة إلى الماهيات المختلفة»؛ «وعند الفلاسفة حقيقة مختلفة بالذات»؛ «(قوله أو لفظي)»؛ «نسب إلى الشيخ أبي الحسن الأشعري».
records.english: On “shared in meaning”: this is the majority position. Yet for the theologians, existence is one reality differentiated by its relations to various quiddities, whereas for the philosophers it is a reality diversified in itself. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage93_prior_working_overview: On “meaning”: according to one account associated here with certain theologians, existence is one common intelligible content differentiated by its relations to distinct quiddities. Philosophers, the gloss reports, may instead understand particular modes of existence to differ in reality while sharing an abstract predicate. The author distinguishes such positions from the thesis that the term “existence” is **merely homonymous**. He reports an attribution of a stronger difference in the meaning of existence to al-Ashʿarī and asks how it is to be understood, rather than simply accepting that the two doctrines are equivalent. The closing remark on what it means to “join the special to the common” goes on to I:38.

records.title: Shared meaning and division
records.arabic: ثم اختلفوا في أن اشتراك الموجودات في الوجود معنوي أو لفظي
records.arabic_anchors: «أن اشتراك الموجودات في الوجود معنوي أو لفظي»؛ «بأنه على اشتراك معنوي»؛ «وجود (الواجب) ووجود (غيره)»؛ «التقسيم المشترك لا يقال للوجود».
records.english: They then differed as to whether existing things share the meaning of existence, or only a common verbal designation.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The question is whether the things said to exist share the word “existence” merely by homonymy or share an intelligible **meaning**. The position defended here is that existence is said of them through a common meaning, though the particular modes of existence differ. The text identifies several ways to analyze this distinction and warns that the common meaning should not be confused with one numerically identical extramental entity distributed among individuals. The Necessary and what is other than it must both fall under the relevant expression if the division is to be intelligible.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «أن اشتراك الموجودات في الوجود معنوي أو لفظي»؛ «بأنه على اشتراك معنوي»؛ «وجود (الواجب) ووجود (غيره)»؛ «التقسيم المشترك لا يقال للوجود».
records.stage85_source_caution: The following arguments for either position remain outside this selected excerpt.

records.title: The threefold division
records.arabic_anchors: «(بنيه على اشتراك معنوي)»؛ «(صح التقسيم إلى) وجود (الواجب) ووجود (غيره)»؛ «وجود القسمة مشترك بين جميع أقسامها»؛ «كالجوهر والعرض».
records.english: The proof takes the form of a valid **division**: existence is divided into the existence of the Necessary and the existence of others, and the latter admits further divisions, such as substance and accident. A division requires that the divided term be intelligibly common to its members; it does not prove that the thing divided exists as a separate reality alongside all the members. The distinction between a logical common notion and an independent common entity is therefore crucial.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: No external universal is established by common predication
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله بل كان له في كل معنى الخ)»؛ «على تقدير أن يكون مشتركا لفظيا»؛ «خصوصية مختلفة»؛ «المفهوم»؛ «مطلق الماهية والتشخص».
records.english: The gloss differentiates the sharing of an **expression** from the sharing of an intelligible content. A single word may designate entirely different objects, but then it does not provide the common content needed for the proposed division. Conversely, when one grasps the common content of “existence,” one has not thereby established a universal existence outside the mind, over and above the particular existents. The author asks whether specialization is something added in the concept or something constituting each existing thing as that thing. Merely treating particularity as an accident of an independently existing universal would beg the question.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Two questions hidden in “existence”
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله ما اتصف بالوجود)»؛ «(قوله فأي مفهوم من معانيه)»؛ «الوجود بأحد المعاني»؛ «المعنى الاعتباري»؛ «الإنسان».
records.english: On “whatever is qualified by existence”: the question is **which sense** of existence is being predicated. If one means a mental or relational meaning, this can be commonly conceived; if one means the reality by which the individual is actual, it does not follow that every individual actualizes one numerically identical external being. The gloss contrasts those possibilities through the example of “human being” and asks which predicate makes it proper to say that a person exists rather than does not. The final objection continues onto I:39.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: What is shared and what differs
records.arabic_anchors: «لا تتوقف على الوضع والعلم ولذلك لا تختلف باختلاف اللغات»؛ «مع الاشتراك اللفظي»؛ «(الأمر الثاني)»؛ «(يلزم مع التردد في الخصوصية)».
records.english: What is shared in meaning is not established simply by a convention of language; cognition of existence, on this argument, is not confined to the accidental distinctions among languages. Nevertheless, the fact that a term is used in several cases does not by itself prove that those cases contain one and the same external entity. The second argument considers the intelligibility of differences among the **specializations** of existence and the possibility of reflecting on them while retaining a general notion.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Possible, necessary and nonexistent
records.arabic: لو لم يكن الوجود مشتركا معنويا
records.arabic_anchors: «(تمام الحصر في الموجود والمعدوم)»؛ «ولو لم يكن الوجود مشتركا معنويا»؛ «لزم الحصر في قولنا الإنسان إما موجود أو معدوم»؛ «المعدوم».
records.english: If existence were not shared in meaning …
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: An exhaustive contrast such as “the human being is either existent or nonexistent” presupposes that we understand the negation being made. The opponent cannot explain that opposition solely by ascribing unrelated meanings to “existence” in the cases to which it applies. The text also considers the division of what exists into Necessary and possible. But this reasoning must be handled carefully: the terms of a division can be intelligible in the mind even where not every term names something actual outside it.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(تمام الحصر في الموجود والمعدوم)»؛ «ولو لم يكن الوجود مشتركا معنويا»؛ «لزم الحصر في قولنا الإنسان إما موجود أو معدوم»؛ «المعدوم».
records.stage85_source_caution: The consequence is left unfinished here; this is a selected opening clause, not a complete argument.

records.title: What does the denial actually deny?
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله يجوز الاتصاف بالوجود بمعنى آخر الخ)»؛ «مفهوم العدم»؛ «الوجود والماهية هو تغايرهما بحسب المفهوم دون الهوية»؛ «(قوله أي عن الماهية الخ)»؛ «سلب مبدا الاشتقاق».
records.english: The lower commentator says the argument depends on **what it is that is denied**. To say that a possible quiddity is nonexistent is not to deny that the concept of that quiddity can be thought, nor to place an external thing called “nonexistence” where actual existence should be. The difference in meaning between existence and quiddity may warrant denying one predicate of the other in thought, without proving an external quiddity lacking existence. The gloss distinguishes denial of a **derived predicate** from denial of the underlying source or principle of the predicate, and asks whether the inference from the former to the latter is licensed.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Necessary and possible existence remain different
records.arabic_anchors: «الفرق بين معنى الوجود والماهية»؛ «سلب الوجود عن الماهية»؛ «المعنى المصدري الانتزاعي»؛ «المحقق»؛ «الوجود المقابل للعدم».
records.english: The writer returns to the distinction between the abstract verbal or intellectual meaning of existence and the actuality that stands opposite nonexistence. If existence is understood in the abstract derivative sense, it can be conceptually set aside; doing so does not itself establish that the thing's concrete reality is removed or that the thing remains externally real in its absence. If the sense is actual existence, the matter is different. The objection is directed against sliding between these senses while asserting that one and the same entity can be both present and absent. [The final sentence runs into the causal argument on I:40.]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: A shared meaning does not prove that every nonexistent is a thing
records.arabic: لجواز الاتصاف بالوجود بمعنى آخر فلم يكن معدوما ولا موجودا بالمعنى الذي أريد
records.arabic_anchors: «يجوز الاتصاف بالوجود بمعنى آخر فلم يكن معدوما ولا موجودا بالمعنى الذي أريد»؛ «(على زيادته على الماهية ذهنا)»؛ «أن العقل يلاحظ الوجود دون الماهية»؛ «ثم الوجود له (عنها)».
records.english: It might bear the predicate “existent” in a different sense; thus it would be neither nonexistent nor existent in the sense originally intended.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: It is possible for one and the same thing to be spoken of under different senses of “existent”; this does not mean that a thing is at once existent and nonexistent *in the same respect*. An argument that existence is **additional to quiddity in the mind** starts from the intellect's ability to consider existence without considering the particular quiddity, and vice versa. This difference of conception is not yet a proof of two extramental realities.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «يجوز الاتصاف بالوجود بمعنى آخر فلم يكن معدوما ولا موجودا بالمعنى الذي أريد»؛ «(على زيادته على الماهية ذهنا)»؛ «أن العقل يلاحظ الوجود دون الماهية»؛ «ثم الوجود له (عنها)».

records.title: Two arguments for mental distinction
records.arabic_anchors: «(الأول)»؛ «(صح تسلبه) أي الوجود (عنها)»؛ «أي عن الماهية»؛ «فلو كان عينها لما جاز ذلك لامتناع سلب الشيء عن نفسه»؛ «(و) الثاني».
records.english: One argument is that the mind can **deny existence** of a quiddity: a quiddity can be conceived as nonexistent. If existence were identical with the quiddity in every sense, denying it would seem to be denying the thing of itself, which is impossible. The second argument appeals to the distinction between what the mind understands by the quiddity and what it understands by existence; the significance of that distinction is considered across I:39–40. The upper stream is explicit that the thesis under investigation concerns **addition in intellect**, not necessarily an added external accident.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Does giving existence cause a regress?
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لأن جعل الشيء على نفسه الخ)»؛ «الحمل هنا أيضا هو الحمل الاشتقاقي»؛ «لا حمل المواطأة»؛ «حقيقة الوجود ...»؛ «الوجود الزيادة».
records.english: The marginal writer says the alleged self-predication is not always a case of strict identity: the predication in question may be **derivative**, not a claim that the subject and predicate are one in every respect. A quiddity's being qualified by existence is therefore not exactly the same sort of proposition as the quiddity's being identical with itself. Yet if one makes a distinct extramental “existence” into a further thing, it must in turn have existence and the regress returns. The distinction must be located at the level of explanation rather than by multiplying external entities.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Why the possible is not thereby Necessary
records.arabic_anchors: «لزم احتياجه إلى غيره والاحتياج إلى غيره ممكن»؛ «الماهية لا يمكن أن تكون من غير الوجود ...»؛ «وإذ ذاك يكون وجوده نفس الماهية»؛ «فيكون المعنى ...».
records.english:
The gloss presses the objection: if a possible thing's “existence” is merely an intellectual addition, why does it still require an efficient cause, whereas the Necessary does not? The reply must distinguish **dependence on an external cause** from dependence on an independently existing accident named existence. An object whose actuality is given by another is possible, even though its quiddity and concrete existence are not two separately actual items. The Necessary is understood as having no such external causal dependence. The author notes that a purely terminological answer will not suffice; he proceeds to the problem of the Necessary's quiddity and the causal priority of essence in I:41.

records.title: Causation presupposes priority
records.arabic: ولو كان عينا لها فلأن حمل الشيء على نفسه غير مفيد
records.arabic_anchors: «(إفادة محله عليها)»؛ «ولو كان عينها لأفاد المحل الشيء على نفسه»؛ «(و) الثالث (اكتساب ثبوتها)»؛ «يقتقر إلى كسب الوجود»؛ «ثبوت الماهية».

records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh

records.stage85_prior_overview: The third argument concerns the quiddity's acquiring the establishment or actuality which it lacks in itself. If existence were simply the quiddity, would not the cause be causing the thing **as itself**, a peculiar causal self-reference? The argument appeals to the way the thing acquires existence; the analysis of what it is for a cause to confer existence must distinguish a thing's receptive capacity and an efficient agent. The text invokes the notion of “acquiring” being, but it does not follow that a pre-existing quiddity must already occupy the external world as its own causal recipient.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(إفادة محله عليها)»؛ «ولو كان عينها لأفاد المحل الشيء على نفسه»؛ «(و) الثالث (اكتساب ثبوتها)»؛ «يقتقر إلى كسب الوجود»؛ «ثبوت الماهية».

records.title: The theologians' response concerning the Necessary
records.arabic_anchors: «واستدل بها ... اختلاف ثبوت الماهية»؛ «(والحكم على أن حقيقة الواجب وجوده خاص)»؛ «فالوجود عندهم نفس الماهية في الواجب»؛ «قالوا لو كان الوجود في الواجب زائدا على الماهية».
records.english: The theologians have been represented as holding that the reality of the Necessary is its **special existence**. On that interpretation, in the Necessary existence is not additional to a separate quiddity. They argue: if its existence were an added feature of a quiddity, it would depend on something other than that quiddity, which would destroy the claim that it is necessary through itself. The discussion thus turns on whether necessity is explained by the thing's actual being or by an additional attribute that itself needs explanation. The last sentence joins I:41.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The distinction between a possible thing and its existence
records.arabic_anchors: «متغايرين بالمفهوم والاعتبار لكنهما في الخارج موجود له هوية واحدة»؛ «الإمكان الذاتي للوجوب»؛ «غير محتاج إلى غير ذاته»؛ «اتصاف الذات بالوجود».
records.english: A quiddity and its existence can differ in concept and mode of consideration while having a **single identity externally**. There is then no further item outside the mind by whose addition the thing is first made an existent. The gloss warns that an argument from possible existence to necessary existence must not assume the very external duality that is under dispute. If possibility attaches to a thing considered through itself, this does not mean a real quiddity is already present outside the mind, waiting for an extramental accident called existence. Likewise, necessary existence through itself must not be described as though a separately actualized existence were attached to a preceding subject. The discussion concerns how our concepts are applied to what is necessary and what is possible, and whether the proposed distinction is merely intellectual or requires a second actual thing.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: A question about the priority required of causes
records.arabic_anchors: «الممكن الذاتي»؛ «الواجب ما يحتاج في ثبوت الوجود له إلى غير ذاته» [read against surrounding lines: **the exact negation/wording must be checked**]؛ «(قوله تقدم ماهية الممكن الخ)»؛ «القابلة للوجود».
records.english: The gloss further contrasts the possible thing, whose existence is dependent on something else, with that which exists by itself. It distinguishes the priority of an efficient cause from the status of a thing capable of receiving existence: the receptacle cannot simply be treated as an independently existent cause of that same existence. The margin's compressed formulation of the relation between what is necessary through itself and what is dependent on an efficient cause still needs a word-for-word second proof; the distinction is recorded without supplying a fictitious variant.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Separate short note
records.arabic: (قوله هو العلة الفاعلة) دون القابلة، بناءً على أن قيامه بالماهية في الممكن إنما هو ذهناً لا خارجاً كما يأتي. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله هو العلة الفاعلة) دون القابلة بناء على أن قيامه بالماهية في الممكن إنما هو ذهناً لا خارجاً كما يأتي اه منه».
records.english: On “it is the efficient cause”: This is in contrast to a receptive cause, on the assumption that its inherence in the quiddity of a contingent thing occurs in the mind only, not extramentally, as will be explained later. [End of the printed ruled note.]

records.title: Main text, beginning in I:40
records.arabic: الواجب في وجوده محتاجا إلى غيره فلا يكون واجبا
records.arabic_anchors: «الواجب في وجوده محتاجاً إلى غيره فلا يكون الواجب واجباً»؛ «أن تكون نفس الماهية والعلة متقدمة بالوجود على المعلول»؛ «فيلزم تقدم الماهية بالوجود على الوجود وذلك محال»؛ «وأجيب بأن العلة متقدمة ...».
records.english: [If] the necessary existent depended on something else for its existence, it would not be necessary.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: [Were the Necessary to depend for its existence on something other than itself,] the Necessary would be dependent on another and would not be necessary [in itself]. Another alternative is that the very quiddity acts as the cause. But a cause precedes its effect with respect to existence, so this would entail that the quiddity exists prior to its own existence, an impossibility. The reply distinguishes the sort of priority required here. It is the *efficient* cause that must precede the effect in existence, not every condition or receptacle in which existence may be said to obtain. [The text turns to how the possible's quiddity is conceived as a subject for existence; the last clause runs onto I:42.]
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «الواجب في وجوده محتاجاً إلى غيره فلا يكون الواجب واجباً»؛ «أن تكون نفس الماهية والعلة متقدمة بالوجود على المعلول»؛ «فيلزم تقدم الماهية بالوجود على الوجود وذلك محال»؛ «وأجيب بأن العلة متقدمة ...».
records.stage85_source_caution: Source sentence is part of a conditional objection; quoted beginning is already dependent on surrounding words.

records.title: Why an efficient cause must be conceived as existent
records.arabic_anchors: «ما لم يلاحظ كون الشيء موجوداً امتنع أن يلاحظ مبدأ الوجود ومفيداً له»؛ «بخلاف القابل للوجود»؛ «وإلا لزم حصول الحاصل»؛ «ولا العدم وإلا لزم اجتماع النقيضين».
records.english: Before the intellect can consider a thing as the **source or giver of existence**, it must consider that thing as existent. A thing understood merely as receptive of existence is different: it must not be presumed already to have the very existence that it is supposed to receive, for that would amount to bringing about what is already realized. Nor can one simply put it under nonexistence while ascribing to it the standing of an actually existent subject; that risks combining contradictories. The gloss is concerned with the exact stage and sense in which something is called a “subject,” “cause,” or “receptacle,” not the crude claim that a nonexistent thing performs a causal act.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The distinction between an *iʿtibārī* predicate and an external constituent
records.arabic_anchors: «الماهية على التقدير المذكور تصير علة اعتبارية لا خارجية»؛ «القائلين بزيادته»؛ «أقول فتقرر في المباحث السابقة»؛ «الاتحاد في المفهوم»؛ «مغايرة له من حيث المفهوم».
records.english: On this account, the priority assigned to quiddity for the purpose of predicating existence is a priority **within consideration**, not the priority of an independently present extramental efficient cause. Thus the common assertion that existence is “additional to quiddity” must be situated within a precise theory of what the addition means. It need not assert two separate things outside the mind. The marginal critic presses the question of how this can be reconciled with the philosophers' account of the unique Necessary, and with the many possible things whose existence is spoken of in a shared manner. When the Necessary's existence is called identical with its quiddity, this is not simply saying that the *concept* of existence and the *concept* of quiddity are indistinguishable; the argument concerns the reality indicated by each.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The argument and its answer
records.arabic: تقدير إمكانه يحتاج إلى فاعل فيلزم المحال
records.arabic_anchors: «تقدير إمكانه يحتاج إلى فاعل فيلزم المحال»؛ «لكن الوجود عند القائلين بزيادته أمر اعتباري لا يحتاج إلى موجود فلا إشكال»؛ «قائم بنفسه متميز من غيره مخالف لوجود الممكن في حقيقته»؛ «مع تفرده ... بالقيام بالماهية».
records.english: If it were supposed possible, it would require an agent, and the impossibility would follow.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: If the added existence itself had to be a possible existing entity, it would require an agent and the difficulty would recur. But those who say existence is additional [to quiddity] take that addition, in the relevant sense, to be **an intellectual consideration**, not an independently existing entity requiring its own further existence. So the objection does not arise in that form. The Necessary's existence is described as subsisting through itself, distinct from what is other than it and different in reality from the existence of the possible. This is so despite the existence of the possible being conceived as standing in a quiddity. The relevant distinction is between the unique self-subsistence of the Necessary and the possible's mode of dependence, not simply between two things represented by the same universal concept.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «تقدير إمكانه يحتاج إلى فاعل فيلزم المحال»؛ «لكن الوجود عند القائلين بزيادته أمر اعتباري لا يحتاج إلى موجود فلا إشكال»؛ «قائم بنفسه متميز من غيره مخالف لوجود الممكن في حقيقته»؛ «مع تفرده ... بالقيام بالماهية».
records.stage85_source_caution: “It” has an antecedent in the previous discussion of the existence of the Necessary.

records.title: What abstraction cannot mean
records.arabic_anchors: «مع تفرده»؛ «بالقيام بالماهية»؛ «لأن مقتضى الذات الذي لا يتخلف عنه»؛ «فيكون وجود الممكن مجرداً أيضاً وهو باطل»؛ «فلا يرد أن تجرد الوجود عن الماهية ...».
records.english: One must not say that existence, considered through its own nature, is necessarily abstracted from every quiddity; whatever follows essentially from a nature would then accompany it in every case. The possible's existence too would have to be independent of quiddity, contrary to the very contrast being drawn. The possible quiddity, as possible in itself, admits nonexistence; its possibility is not abolished merely by abstractly conceiving its existence. [The upper discourse continues into I:43.]
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Does denying extramental addition deny the quiddity itself?
records.arabic_anchors: «ضرورة توقف وجوده على تجرده»؛ «التجرد ... عن المقارنات»؛ «قائم به في الخارج»؛ «أن ما هو في الخارج زيادة عليه خارجاً معنى تنافيهما»؛ «المعروض له ليس في الخارج شيء واحد».
records.english: The marginal commentator tests the assertion that a quiddity “subsists” and that existence stands in it. A requirement that the thing be separated or individuated does not by itself prove a **second independent being** alongside the individuated thing. If the reality is one outside the mind, the two analyses—“quiddity” and “existence”—may designate it under different considerations without being two substances or an accident and a substance. The critic asks whether the proposed explanation surreptitiously makes one of those conceptual factors actual before the other. Such an account would fail to explain how a single existent has the identity it does.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The whiteness-and-body analogy
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن كان المعروض له ليس في الخارج شيء واحد يطلق عليه البياض والجسم»؛ «بل شيئان كل منهما متحقق على حدة»؛ «لكن لا تسلم إن الماهية مع الوجود بعد عروضها لها ...»؛ «فلا يلزم ما ذكر».
records.english: When a body is white, whiteness and body are not merely two interchangeable names for one individual in the way under dispute: they are distinct grounds of predication, each considered as having its own mode of realization. But one cannot simply transfer this relation to quiddity and existence. The gloss insists on distinguishing the concept of what the thing is from the concept of its being, without inferring that its existence must be another extramental item attached to an already actual quiddity. The analogy therefore needs a careful qualification. [The long final clause continues on I:44.]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Separate short objection
records.arabic: (قوله إذ لا تنفرد إلخ) بناءً على أنه ليس الهوية المتحدة مع الماهية في الخارج، لأنه أمر اعتباري لا تحقق له في الخارج كما هو عند المتكلمين، فافهم. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله إذ لا يتقرر الخ) بناء على أنه ليس الهوية المتحدة مع الماهية في الخارج لأنه أمر اعتباري لا تحقق له في الخارج كما هو عند المتكلمين فافهم اه منه».
records.english: On “since it is not separately established, etc.”: This proceeds on the view that it is not an identity united with quiddity outside the mind: rather, it is a consideration of the intellect, having no extramental realization, as the theologians maintain. Understand this. [End of the printed ruled note.]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
