records.title: The special existence is not the universal concept
records.arabic: فلا يكون واجبا ولا رادا بأن الوجود معلوم بالضرورة وحقيقة الواجب غير معلومة
records.arabic_anchors: «فلا يكون واجباً ولا راداً بأن الوجود معلوم بالضرورة وحقيقة الواجب غير معلومة اتفاقاً»؛ «البحث ليس في الوجود المشترك بل في الوجود الخاص المخالف لسائر الوجودات في الحقيقة»؛ «والمجرد هو الثاني والمعلوم بالضرورة هو الأول».
records.english: [On this view] it would not be necessary; nor is the objection answered merely by saying that existence is immediately known while the reality of the Necessary is unknown.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: [If the possible's existence were separated from quiddity in the same manner,] it would not thereby become necessary, and the objection that “existence is necessarily known, whereas the reality of the Necessary is agreed to be unknown” does not reach the intended point. The discussion is **not about existence as a concept shared by many things**. It concerns the *special existence* differing in reality from all other existences. The existence described as independent or separated [from quiddity] is the latter; the existence grasped necessarily is the former, common notion. They must not be interchanged in the objection.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «فلا يكون واجباً ولا راداً بأن الوجود معلوم بالضرورة وحقيقة الواجب غير معلومة اتفاقاً»؛ «البحث ليس في الوجود المشترك بل في الوجود الخاص المخالف لسائر الوجودات في الحقيقة»؛ «والمجرد هو الثاني والمعلوم بالضرورة هو الأول».
records.stage85_source_caution: The original includes further context on mental distinction and external existence.

records.title: What “inhering in quiddity” signifies
records.arabic_anchors: «ذهناً لا عيناً»؛ «إذ لا يتقرر كل متحقق على حدة في الخارج»؛ «كبياض الجسم»؛ «فإنه قائم في الخارج»؛ «فلا يلزم أن تقوم الماهية ...».
records.english: The possible's existence is said to subsist in quiddity **in the mind, not as two separately actualized things outside it**. One must not picture the quiddity as first possessing an independent extramental existence, and then receiving the accident of existence, like the colour white borne by a body. The illustrative analogy with whiteness is thus qualified. It is the mind that distinguishes what it conceives as the thing and as its being; outside the mind there is no need to posit a second, already existent quiddity that serves as a host for an equally independent existence. “The existence of everything is additional to it ...” passes into the next leaf.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The priority of quiddity and the Necessary's existence
records.arabic_anchors: «الفرق الظاهر بين الصورتين هو أن قيام البياض بالجسم مسبوق بوجود الجسم بخلاف قيام الوجود بالماهية»؛ «الوجود الواجبي عين الماهية»؛ «معنى كون وجود الواجب نفسه»؛ «غير محتاج إلى وجود آخر».
records.english: The obvious difference between the two cases is that whiteness comes to stand in a body whose existence is already presupposed. The supposed standing of existence in a quiddity cannot be treated in the same manner. For the Necessary, saying that existence is its very reality is intended to deny that its being depends on another existence. If every actual existence had to be supplied by some further existence, no existence would ever be explained. It is therefore no objection merely to say that we distinguish the notion of the Necessary's essence from our notion of existence; the point is whether the being of that essence requires some second actual thing.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: A critical test of the explanation
records.arabic_anchors: «إنه غير محتاج إلى وجود آخر يقوم به»؛ «لا معنى للواجب سوى ما يكون تحققه بنفسه»؛ «كان الممكن ... لم يفتقر إلى وجود آخر»؛ «المصنف في شرح المقاصد»؛ «هذا المذهب إلى الضلال البعيد».
records.english: A thing whose existence is through itself does not require a further being to make it actual; that is how the claim about the Necessary is explained. But the marginal writer then presses a difficulty: if “being by itself” merely means not needing a separately added existence in the same way as a possible thing does not require a new extramental item called its existence, the proposed account risks losing the difference between what is necessary and what is possible. The possible still depends on a cause; the Necessary does not. The critic invokes the author's discussion in *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid* and contests the attribution of a particular metaphysical thesis to it. The concluding polemical expression about a doctrinal view being “far astray” is **reported as the marginal writer's claim**, not endorsed here. [Some compressed words before the final formula require checking against a clearer image or second print.]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The end of the rebuttal
records.arabic: وأيضا الماهية المعروضة إما معدومة فمتناقض أو موجودة فدور أو تسلسل
records.arabic_anchors: «وأيضاً الماهية المعروضة إما معدومة فمتناقض أو موجودة فدور أو تسلسل»؛ «ليس كقيام البياض بالجسم»؛ «وجود الواجب له ...»؛ «والوجود المشترك ...»؛ «بالتشكيك».
records.english: Moreover, the quiddity receiving the predicate would either be nonexistent, which is contradictory, or existent, which produces a circle or an infinite regress.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: If the quiddity supposedly receiving existence were **nonexistent**, the position would be contradictory; if **already existent**, the argument would move in a circle or require an endless regress. Hence the addition of existence is not to be understood exactly as whiteness inhering in a body. The Necessary has its special existence, while the common notion of existence can be predicated across things that are not identical in their modes of realization. It is in this setting that the text speaks of the common predicate and of gradational predication (*tashkīk*). The marginal discussion asks what kind of unity this common predicate has, rather than presupposing a single external genus of existents.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «وأيضاً الماهية المعروضة إما معدومة فمتناقض أو موجودة فدور أو تسلسل»؛ «ليس كقيام البياض بالجسم»؛ «وجود الواجب له ...»؛ «والوجود المشترك ...»؛ «بالتشكيك».
records.stage85_source_caution: Selected disjunction within a larger argument about the relation between existence and quiddity.

records.title: The distinction between the shared predicate and its realization
records.arabic_anchors: «هو الوجود المشترك المقول على الوجودات الخاصة (بالتشكيك)»؛ «المحلول في الجوهر أو ...»؛ «كالبياض ... كالحركة»؛ «فالوجود عارض الماهية ... بالتشكيك».
records.english: The existence predicated of particular existences is a **common meaning**, predicated with gradation. If it is spoken of as something “inhering,” the intended inherence varies with the category under consideration; comparison with whiteness and with motion should not be confused with a proof that every particular existence is itself a separately existing recipient of an accident called *being*. The analogy is a way of explaining shared predication despite different instances, and the precise force of “gradation” remains part of the ensuing controversy.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The nominal character of the common predicate
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله جاز كون واحد من الوجودات الخاصة الخ)»؛ «ما ثبت من اشتراك الكل في مفهوم الوجود لا يقتضي تصادق أفراده»؛ «كأفراد الماني من أنواع الحيوانات»؛ «الوجود المطلق صادق على الوجودات الخاصة المختلفة الحقائق».
records.english: The gloss objects that sharing in the **concept of existence** does not require distinct actual existences to coincide or be identical. The common term “animal” can be said of many living kinds without those species becoming one external thing; so “existence,” too, may be said of existences different in their particular realities. But one must distinguish a concept shared by things from a single actual entity shared among them. In such cases, what is common is the mode of predication, not an additional piece of reality lying between the individuals.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Existence, the subject, and the universal
records.arabic_anchors: «الحقيقة الواحدة صادقة على الوجودات الخاصة المختلفة الحقائق»؛ «التواطؤ»؛ «التشكيك»؛ «الموجود»؛ «الوجود لا الوجودات»؛ «كأفراد المفهوم».
records.english: There remains a difficulty if the particular existences are treated as radically different realities and the shared predicate “existence” as a real genus. What is supposed to be common is not literally the same as what individuates each thing. The note asks whether predication here is univocal (*tawāṭuʾ*), gradational (*tashkīk*), or only common in name. The distinction between the concept of “what exists” and the existence of the individual is important: the former is a mental universal, while the latter is the actuality of that individual. The writer then considers the opponent's suggestion that establishing the particular existences requires an additional “being” and rejects inferring a separate accident simply from this language. The argument continues on I:46.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: What the upper text means by “establishment”
records.arabic: (قوله بمعنى الثبوت) مع أن الظاهر أن حمله عليه لا يكون إلا بهذا، وإلا كان لفظ الوجود مشتركاً لفظياً. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله بمعنى الثبوت) مع أن الظاهر أن جعله عليه لا يكون إلا بهذا»؛ «لفظ الوجود مشتركاً لفظياً»؛ «جعل الكون على الوجودات».
records.english: On “in the sense of establishment”: It would appear that predicating it in this sense cannot be done except in this way; otherwise the term “existence” would be purely equivocal. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On “in the sense of establishment”: the marginal writer notes that the interpretation appears unavoidable if the term is to retain a meaning across particular instances. Otherwise “existence” might become a merely equivocal word, with no conceptual unity. But interpreting it this way makes the relation of predicate and subject problematic. A verbal or conceptual distinction alone does not amount to one real item supervening on another.

stage92_source_note.limitations: Only the opening objection in the ruled band. Its further discussion of predicating “being” by derivation remains untranscribed.

records.title: The nature of gradational predication
records.arabic: أن الوجود الخاص لكل شيء إن كان عبارة عن ثبوته
records.arabic_anchors: «فهو له المقول على الوجودات ... بمنزلة العلة»؛ «ليكون الكون عارضاً»؛ «ولا يلزم من ذلك تكثر الوجودات الخاصة»؛ «لأن زيادة العارض لا تستلزم زيادة المعروض».
records.english: If the particular existence of each thing means its being established …
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The predicate common to the particular existences is spoken of according to a gradational or derivative predication. On the account in question, *kawn*—the fact of being—is treated as an accident. It does not follow from its being predicated of many existents that the individual existences themselves multiply in exactly the same way, for multiplicity of the predicate or accident does not entail multiplicity of what bears it. The particular existences are each distinguished in their realities; this is the problem that the common concept has to account for.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «فهو له المقول على الوجودات ... بمنزلة العلة»؛ «ليكون الكون عارضاً»؛ «ولا يلزم من ذلك تكثر الوجودات الخاصة»؛ «لأن زيادة العارض لا تستلزم زيادة المعروض».
records.stage85_source_caution: The full ensuing alternatives are not translated here.

records.title: The accident–substrate difficulty
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن كون واحد من الوجودات الخاصة قائماً بنفسه»؛ «لكن لا يخفى أن الوجود الخاص لكل شيء»؛ «فلا يرد أنه لو كان ... فلا يصح جعل الكون بمعنى الثبوت عليهم»؛ «كالنور على الأنوار».
records.english: If the particular existence of a thing means nothing over and above its **actual establishment**, then saying that being inheres in it risks making the predicate and its subject the same thing under two descriptions. That difference of consideration is insufficient for a real accident standing in a real substrate. If particular existence is a reality besides actual establishment, however, the proposal that *kawn* means establishment when predicated of it becomes obscure. The analogy, “as light is predicated of lights,” cannot simply settle the question; the comparison is continued on I:46.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: How “existence” is used
records.arabic_anchors: «وجود الوجود لفظاً»؛ «حمل الخلاف في الوجود»؛ «المعنى النسبي»؛ «الماهية»؛ «مبدأ الآثار»؛ «المشتق ... مشتق معنوي أو لفظي».
records.english: The marginal writer examines the possibility that the disagreement about the addition of existence is in part **verbal**. Those who assert an addition may be speaking of the relational or mental meaning of existence, whereas those who say existence and quiddity are identical mean the concrete reality which grounds effects. The note then asks whether the common predicate is a genuine conceptual derivative, or only a linguistic extension; how can it be predicated of existences which are supposed to differ in reality? The answer cannot be obtained simply by saying that the word “existence” occurs in both accounts. The sense of the predicate must be specified.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: What follows from the attribution to al-Ashʿarī
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فيعارض النور المطلق)»؛ «(قوله كأنه لهذا قال المعدوم الخ)»؛ «المصنف في شرح المقاصد»؛ «العدم ممتنع على القول بزيادة الوجود».
records.english: On the analogy with unrestricted light, the critic wonders whether the general predicate is superadded to individual lights in external reality, or belongs to them as something the intellect understands. On the suggestion that al-Ashʿarī denied the thinghood of the nonexistent: this may follow if existence is the very reality of the thing; but it does not follow simply from a verbal definition. The note appeals to the author's discussion elsewhere in *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid*, and points out that some interlocutors affirm the **possibility of nonexistent quiddities being things** precisely because they regard existence as additional. The detailed inference continues on I:47.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Distinguishing external reality and an extracted concept
records.arabic: […] كون الوجودات الخاصة موجودة حقيقة، لأن اللازم من ذلك كونها كائنة لا موجودة، لأن الوجود حقيقة فيما هو أثر الفاعل في الممكنات وعين الذات في الواجب تعالى. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «تلك الوجودات الخاصة موجودة بحقيقة لأن لازم ...»؛ «الوجود حقيقة فيها هو أثر الفاعل في الممكنات وعين الذات في الواجب تعالى»؛ «الكون العارض إنما هو بطريق التجوز»؛ «أمر اعتباري انتزعه العقل».
records.english: […] [This would suggest] that particular existences are themselves truly existent. Yet what follows is that they are actual, not that they are [further things] possessing existence: “existence,” strictly speaking, belongs to what is the effect of an agent in contingent things and is identical with the divine essence in the Necessary Existent. […]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: Those particular existences are actual in virtue of their individual reality: in possible things, the reality of existence is the effect of an efficient cause; in the Necessary, it is identical with the essence. To call an intellectually extracted predicate—*kawn* or “being”—an additional existing accident is, on this account, to speak figuratively. The intellect has drawn out a feature from what is genuinely existent. The writer emphasizes that reality as the **principle of effects** must be distinguished from an abstracted consideration to which a similar name is applied. [The small final connective phrase in the ruled note requires a second literal reading.]

records.title: The light analogy
records.arabic: (نفس الماهية) كما نسب إلى الشيخ الأشعري رحمه الله
records.arabic_anchors: «أنوار الشمس ونور القمر ونور السراج مختلفة بالحقيقة مشتركة في عارض النور المطلق»؛ «فما مثاله»؛ «في الكل»؛ «عن الواجب والممكن».
records.english: “Identical with the quiddity,” as has been attributed to Shaykh al-Ashʿarī—may God have mercy upon him.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: The light of the sun, the light of the moon and the light of a lamp differ in reality, yet [it is asserted that] they share the accident or common predicate of “light” without qualification. This supplies the proposed analogy for predicating existence of diverse instances. “In all” means: in the Necessary as well as in the possible. The force of the comparison depends on whether that shared light is an independent accident or a common intelligible description; the printed discussion does not permit those alternatives to be silently identified.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «أنوار الشمس ونور القمر ونور السراج مختلفة بالحقيقة مشتركة في عارض النور المطلق»؛ «فما مثاله»؛ «في الكل»؛ «عن الواجب والممكن».
records.stage85_source_caution: An attribution within the printed commentary, not an independent historical verification.

records.title: The Ashʿarī attribution
records.arabic_anchors: «(نفس الماهية)»؛ «كما نسب إلى الشيخ الأشعري رحمه الله»؛ «وكأنه لهذا قال المعدوم ليس شيئاً».
records.english: Another view makes existence **the very quiddity itself**, a position here attributed to Shaykh al-Ashʿarī—may God have mercy on him. The text suggests that this is why he said that “the nonexistent is not a thing.” The claim is reported as an attribution in the source, not assumed to settle every dispute about what the Ashʿarī school itself teaches.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The critic on existence as an intellectual meaning
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله كأنهم قالوا ... الخ)»؛ «الوجود الصدري الاعتباري»؛ «الماهية»؛ «ليس في الخارج تحقق واحد»؛ «الوجود الاستحقاق» [last printed phrase uncertain].
records.english: The gloss says that some of the reported positions about the nonexistent may have arisen from a failure to distinguish **considered existence** from independently actual existence. One may grant a quiddity mental establishment in order to think about it without thereby positing its actuality in the external world. But the objection remains: if existence is regarded as an added feature, exactly where does the alleged addition take place? If there is no separately actualized existence, one cannot explain the doctrine by making the non-existent quiddity into a real extramental subject already prepared to receive an accident. [An expression near the first lines of the gloss is unclear; the argument is retained provisionally without supplying a conjectural reading.]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Restriction of “one realization”
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فإن نفاه نفسه)»؛ «تحقق هو الموجود لا هو والوجود بتحققين»؛ «أم حاصلها أن المقصود كون وجود الشيء هو أنه إذا عرض الوجود على الماهية»؛ «لم يحصل هناك موجود واحد بوجود واحد»؛ «الاتصاف بالوجود».
records.english: Saying that the thing and its existence do not have two distinct external realizations does not mean that the **concept of existence** is the **concept of quiddity**. Nor should it be construed as the claim that an independently existing accident and its independent substrate have fused into one. The objector illustrates the problem: if one says that existence comes to a quiddity, and a single existent then results, one has already smuggled in the idea of the pre-existing quiddity and of something additional. If existence itself is only the intellectual relation used in judgement, it cannot do the causal work that a real principle of effects would have to do. The margin follows this question across to I:48.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The contrast of the positions
records.arabic: فإن الوجود إذا كان نفس الماهية فإذا ارتفع ارتفعت
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن الوجود إذا كان نفس الماهية فإذا ارتفع ارتفعت»؛ «فكان المعدوم نفياً صرفاً»؛ «بخلاف ما إذا قيل بأنه زائد عليها كالمعتزلة»؛ «فإن ارتفاعه لا يلزم ارتفاعها»؛ «فإن ارتفاع العارض لا يستلزم ارتفاع المعروض».
records.english: If existence is the very quiddity, then when existence is removed, that quiddity is removed as well.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: For, if existence is the very quiddity, then when existence is removed, the quiddity itself is removed. The nonexistent is then sheer negation. That is unlike the view of those who say existence is additional to quiddity, such as the Muʿtazila: the removal of existence does not necessarily remove quiddity, just as the removal of an accident does not necessarily remove that in which it inheres. This is the reason that some of them affirm that the nonexistent is a thing, or possesses establishment [of a qualified sort]. The text is reporting the connection between the two theses, not assuming that everyone who calls existence additional must accept extramentally existent nonexistent things.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «فإن الوجود إذا كان نفس الماهية فإذا ارتفع ارتفعت»؛ «فكان المعدوم نفياً صرفاً»؛ «بخلاف ما إذا قيل بأنه زائد عليها كالمعتزلة»؛ «فإن ارتفاعه لا يلزم ارتفاعها»؛ «فإن ارتفاع العارض لا يستلزم ارتفاع المعروض».
records.stage85_source_caution: Conditional statement only, not a full proof of the position.

records.title: Not numerical identity of the concepts
records.arabic_anchors: «(في المعنى) أي المفهوم من الوجود هو المفهوم من الشيء»؛ «(يعني أنه لا ينفرد كل) من الوجود والماهية»؛ «(بتحقق على حدة في الخارج)»؛ «(وأما هو) أي ليس الشيء هوية ولعارضه المسمى بالوجود هوية أخرى».
records.english: “In meaning” could be taken to imply that what is understood by existence is the same as what is understood by the thing; but that is not what is intended. Rather, existence and quiddity do not **each possess a distinct realization outside the mind**. There is not a quiddity with one extramental identity and an additional accident called existence with another extramental identity. Nor does the rejection of two identities make the notions synonymous; it is precisely the difference between conceptual distinction and external separation that matters here.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The intention behind “I say ...”
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أقول الخ) حاصله أن ما ذكر مبني على أن المراد من الوجود هو الأمر الاعتباري»؛ «أما لو أريد به ما به التحقق فلا حاجة في القول بعينية الوجود للماهية»؛ «دور الماهية»؛ «القول بأنه اعتباري».
records.english: The marginal writer says the previous difficulty arises if “existence” is taken as a **considered or relational item**. But if the intended meaning is what makes something genuinely actual, then the statement that existence is identical with the thing's quiddity requires a different treatment. It is not enough to repeat that “existence is additional,” since the sense of the addition is precisely at issue. Nor does the rejection of an additional independently existing feature establish that the two ideas—existence and whatness—mean exactly the same thing.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: Two senses of predicating existence of a quiddity
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله ولأنت الخ)»؛ «(قوله بالإضافة إلى ذات الشيء وحقيقته)»؛ «إذا قيل للإنسان مثلا وجود في الخارج ووجود في الذهن»؛ «الوجودين»؛ «البياض والجسم»؛ «الإنسان وحقيقته».
records.english: The gloss asks how to interpret the statement that the same quiddity has both **external existence** and **mental existence**. One must not imagine that there are necessarily two separately real entities called “the human being” merely because the human being can be conceived in the mind and realized outside it. Nor does the analogy with whiteness and body establish that mental existence is a further accident borne by a pre-existing thing in precisely the same way as an extramental colour is borne by a body. Rather, both the identity and the difference of the two modes must be explained: external actuality belongs to the thing in the world, while a mental form realizes the content for the knower. This resolves part of the equivocation without turning the individual quiddity itself into a universal that lives outside the mind.
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The literal gloss continues into I:49
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله بل الموجود في اللفظ الخ)»؛ «الوجود في اللفظ»؛ «الوجود في الخط»؛ «حقيقة الإنسان».
records.english: When the text moves to “what exists in the word,” the commentator warns that the expression is not univocal. Spoken and written signs exist externally as sounds and traces, but the human quiddity designated by them does not thereby exist **as that human** within the sound or inscription. The precise remaining argument begins again on I:49; the continuation should be joined with that page during the later literal proof. [Final short printed words on the lower margin need reinspection; this is an intentionally bounded provisional unit.]
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: The sense of existence relevant to effects
records.arabic_anchors: «أقول أنا لم أرد بالوجود المعنى النسبي الذي لا تحقق له في الخارج وإنما أريد به ما هو مبدأ الآثار وهو الهوية»؛ «ولا شك أنه بهذا المعنى نفس الشيء بلا تحقق» [final phrase imperfectly legible].
records.english: I say: I did not intend by “existence” the **relative meaning** which has no independent external realization. I intended that which is the *principle of effects*: the actual reality or identity of the thing. There is no doubt that existence in this sense is the thing itself. This is different from the abstract relational predicate which can be asserted of it; the author is identifying actuality in the relevant sense with the very existent, not with a second accident alongside it.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: External and mental existence
records.arabic: ثم الوجود منقسم إلى العيني
records.arabic_anchors: «(ثم الوجود منقسم إلى العيني)»؛ «وهو الوجود المتأصل المقصود عليه الذي به تتحقق ذات الشيء ... في الخارج»؛ «(وإلى الذهني)»؛ «وجود غير متأصل بمنزلة الظل للجسم»؛ «والصورة المطابقة للشيء عيني إنها لو تحققت في الخارج لكانت ذلك الشيء».
records.english: Existence is then divided into existence in external reality …
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.
records.stage85_prior_overview: Existence is then divided into **external** and **mental**. External existence is primary or original existence, by which a thing's essence obtains in the external world—indeed, it is the external realization of that essence. Mental existence is non-primary, resembling the relation of a body's **shadow** to the body. What is present in the mind is a form corresponding to the external thing: were the form itself actualized outside the mind, it would be that thing. Likewise, if a body's shadow were to become a body [in the proposed analogy], it would be that body's counterpart. This analogy does not equate the mental form with a separately existent person or object.
records.stage85_prior_anchors: «(ثم الوجود منقسم إلى العيني)»؛ «وهو الوجود المتأصل المقصود عليه الذي به تتحقق ذات الشيء ... في الخارج»؛ «(وإلى الذهني)»؛ «وجود غير متأصل بمنزلة الظل للجسم»؛ «والصورة المطابقة للشيء عيني إنها لو تحققت في الخارج لكانت ذلك الشيء».
records.stage85_source_caution: The classification continues with mental, verbal and written existence; not all of that continuation is entered here.

records.title: Word, writing and the kind of reality intended
records.arabic_anchors: «(حقيقة)»؛ «(و) منقسم (إلى اللفظي والخطي مجازاً)»؛ «(إذ ليس الموجود في اللفظ والخط من الإنسان)»؛ «(الشخص)»؛ «(ولا الماهية)»؛ «(في الخارج)»؛ «(في الذهن)»؛ «(بل)».
records.english: Mental existence can be called genuine with respect to the thing's quiddity and its reality as apprehended. “Verbal” and “written” existence, by contrast, are **figurative** modes of speaking about the existence of the thing: what exists in the spoken or inscribed word “human” is neither an external human individual nor the quiddity present as an intelligible form in the mind. What exists in speech is an utterance; what exists in writing is an inscription. These signify the thing but are not themselves that thing. The last printed “rather ...” continues at I:49, where the relation of the sign to the signified is clarified.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Printed page examined manually; marginal English remains partly interpretative; no independent second proof; not a complete page.

records.title: the inscription may point to words without being words
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله نعم لو أضيف إلى اللفظ الموضوع الخ)» · «الوجود اللفظي المجازي» · «الوضع» · «النقش».
records.english: On the remark that the name might be added to the expression established by linguistic convention, the marginal writer clarifies the difference between the *conventional association* that makes an utterance significant and the *graphic inscription* that reproduces its shape. A written word is related to a spoken word, but the writing's existence on paper is not the spoken sound's existence in the air. It is a derivative or figurative mode of the word's availability to the reader.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: does the representation preserve its object's identity?
records.arabic_anchors: «الألفاظ» · «الصور الذهنية» · «الأعيان الخارجية» · «اختلاف الأوضاع والأشخاص».
records.english: The discussion examines a chain: object in external existence, the form by which one apprehends it, a spoken expression and a written mark. The links may be used to identify an object, but the identity of the thing represented must not be confused with identity of the representations. In particular, the same written or spoken name can refer to different particulars, whereas different names may indicate one referent. Consequently, one cannot demonstrate mental existence simply by asserting that the image and external object must share the same individual existence.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: information about a nonexistent object
records.arabic_anchors: «الحكم على الأشياء» · «الصورة الحاصلة في الذهن» · «الأمور المعدومة» · «العلم».
records.english:
The commentator then draws attention to judgement about absent or nonexistent objects. A person may acquire information about a thing not before the senses, because the concept or form is available for intellectual consideration. Yet the availability of this concept requires explanation: does it give the quiddity another mode of being, or does it supply a sign or likeness capable of sustaining judgement? The author indicates that the answer determines whether the opponent has proved the thesis of mental existence or only the more modest fact of conceiving what is absent.

**Incomplete:** the last lower sentence breaks at the next leaf and its distinctive grammatical example needs exact retranscription.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: from name to written mark to the thing signified
records.arabic: (الاسم و) في الخط (صورته) المرقومة
records.arabic_anchors: «(الاسم)» · «(و) في الخط (صورته) المرقومة» · «لو أضيف إلى اللفظ الموضوع» · «الوجود في الأعيان».
records.english: “The name,” and, in writing, “its inscribed form.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: [The author completes a comparison involving the] **name** and its representation **in writing**, the inscribed shape of the expression. If the word signifies something, an inscribed form can signify the word, and through it lead us to what the word designates. But the ink or written pattern is not numerically identical with its spoken expression or the external object. The different relations of signification need to be distinguished from the actual mode of existence of the object signified.
records.stage86_source_note: Bounded upper-text lemma; ensuing distinctions between word, writing, and signified are not transcribed.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:49, physical combined PDF p.62
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the mental status of what cognition is about
records.arabic: (والدليل على) الوجود (الذهني)
records.arabic_anchors: «(والدليل على) الوجود (الذهني)» · «مع أن كون العلم سواء» · «في الأعيان».
records.english: “The proof for mental existence” [begins here].
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The argument for **mental existence** draws upon the fact that an object can be known and judged concerning even when the external thing is not present. It is possible to form an intelligible object of cognition, but the inference from that possibility to the **real presence of the object's quiddity in the mind** needs to be tested. Merely having a sign, or even a mental image, does not yet establish the exact metaphysical thesis.
records.stage86_source_note: Only the start of the proof; do not treat as a translation of the full proof.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:49, physical combined PDF p.62
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the claim need not be that the identical external object exists mentally
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله مقتضيا الثبوت الخ)» · «الوجود الذهني» · «ملاحظة» · «لا حاجة إلى الدليل».
records.english: The lower commentator objects that the proof may establish no more than a meaningful presentation of a non-external object. The mind can attend to the subject and predicate and judge their relation. This does not by itself show that the very same quiddity, with all the attributes of an external existent, has migrated into another receptacle. Without distinguishing conceptual availability from extra-mental actuality, one risks making the conclusion true by definition rather than establishing it by demonstration.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the phoenix and the proposed 'mental subject'
records.arabic_anchors: «العنقاء» · «موجودا في الذهن» · «لم يكن حاصلا في الخارج» · «الوجود الذهني».
records.english:
The author's reply is that a concept of the phoenix is possessed by the knower, and a judgement may be made with respect to it. But the mental concept is not thereby shown to have all the external predicates of a creature. In particular, saying “the phoenix is an animal” does not make a phoenix breathe in the room. The discussion is thus about the scope of predication and the dependence of cognition on a representation, not about a straightforward instance of an external relation.

**Incomplete:** the final lower argumentative chain includes a difficulty about the subject–predicate relation; its intermediate clauses have been condensed.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: affirmative predication is not an ordinary external inherence
records.arabic: (قوله مقتضياً لثبوت إلخ) لكن لا يلزم أن يكون ذلك هو الوجود الذهني؛ لجواز أن يكون ذلك الأمر نفس المعلوم، بل مرآة الملاحظة، كما هو عند القائلين بالوجود الذهني. […] (قوله حتى يجري إلخ) وحينئذ لا حاجة إلى الدليل عليه. […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله إذ نحكم على الممتنعات الخ)» · «الحكم في السلب» · «ثبوت».
records.english: On “entailing establishment, etc.”: It does not follow that the relevant matter must itself be mental existence, for it might be the known thing, serving as the mirror through which it is considered, as maintained by those who affirm mental existence. […] On “so that it may apply, etc.”: In that event there is no need to argue for it. […]
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: The separately marked note qualifies the inference from affirmative judgement: an affirmative proposition involving an impossible subject is not the same as the external inherence of an accident in an existing substance. The intellect may combine concepts in a judgement; the ontological status of the object of that judgement remains the matter to be demonstrated.

stage92_source_note.witness: Būlāq 1318 AH printed Volume I (single printed copy, no manuscript collation)
stage92_source_note.scope: selected contiguous source phrases, omissions explicitly signaled
stage92_source_note.limitations: Two printed subnotes from one ruled band. The third subnote, on judgment concerning impossibilities, is not fully transcribed.

records.title: the intellect can affirm what is not externally possible
records.arabic: إذ نحكم على الممتنعات
records.arabic_anchors: «(أنا نعقل الأمور الثبوتية في الخارج إذ نحكم على الممتنعات)» · «إيجابا» · «الممتنع» · «من المفهومات».
records.english: “For we make judgements concerning impossibilities.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The intellect forms concepts and even makes **affirmative judgements about impossibilities**. An object of judgement can therefore be present to thought without being an external thing. If the judgement contains a positive predicate, it is not enough simply to say that a positive judgement requires its subject to exist externally, since the very instances under discussion are said to be impossible externally. What exists in the mind may be the concept or representation under which the judgement is made.
records.stage86_source_note: Selected clause within the mental-existence demonstration.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:50, physical combined PDF p.63
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the possible and impossible under a concept
records.arabic: كقولنا كل عنقاء حيوان
records.arabic_anchors: «(ولا)» · «لا وجود لموضوعها في الخارج أصلا» · «كقولنا كل عنقاء حيوان».
records.english: “As when we say: ‘Every phoenix is an animal.’”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: Consider a proposition about a phoenix: “Every phoenix is an animal.” The subject-expression can be understood and the predicate related to it in judgement although no phoenix need exist outside the intellect. The argument demands an explanation of what, exactly, is the subject of that predicate. Treating the conceptual subject as a presently existing external animal would be to misunderstand the example.
records.stage86_source_note: Example only; conditions of affirmation and external existence are not exhaustively rendered.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:50, physical combined PDF p.63
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: what is meant by 'the intelligible is present'
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله والفهم والتميز عند العقل الخ)» · «وجوده في الخارج» · «وجوده في الذهن» · «الوجود المجرد».
records.english: The longer gloss explains that *intelligible presence* need not mean actual presence of the external subject. The mind may understand a proposition about a thing absent from the senses. If the thesis is only that a concept is present in cognition, it will hardly be disputed; if it is that the quiddity itself obtains a genuine additional form of existence, the argument needs premises that discriminate the two. The author considers a reply that the same quiddity can exist in different modes, while its externally associated accidents need not follow it into the mind.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: a claimed additional existence and the danger of circularity
records.arabic_anchors: «حاصل تجرد» · «الوجود في الذهن» · «الإضافة بين العاقل والمعقول» · «لا إثبات في الخارج».
records.english: The gloss examines whether the relation of knower and known can be established before the mental presence of the known object is proved. If the relation is used as evidence for mental existence, one cannot simply define its terminus as a mentally existent instance of the object; that would assume the conclusion. Yet some relation appears involved in the cognitive act. The issue is whether its terminus must be an externally existing thing, an existent mental form, or an object given through the mind's intellectual act. The author's reply remains conditional on the interpretation of cognition.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: ending of the proof and transition to the objection
records.arabic_anchors: «حصول الصورة» · «الثبوت في الخارج» · «المعقول» · «الوجود».
records.english:
The marginal passage closes by requiring the reader to distinguish the existence of a *form of what is known* from the external actuality of the *thing itself*. The proponent regards the mental form as supplying the predicate-relation; the opponent may grant the form without granting what the proponent wishes to infer about the known object. The objection on I:52 will ask why, if the real object's essence is mentally present, it does not undergo all the same qualifications it would undergo in the external world.

**Incomplete:** several lower sentences concerning the source of the cognitive relation require their original sequence reconstructed without condensation.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: only an affirmative relation, not an externally subsisting accident, is required
records.arabic: كل جسم حادث
records.arabic_anchors: «كل جسم حادث والقضية» · «فالتعقل» · «(إن كان بالمحمول)» · «في الذهن» · «إضافة».
records.english: “Every body is originated.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: In a judgement such as “Every body is originated,” the intellect understands the subject and the predicate and affirms their relation. But the **act of understanding** is not identical with the external coming-to-be of each subject to which the judgement applies. If the relevant relation is obtained through the predicate's belonging to the subject conceptually, one must explain whether that belonging is an external accident or the relation employed by the mind in judging.
records.stage86_source_note: Single example proposition within a longer argument about understanding a proposition.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:51, physical combined PDF p.64
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: predication and addition are not the same
records.arabic: فلا محالة يقتضي التعقل إضافة بين العاقل والمعقول
records.arabic_anchors: «ولا يكن محصله فيه» · «(فلا محالة يقتضي)» · «التعقل (إضافة)» · «بين العاقل والمعقول».
records.english: “Understanding must therefore imply a relation between the knower and what is understood.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: A proposed proof says that cognition requires a kind of **relation** (*iḍāfa*) between a knower and what is known. In the absence of the known thing externally, this relation must have a terminus in the mind. The respondent demands clarification: does the claim concern the existence of the known object itself, the presence of a concept through which it is known, or simply the logical relation expressed by the proposition? These are different claims, and their differences matter to the argument for mental existence.
records.stage86_source_note: Bilingual excerpt; distinction between relation and predication still to be fully checked.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:51, physical combined PDF p.64
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: forms need not be mental instances of every non-external object
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله قد يحصل المثال الخ)» · «المعقولات التي لا وجود لها في الخارج» · «صورة المعقول» · «العقل الفعال».
records.english: The commentator cites a discussion in the *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid* about intelligibles that do not exist externally. A concept of a nonexistent or impossible thing is not a reason to suppose that the object itself has an external instance. The theory that mental forms are impressed or supplied through an intellectual cause must also explain how incompatible or impossible objects can be known without requiring those things to be realised. The objection is a problem for a simplistic account of mental existence, not a demonstration that there can be no representation of nonexistents.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: how the known form can be present without inhering as the thing's external nature
records.arabic_anchors: «صور الكائنات في العقل الفعال» · «الصفات» · «الوجود في الأعيان» · «المفهومات».
records.english:
The author distinguishes the being of a form **in an intellect** from the thing's existence among external individuals. An intelligible can be available to the mind without the mind being an instance of every property predicated of the object. If one says the form is present as an intelligible, that requires no such external inherence; but if one says that the object itself is reproduced there in the complete manner of its external existence, the absurdities alleged by the opponent return. The debate continues at I:53 with the question whether the mental form and what the form depicts are identical.

**Incomplete:** the dense lower text contains additional argument about the Active Intellect and mental conjunction that has not been translated word for word. The printed lower author's individual identity remains unassigned.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the familiar paradox of contradictory external properties
records.arabic_anchors: «إذا قد حصل الأمر المطلوب بحصول المثال هذا» · «لو كان المعقول وجود» · «في الذهن» · «الأعراض المتصورة حتى المتضادات».
records.english: The opponent asks: if the actual object known really comes to exist in the mind, why do the accidents ordinarily associated with the object not arise there? Mental representations can include **contrary descriptions** or things whose external conjunction is impossible. Yet the mind does not thereby become the site of incompatible external qualities. Therefore the argument must make clear what “mental existence” means, rather than transferring the rules of external inherence into cognition without qualification.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the representation is present without the external attribute inhering
records.arabic: وهو وجود غير متأصل … لا يقتضي الاتصاف
records.arabic_anchors: «(وهو وجود غير متأصل)» · «(لا يقتضي الاتصاف)» · «كالكون يتصور الكفر».
records.english: “It is an existence that is not independently rooted … [and] does not entail the subject’s being qualified by the property.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The response is that mental existence is **not the same kind of rooted, independent external existence**. Thus the mind's conceiving a quality does not entail that the mind becomes externally qualified by that quality. The one who conceives disbelief does not thereby become an unbeliever, just as someone may conceive a colour or a contradiction without inheriting the external attribute described. The consequence at issue is limited to apprehension, not to the occurrence of the objects' real physical properties in the knower.
records.stage86_source_note: Two separately located phrases on the same upper text, not asserted to be contiguous.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:52, physical combined PDF p.65
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: water in a house versus water in a mind
records.arabic: كالماء في البيت
records.arabic_anchors: «(كالماء في البيت)» · «بواسطة الكون» · «وجود الشيء في وجود أصيل».
records.english: “Like water in a house.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: A comparison is drawn with water in a house. The water's occupying a room is an externally realised spatial relation: its actual location in that room accompanies a particular condition of existence. When the *water* is apprehended by the mind, this does not mean that the very same water now occupies a corner of the brain as it occupies the house. The difference between external emplacement and intellectual representation explains why external attributes are not all transferred into cognition.
records.stage86_source_note: Example only; accompanying explanation not exhaustively rendered.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:52, physical combined PDF p.65
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the narrower character of the mental-existence agreement
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فإن الكل متفق في الصورة الخ)» · «الفلاسفة» · «الصورة الحاصلة في الذهن» · «حقيقة».
records.english: On “All agree concerning the form”: the glossator observes that this common ground does not remove the disagreement. The philosophers' claim of union between the intelligible form and what is known may be meant in the level of quiddity or truth, whereas those denying mental existence understand the known form as a description or representation. If the union is stated without fixing the relevant respect, a merely verbal accord conceals a substantive ontological divergence. One must ask whether it is the genuine quiddity, or only something resembling it, which becomes present in understanding.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: philosophers, theologians and the relation between the form and its object
records.arabic_anchors: «هل هي عين ذي الصورة» · «وحدتها كماله عليه أهل التحقيق» · «الوجود الذهني» · «الوجود الحقيقي».
records.english: The marginal author compares the accounts attributed to philosophers, verifying scholars and those who deny the identity. The questions are whether a mental form possesses the same essence as its external object, whether mental and external existence are two manners of realizing one quiddity, and whether the form is only an analogical representation. If the form is merely another thing, then the object known may remain absent; if the object itself is asserted to be present, it becomes necessary to distinguish its mental mode of presence from the properties of its external occurrence.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: 'everything established is existent' and its dialectical limits
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فكل ما هو موجود معدوم الخ)» [opening uncertain] · «الوجود والثبوت والعدم» · «عندهم» · «الواسطة».
records.english: The lower gloss reports that theologians differ over whether nonexistents can have a fixed status that is not existence. One camp holds the division between existence and nonexistence to be exhaustive. Another proposes the so-called fixed nonexistent, arguing from the meaningfulness of distinctions and judgements about absent things. The author's challenge is to say what this supposed middle rank adds to conceptual differentiation without simply renaming a mode of existence. [The final objection continues on I:54.]
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: what is being disputed about the mental form
records.arabic: فإن الكل متفق في الصورة إلا أن القائلين بالوجود الذهني يقولون باتحاد الصورة وذي الصورة
records.arabic_anchors: «الخلاف في الوجود الذهني بالقطع» · «الكل متفق في الصورة» · «القائلين بالوجود الذهني» · «باتحاد الصورة وذي الصورة».
records.english: “Everyone agrees about the [mental] form, but those who affirm mental existence maintain the identity of the form and that of which it is the form.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The disagreement concerns **mental existence**. Everyone, it is said, accepts the presence of a *form* in cognition; the proponents of mental existence maintain that the form and what it is a form of are united under the relevant consideration. The opponents do not accept that identity. The issue is not whether anyone ever thinks of things, but whether the thing known is itself present mentally or whether a form distinct from it supplies the act of cognition.
records.stage86_source_note: Selected argument; the contrary position continues in the original.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:53, physical combined PDF p.66
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: being, fixity and the denial of intermediates
records.arabic: فكل ما هو ثابت فهو شيء وموجود وبالعكس
records.arabic_anchors: «ثم المعقول من الوجود والشيئية» · «الثبوت» · «ضرورة فكل ما هو ثابت فهو شيء وموجود وبالعكس» · «(و) المعقول (من العدم)».
records.english: “Everything that is established is a thing and an existent, and conversely.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: It follows that, on the account being defended, **existence, thinghood and establishment** are not three independently distinct ontological ranks. Whatever is established is a thing and is existent, and conversely. The notion signified by *nonexistence* is the contrary of existence; consequently one cannot assume an unargued middle state in which the object is at once absolutely nonexistent and yet positively established as a thing.
records.stage86_source_note: A bounded claim about establishment, thinghood and existence.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:53, physical combined PDF p.66
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: logical intermediates and real intermediates are not interchangeable
records.arabic_anchors: «يلزم الترادف» · «(قوله والنزاع ... الخ)» · «الثبوت» · «النفي» · «الوجود».
records.english: The glossator asks whether denying an intermediate level forces existence and positive fixity to be completely synonymous. Even if they are equivalent in extension under the disputed account, it need not follow that every use of their words has precisely the same meaning. The proposed intermediate rank may also conceal an ambiguity: an object can be known, named or considered mentally while being nonexistent externally, but none of these facts alone supplies a third ontological condition between existence and nothingness.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: blackness, whiteness and the basis of an affirmative predication
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله إذ هو بحيث يتلوه الخ)» · «اللفظ» · «حقيقة في الوجود» · «المعدوم».
records.english: The objection presses the interpretation of the opponent's examples. If the absolutely nonexistent can have the attribute of blackness or whiteness as an externally established property, the subject must be explained; if only the possibility of the predicate is intended, the argument does not establish the third rank. A difference among words, among conceived predicates, or among possible future instances must be distinguished from an actual difference among external entities.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the refusal of positive fixity for absolute nonexistence
records.arabic: فكذا المعدوم ليس بشيء ولا ثابت
records.arabic_anchors: «شيء ولا ثابت» · «(فكذا المعدوم ليس بشيء ولا ثابت)» · «المعدوم في الخارج» · «بالوجود الذهني».
records.english: “Likewise, what is nonexistent is neither a thing nor established.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: —[The argument denies that the nonexistent can be a thing in the relevant sense or positively fixed.] Thus “the nonexistent is neither a thing nor established.” Admittedly, something nonexistent in **external** reality can be the subject of a judgement in the **mind**, on the theory of mental existence. But this does not make the absolutely nonexistent an existing thing outside the intellect. The dispute concerns the type of establishment claimed for it.
records.stage86_source_note: Only the conclusion of the immediate argument; mental/external existence qualifications remain.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:54, physical combined PDF p.67
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the argument for an intermediate rank
records.arabic: لا واسطة بين الثابت والمنفي
records.arabic_anchors: «(لا واسطة بينهما)» · «بين الوجود والعدم» · «(ومنهم من أثبتها)» · «المعدوم» · «السواد».
records.english: “There is no intermediate state between the established and the negated.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The author first denies any intermediate state between existence and nonexistence, then reports those who **affirm such a middle condition**. They say that an object may be *established* although not existent, so that the affirmation of a predicate may be made concerning something that has not yet been externally realised. The argument is tested with predicates like blackness and with the supposed fixed nature of a nonexistent possible thing.
records.stage86_source_note: Short polemical lemma; subsequent report of a contrary view still untranscribed.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:54, physical combined PDF p.67
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the regress objection depends on a particular interpretation of qualification
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله أو ما يصدق عليه الخ)» · «التفسير» · «اتصاف» · «عدم».
records.english: The lower commentator argues that the regress arises under a specific interpretation of a subject's receiving existence. It may be true that an externally subsisting accident requires a subject, but the controversial question is whether existence itself is just another accident of this sort. If the subject has to exist prior to its being qualified as existent, the account becomes circular; if not, the meaning of the attribution needs to be distinguished from ordinary inherence. The explanatory terms cannot be substituted for one another without argument.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: why the other side also fails if it simply makes nonexistence a positive attribute
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وأنا نقضه اللاوجود)» [reading uncertain] · «لا يصح» · «نقيض» · «الثبوت والعدم».
records.english: The glossator tests the opposing account: if nonexistence is made a positive attribute, a nonexistent subject will have to obtain the attribute in some way, and the same puzzles recur. But if nonexistence means simply the absence of existence, there is no need to imagine a further quality inhering in a fixed object. The difference between negating a predicate and affirming an opposite positive property remains indispensable.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: blackness and whiteness as misleading analogies
records.arabic_anchors: «السواد والبياض» · «الصفات الثبوتية» · «الصفات السلبية» · «لهم».
records.english: Blackness and whiteness are positive qualities that can belong to a body. Nonexistence, by contrast, cannot be placed in the same class merely because the grammar of a proposition allows it to be predicated. A subject can be described as not black without acquiring a new positive accident called *not-blackness*. Similarly, to say that something does not exist may deny its being rather than give it another positive quality. This helps expose the difference between contradictories, contraries and the denial of an attribute.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: existence as an attribute of an already established subject
records.arabic: تسلسل الوجودات
records.arabic_anchors: «(قال)» · «يجعل الوجود صفة إذا وجد تسلسل» · «الوجودات» · «أو عدم اتصاف بالنقيض».
records.english: “An infinite regress of existences.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: “They say”: if existence is treated as an additional positive attribute which must itself become existent, then one seems required to posit another existence for it, and so on without end. Alternatively, if nonexistence is said to be simply the subject's being qualified by a contradictory predicate, the account must explain how the subject is present in order to receive that contradictory qualification.
records.stage86_source_note: Only the printed term concluding the regress objection; explanatory reconstruction deliberately withheld.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:55, physical combined PDF p.68
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: replies to the regress and to the paradox of the subject's being absent
records.arabic: لا نسلّم لزوم التسلسل
records.arabic_anchors: «(ورد)» · «أنه موجود» · «(لا أن وجوده عينه)» · «(عدم)».
records.english: “We do not concede that an infinite regress follows.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The reply notes that an account of existence as an attribute need not grant that every attribution has the same form as an accident inhering in a substance. Without first resolving what it means for the subject to be there, one cannot pass immediately to an infinite series. Likewise, speaking of an object's nonexistence does not necessarily establish an independently existent contradictory accident in that object. These are competing explanations of one and the same predication.
records.stage86_source_note: Bounded phrase from the reply; the argument is not complete.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:55, physical combined PDF p.68
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the two formulae 'existence is not there' and 'the nonexistent is there'
records.arabic_anchors: «اللاوجود عند القائلين بالواسطة» · «المعدوم عند المثبتين» · «عند النافين» · «العدم».
records.english: The marginal commentator distinguishes the views of those who posit an intermediary rank from the views of those who deny one. The former may call the nonexistent *established* but not *existent*, allowing possibility and conceptual predication without external being. The latter refuse to grant anything outside the exhaustive pair existence/nonexistence. The gloss warns that both sides use the term “established” and the term “nonexistent” under varying specifications; to argue against one formulation while quietly using another is not a sound refutation.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: being a subject of denial does not establish a subject in actuality
records.arabic_anchors: «(وأقول)» · «كان الوجود معدوما» · «لو كان حالا» · «كلا».
records.english: “I say”: even if a possible thing receives the judgement that existence is absent from it, this does not force the existence of a substrate in which that absence subsists. The difference between the *subject as conceived* and the *subject as externally fixed* matters at every step. The gloss considers the objection that nonexistence must occur as a positive state and replies that doing so would contradict the very point of denying an extra-mental existent.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: what does it mean to be an intermediate condition?
records.arabic_anchors: «الواسطة» · «ليست موجودة ولا معدومة» · «لا يمكن» · «الوجود لا صفة».
records.english: The alleged intermediary between the existent and the nonexistent may be said to be neither positively existent nor absolutely nonexistent. But if the intermediary itself is a subject of predication, the argument still owes an account of its ontological status. Is it an objective condition, a mental consideration, or a change in terminology? The commentator disputes whether the original formulation truly supplies a third alternative or only shifts the meaning of its terms.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the marginal author's cautious conclusion
records.arabic_anchors: «وهو بين البطلان» · «من شرح المقاصد» · «بطريق التفسير واللطف» · «تحقيقه من رسالتنا».
records.english:
The gloss finally suggests that much of the difficulty may arise from the way the rival schools explain their terms. The same surface expressions are employed differently by those who admit an intermediary and those who reject it. A reconciliation is possible only if one shows that their actual ontological claims coincide; otherwise the differences cannot be dissolved by linguistic adjustment alone. The writer refers to another, more detailed treatment of the point and closes the discussion before the illustration at I:57.

**Still unresolved:** the bottom third of I:55 and most of the lower argumentative chain on I:56 need exact, uncompressed translation. These pages are **not** certified first-pass complete despite the connected reading above.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the alleged logical contradiction
records.arabic: نقيضه العدم لا المعدوم
records.arabic_anchors: «(و)» · «اتصافه بالنقيض بل بالمعدوم» · «(نقيضه العدم لا المعدوم)» · «بطرق الاشتقاق».
records.english: “Its contradictory is nonexistence, not the nonexistent thing.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The dispute is sharpened by distinguishing **nonexistence** (*ʿadam*) from **the nonexistent thing** (*maʿdūm*). If the contradiction of existence is nonexistence, it does not follow that “the nonexistent” is the same sort of predicate. The latter is a derived description applied to a subject; the former expresses negation of being. Arguments that treat them as interchangeable may therefore depend on an unnoticed shift from an abstract contradictory to a derived adjectival predicate.
records.stage86_source_note: Critical terminological distinction, with the remaining proof still open.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:56, physical combined PDF p.69
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: why existence and nonexistence cannot be treated as two substances
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن كل صفة فائقة شيء» [source reading uncertain] · «الوجود» · «العدم» · «نقيض».
records.english: An apparent paradox arises if both existence and nonexistence are handled as independently positive qualifications. The author asks whether an attribution of existence makes the subject independently existent beforehand, and whether attributing nonexistence does likewise. The regress and contradiction can be avoided only by fixing the relevant sense of qualification. The upper text ends by opposing the *actual negation of existence* to the supposedly positive *object described as nonexistent*.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: whether 'the body is a nonbody' follows
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله كالسواد الخ)» · «اتصاف الوجود بالعدم» · «لا يكون الوجود موجودا» · «لا عذر فيه».
records.english: The longer commentator returns to the proposed example: in a body the qualification by blackness leaves the subject's existence intact, but an attribution of nonexistence to existence is not of that sort. The relevant inference depends on what precisely the subject is said to lack. If the predicate negates the subject considered in its very identity, the analogy breaks down. The objection thus turns not on the grammar alone but on the difference between a separable or accidental predicate and a contradiction in the subject's being.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: does the formula 'not possible' differ from the absence of possibility?
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله لعدم الفرق بين الإمكان له والإمكان لغيره الخ)» · «الإمكان» · «منفيا في نفسه» · «نفي ثبوته».
records.english: A further gloss distinguishes the negation of possibility from the possibility of negation, as well as “the thing has possibility” from “possibility is affirmed for something else.” The author stresses that an assertion involving the possible does not by itself make the possible object existent. Saying that a thing may exist is consistent with its presently not existing. One cannot, without another premise, move from the stability of a conceptual distinction to the established existence of its subject.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the force of the blackness analogy
records.arabic: (قوله كالسواد إلخ) فإن قيل: اتصاف الوجود بالعدم ليس كاتصاف الجسم بالسواد مثلاً، لأن اتصاف الوجود بالعدم يقتضي أن لا يكون الوجود موجوداً، واتصاف الجسم بالسواد […]
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله كالسواد الخ)» · «اتصاف الوجود بالعدم» · «اتصاف الجسم بالسواد» · «المعدوم في نفسه».
records.english: On “like blackness, etc.”: One might object: Existence being characterized by nonexistence is not like a body being characterized by blackness. For existence being characterized by nonexistence would entail that existence is not existent, whereas a body’s being characterized by blackness […]
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On the blackness analogy, the smaller gloss denies that the relation of existence to nonexistence can simply be treated as equivalent to the relation between a subject and the blackness inhering in it. To say that existence receives nonexistence may negate the very existence under discussion, whereas a body's receiving blackness does not negate its being a body. An appeal to an ordinary attribute therefore cannot settle a dispute over the contradictory of existence itself. The note also challenges the move from a description's being conceived to its object being established in itself.

stage92_source_note.witness: Būlāq 1318 AH printed Volume I (single printed copy, no manuscript collation)
stage92_source_note.scope: selected contiguous source phrases, omissions explicitly signaled
stage92_source_note.limitations: Only the opening objection; the continuation and reply are printed but not completely transcribed.

records.title: the blackness/body counterexample
records.arabic: كالسواد القائم بالجسم
records.arabic_anchors: «كالسواد القائم بالجسم» · «لا جسم مع اتصاف الجسم به» · «الجسم ذو لا جسم» · «الوجود معدوم ولا وجود».
records.english: “Like blackness inhering in a body.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: [The disputed description could attach] as one of the individuals falling under its contradictory—just as blackness inheres in a body. Yet a body qualified by blackness is not, merely for that reason, a nonbody. The reductio is that if one treats the presence of a predicate as the thing's becoming the contrary of itself, one will be forced to say absurdly that the body, precisely while a body, possesses nonbodiness. In the same way, it would be mistaken to infer from a proposed way of speaking about existence that “this existence is nonexistent” or is no existence at all. The point is to test what the claimed opposition actually concerns, not to collapse the levels of predication.
records.stage86_source_note: Analogy only; not the whole reductio.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:57, physical combined PDF p.70
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the differentiability of nonexistents
records.arabic: المعدومات متمايزة … بعضها متصور وبعضها غير متصور
records.arabic_anchors: «(قالوا)» · «المعدومات متمايزة» · «بعضها متصور وبعضها غير متصور» · «بعضها صادق وبعضها كاذب» · «ولا يعقل التميز بدون الثبوت».
records.english: “Nonexistent things are distinguishable … some are conceivable and others are not.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: “They say”: Nonexistent things are **distinguishable from one another**. Some can be conceived and some cannot; some assertions concerning them are true and others false. But differentiation, the argument proceeds, is unintelligible without a kind of fixity or being-established (*ṯubūt*). For one can distinguish two items only insofar as they can be referred to, and reference appears to require something fixed as its object. Thus the opponents attempt to infer a kind of established status for the nonexistent from the fact that it can be thought and described.
