records.stage86_source_note: Two phrases are separated by further source text not transcribed.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:57, physical combined PDF p.70
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: from an object's possibility to its being established
records.arabic_anchors: «ولا يعقل التميز بدون الثبوت» · «(و) كل ممكن ثابت» · «الإمكان» · «ثبوت».
records.english: A second argument is introduced from possibility. Every possible thing, it is said, is “established” in respect of its possibility, even if it is not actually existent. Otherwise possibility and impossibility would have nothing to differentiate them before the thing's realization. This argument requires careful examination, since saying “it is possible that X exists” may be quite different from saying that X already possesses a positive ontological standing. [The final words lead into the objection on I:58.]
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: is the alleged difference already what is being disputed?
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله يعني أن الفرق الخ)» · «وصف الإمكان بالشيء» · «بناء على اعتقاد الخصم» · «ليس أمرا موجودا في نفسه».
records.english: On “That is, the difference ...”: the intended contrast concerns possibility as a description of a subject and possibility attributed to or denied of that subject. But the distinction does not prove itself. It may presuppose the opponent's thesis that there is a fixed subject in which possibility inheres. The one who denies such a subject can still distinguish a statement of possibility from its negation, because the two statements have different significations without requiring the independently existing thing whose possibility is disputed.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the substance of a negative proposition
records.arabic_anchors: «الإمكان في حد ذاته» · «منفيا عن الغير أيضا» · «سلب الإمكان» · «وصف ثبوتي».
records.english: The commentator examines what it means to deny possibility “in itself.” If the possibility is a positive attribute, then denying it of another thing does not necessarily deny the very intelligibility of possibility; nor does its absence from some subject make it a nonentity absolutely. But if the dispute is about a nonexistent possible thing, it is precisely illicit to posit the fixed subject as part of the premise. The distinction between positive and negative descriptions must not beg the question of extramental being.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the form of the objection and the necessary reply
records.arabic_anchors: «ليس فرق بينها» · «التناقض» · «الفرق بين ماهيتين» · «قيل ... عدم الإمكان».
records.english: The gloss presses an alternative: perhaps the meaningful difference is only between affirming and denying an attribution, not between two ontological objects. If so, the opponent has shown a difference between statements, but has not established the subject in the manner required. The author considers the case in which denial of possibility is treated as a real property and the case in which it merely records that the asserted possibility is not available. The latter preserves the distinction without creating a new real existent.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: why a different understanding of the subject changes the argument
records.arabic_anchors: «الممكن» · «في الأذهان» · «الموجود في الأعيان» · «ما لا يمكن».
records.english: It remains open whether the intended subject is the *possible quiddity in the intellect*, a really existing external individual, or something claimed to be fixed while not existing. Those are not equivalent. The marginal author insists that, if the argument changes its sense of “subject” midway, the appearance of a proof from possibility to positive fixity disappears. This opens the next printed page, where the meaning of *thubūt* itself is disputed.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the proposed difference between possibility and its negation
records.arabic: ثبوت الإمكان للشيء … وإن لم يكن موجودا في نفسه
records.arabic_anchors: «للفرق بين الإمكان له ولا إمكان له» · «ثبوت الإمكان للشيء» · «وإن لم يكن موجودا في نفسه» · «(ثبت موصوفه)».
records.english: “Possibility’s being established for a thing … even if the thing itself is not existent.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: [The point is alleged to be] the difference between “it is possible for it” and “it is not possible for it.” That is, possibility can be truly attributed to a thing even if the thing is not existent in itself. But it does not follow that the difference between the two judgements proves that the thing has an independently existing substrate of possibility. The proof's next step claims that, if the attribute of possibility is established, **its subject must be established**; the commentary asks in which sense the subject is being asserted to be established.
records.stage86_source_note: Two bounded phrases, not a complete modal proof.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:58, physical combined PDF p.71
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the absolute nonexistent and the nonexistent-at-present
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فلا يفيد)» · «العدم المطلق» · «لا وجود له أصلا» · «معدوم».
records.english: On “It does not establish the conclusion”: the reason is that the discussion concerns the absolutely nonexistent, not a thing that once existed, or that exists somewhere else, or that is merely absent at the present instant. One must ask whether a thing's absence is absolute or relative to a particular time or description. An earlier or later existent can be spoken of as nonexistent now without becoming an absolutely nonexistent object.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the argument from being fixed in oneself
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله في نفسه)» · «الإمكان» · «غير ثابت أصلا» · «ثبوت معنى».
records.english: The commentator explains that “in itself” may describe the status of a concept under consideration, not an independently established extra-mental entity. If possibility does not exist as an external quality, it is mistaken to infer that the possible object must be established externally. But if the possibility is considered as something intelligible, that does not prove the ontological claim either. The objection turns on precisely this ambiguity.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: why the denial of nonexistence does not yield external existence
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله وإن أردت في الذهن فلا يفيد)» · «وجود الذهني» · «المعدوم» · «الإمكان المنفي».
records.english: If the required establishment is only in the mind, the conclusion is not the one the opponent sought. The mind can hold a concept of something that has no external being. But if an external existence is required, an argument that appeals merely to differentiation among concepts cannot establish it. Thus the reply distinguishes external fixity, intellectual presence and the truth of a statement concerning the possible.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the external sense of existence is not simply being conceded
records.arabic: إن أريد أن التميز يقتضي الثبوت في الخارج فهو ممنوع
records.arabic_anchors: «(قلنا)» · «أن (التميز) يقتضي الثبوت في الخارج» · «ممنوع» · «إنما يلزم أن لو كان بحسب الخارج».
records.english: “If what is meant is that differentiation requires external establishment, that is denied.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: “We reply”: It is denied that the fact of differentiation requires establishment **in external existence**. That consequence would follow only if the difference were itself an external difference between external entities. A distinction made in reason or thought need not have two independently existent objects in the external world corresponding to its two terms. The distinction, therefore, proves less than its advocates require.
records.stage86_source_note: Selected rebuttal on cognitive versus external distinction.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:59, physical combined PDF p.72
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the being of a possible and of an impossible object
records.arabic_anchors: «و(أما)» · «عند العقل» · «اجتماع النقيضين» · «المركبات الخيالية» · «وإن أردت في الذهن».
records.english: At the level of intellect, one may differentiate objects even when they cannot exist externally, such as a combination of contradictories or a composite imagined only in thought. Such differentiation can be meaningful **in the understanding** while its object has no external existence. A thought can therefore distinguish and compare nonexistents without thereby establishing them as external things.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the meaning of possibility's being fixed
records.arabic: الفرق بين نفي الإمكان والإمكان المنفي
records.arabic_anchors: «(وأن الفرق بين نفي الإمكان والإمكان المنفي)» · «في نفسه» · «على تقدير كونه منفيا» · «ثابت أيضا».
records.english: “The difference between the denial of possibility and possibility under negation.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The alleged difference between denying possibility and possibility considered under negation is likewise a difference in what is affirmed or denied. Even if we grant a stable notion of possibility, that stability may belong to a conceptual judgement rather than to the existence of the possible thing. To infer an existent subject from the conceptual distinction would again be to pass illicitly from the mind to the external world.
records.stage86_source_note: Conceptual distinction only; no positive ontological claim implied.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:59, physical combined PDF p.72
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: preventing a slide from conceptual denial to real impossibility
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فلا يلزم من كونه غير ثبوت الخ)» · «إنما ليس من ذلك» · «الصفات الثبوتية والمنفية» · «سلب الشيء».
records.english: The gloss explains that the intended reply is to distinguish the absence of a positive determination from the impossibility of thinking or predicating the thing. Negation may be genuine without itself being another existent positive property. One may deny that something is external or deny a feature of a subject while still entertaining a meaningful proposition concerning that subject. The author therefore resists a reading in which every meaningful negative predicate paradoxically becomes a positive attribute of an existent.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: contrasting contradictory predicates with the subject's actual status
records.arabic_anchors: «الصفات الثبوتية والمنفية» · «الاعتبارات» · «قد يصدق أحدهما» · «كذب الأخرى».
records.english: The difference between contradictories can be expressed by the truth of one statement and falsity of its contrary, without supposing that the contrary is fixed as a second objective quality. Logical opposition belongs to propositions under a given interpretation. The commentary therefore asks whether the negative and affirmative predicates are being used in the same respect, at the same time, and of the same thing; unless these conditions are retained, an alleged contradiction may be only verbal.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the movement toward affirmative predication in I:61
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله كما في وجود زيد الخ)» · «الوجود الذهني» · «عدم» · «في الزمان» · «اللاحق».
records.english: The example of Zayd's existence illustrates the difference between an object's existence at a time and the judgement of its existence. A past or future existent can be treated as absent now, although the expression is not senseless. The later and earlier temporal qualifications must not be allowed to alter silently what the predicate *exists* is taken to mean. This prepares the question addressed on I:61: **what unites the two terms in a true affirmative proposition, and what distinguishes their concepts?**
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: why the possibility of a thing need not make the thing 'fixed'
records.arabic: فلا يلزم من كونه غير ثبوت سلب الإمكان عن الممكن
records.arabic_anchors: «فلا يلزم من كونه غير ثبوت سلب الإمكان عن الممكن» · «ثبوت الشيء لنفسه» · «الخارج» · «الممتنع».
records.english: “Its not being [a positive] establishment does not imply denying possibility of what is possible.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: It does not follow from [a particular item's] not having positive fixity that possibility must be denied of the possible. Nor should the proposition “a thing is itself” be taken as proof that every conceivable thing is externally established. The identity at issue can be preserved in a predicative or conceptual judgement without requiring the independent existence of the subject in the manner claimed by the opposing argument.
records.stage86_source_note: Selective clause; exact syntactic context still requires full upper collation.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:60, physical combined PDF p.73
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: judging a subject as existing, nonexistent or merely conceived
records.arabic: ثم كل من الوجود والعدم قد يقع محمولا
records.arabic_anchors: «(ثم كل من الوجود والعدم قد يقع محمولا)» · «وقد يقع رابطة» · «المحمول للموضوع» · «الحكم الإيجابي» · «وجود المحمول للموضوع».
records.english: “Moreover, both existence and nonexistence may occur as predicates.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: **Existence and nonexistence may each occur as predicates.** A judgement may also make use of a *link* or copula between subject and predicate. When existence is predicated, the judgement is about existence; when a judgement is affirmative with a different predicate, the existence of the predicate *for the subject* is not necessarily the same as the subject's external existence. The distinction is crucial in statements about nonexistent or imagined subjects: the truth or coherence of the predication cannot simply be reduced to the subject's independent external being.
records.stage86_source_note: Source-bound beginning of predicate/copula distinction.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:60, physical combined PDF p.73
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: why merely invoking the 'unity of the terms' does not answer the objection
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله يعني أن يكون ما يصدق عليه في الخارج الخ)» · «المراد اتحاد الطرفين» · «في الوجود الخارجي» · «للتغاير في المفهوم».
records.english: The commentator explains that the phrase “what the expression is true of externally” points back to the explanation of the unity of the two terms. If we take their unity to mean an external identity, that cannot simply be read as the identity of their meanings: the fact that two expressions attach to one existent does not show that their significations are interchangeable. Conversely, an identity secured only through a consideration of the intellect may fall short of the external union a predication is being used to affirm. This is an objection to an overly compressed account of what “unity” is doing in the definition.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the mind's judgement and the external case
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن اتحاد الطرفين ... في الخارج» · «الذهن» · «مع الوجود» · «مع اعتبار العدم» · «اعتزال ماهية المعلومة موجودة».
records.english: If the relation is taken in the external order, there must be an item there under both considerations; if it is taken in the mind, the question becomes whether the very same item can be regarded under incompatible conditions. The objection presses the asymmetry: a subject may be considered under existence, under nonexistence, or simply as a quiddity, but not all these considerations can be treated as independently existing properties of one extra-mental thing. A mental judgement may truly affirm a predicate of a quiddity without the relevant combination being realised in external existence.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: why the subject may not be 'outside' yet remain an intelligible subject
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن الحكم على الذات» · «لا يلزم أن يعتبر فيه أحدهما» · «لأن الحكم على الذات من غير أن يعتبر معه شيء».
records.english: The commentator goes on to reject an inference from an attribution made to the essence to the positive presence of every qualification required to formulate it. The essence is considered without adding an existential condition: ascribing the predicate to it does not force us to posit two real entities, the quiddity and a separate “being-there,” nor does denying existence turn the very subject of the judgement into absolute nothingness. These alternatives would only arise if one mistook a distinction in consideration for an external division.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: final requirements for a true affirmative predication
records.arabic: وافتقر الحمل الإيجابي إلى اتحاد الطرفين ذاتا وهوية
records.arabic_anchors: «وافتقر الحمل الإيجابي إلى اتحاد الطرفين» · «ذاتا» · «وهوية» · «ما يصدق عليه في الخارج أو الذهن عنوان الموضوع» · «هو بعينه الذي يصدق عليه مفهوم المحمول».
records.english: “Affirmative predication requires that its two terms be united in subject and identity.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: —[The previous discussion concludes with what is required for predication.] An affirmative predication depends upon the two terms' being united **in respect of the thing itself and of its identity**. The meaning is that the item of which the subject-expression is true—whether externally or in the mind—is precisely the item of which the predicate-concept is true. A judgement of the form “this is that” is otherwise not warranted where the purported subject and predicate designate two distinct entities.
records.stage86_source_note: Selected requirement for affirmative predication.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:61, physical combined PDF p.74
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: why difference of concepts is nevertheless required
records.arabic: وإلى تغايرهما مفهوما
records.arabic_anchors: «وإلى تغايرهما مفهوما» · «مفهوم عنوان الموضوع مغايرا لمفهوم المحمول» · «ليفيد» · «فائدة يعتد بها» · «وقد يكون فاسدا ... و باطلا».
records.english: “And [it requires] that they differ in concept.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: Yet the concepts signified by the two expressions must also be different: the concept conveyed by the subject-expression must differ from the predicate-concept, **so that the predication conveys a genuine benefit or information**. The author's reasoning considers cases in which this requirement appears to fail, including judgements that are formally true but explanatorily pointless and judgements whose apparent agreement depends upon a merely mental consideration. Thus one must distinguish identity of the *referent* from identity of the *concepts*; to confuse those two identities is to obscure the purpose of affirmative predication. [The exact status of two short transitions in the closing upper lines requires a second reading.]
records.stage86_source_note: Second part of the predication conditions, with explanatory qualifications open.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:61, physical combined PDF p.74
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: whether this account is applicable where there is no existing thing
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله والمراد بالأمر الشيء وبالنفس الذات الخ)» · «قال في شرح المقاصد ما حاصله» · «كيف يتصور هذا فيما لا ذات له ولا شيئية له في الأعيان» · «اجتماع النقيضين محال».
records.english: The commentator introduces a passage from the *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid*: How can the expression be applied to what possesses neither an essence nor thinghood among external things? For we say that the conjunction of contradictories is impossible *in itself*, and that a statement about what is possible is or is not in accordance with what obtains in the thing itself. These claims are not restricted to an independently present external object. The suggested answer is that, upon considering two opposed terms, the intellect discerns an affirmative or negative relation between them—sometimes a necessary relation, sometimes one excluded by necessity, and sometimes one that may obtain or fail. The question is what makes that discernment correct, and whether it is independent of the particular act of judgement.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the two relata and the truth of their connection
records.arabic_anchors: «العقل عند ملاحظة الطرفين» · «نسبة إيجابية أو سلبية» · «مقتضاها الضرورة أو البرهان» · «خصوصية المدرك والمخبر».
records.english: The relation is not exhausted by the fact that somebody conceived it or reported it. Once the parties to the judgement are considered, the mind may discover that one relation follows necessarily, or can be demonstrated, whereas an incompatible relation cannot follow. In this discussion “what is in itself” is therefore invoked to distinguish the **ground of a correct judgement** from the mere occurrence of its being judged. One must not confuse the relation's being intellectually apprehended with its being produced by an arbitrary act of apprehension.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: whether all mental forms must be jointly present
records.arabic_anchors: «صور جميع الكائنات والمعدومات» · «في العقل الفعال» · «لا يكون في نفس الأمر» · «الإيمان» · «الإذعان».
records.english: A further possibility is reported: perhaps all the forms of existent and nonexistent things are present in the Active Intellect, and correspondence is correspondence with those forms. But this does not yet resolve what a true attribution consists in. An affirmation can be held with assent (*iḏʿān*), or presented merely as a conceived proposition; its truth cannot consist in the speaker's act of assent. The author distinguishes the mind's determination of the conceptual terms from the truth of the relation asserted between them. References to assent, existence in the intellect and external realization are not to be collapsed into one claim.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: possible existence and the case of something thought but not realised
records.arabic_anchors: «أن يكون في نفس الأمر» · «في مرتبة الشيء وحد ذاته» · «في الأعيان أو يكون في الأذهان» · «إن لم يكن في الأعيان».
records.english: The final argument returns to the thing's rank or essence, even where what is considered does not exist in external particulars. A quiddity can be conceived, and an essential relation to it can be correctly affirmed without thereby furnishing a corresponding external object. Conversely, a merely imagined relation is not established by the fact that it has been imagined. The discussion therefore separates **external being, mental presence, and truth or necessity belonging to a predicative relation**.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: what is intended by 'the thing in itself'
records.arabic: والمراد بالأمر الشيء وبالنفس الذات … مع قطع النظر عن حكمنا وإدراك المدرك
records.arabic_anchors: «ما في نفس الأمر» · «والمراد بالأمر الشيء وبالنفس الذات» · «في حد ذاته وبالنظر إليه» · «مع قطع النظر عن حكمنا» · «وإدراك المدرك».
records.english: “By ‘matter’ is meant the thing, and by ‘self’ its essence … disregarding our judgement and the perceiver’s apprehension.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: [Truth is discussed by appeal to] what obtains **in the thing itself** (*mā fī nafs al-amr*). By *amr* is meant “thing,” and by *nafs* “essence” or “self.” The intended sense is what we understand when we say, “This thing is such-and-such *in itself*”: that is, with regard to what it is, considered in its own identity, **disregarding our judgement about it and the apprehension of the person who apprehends it**. It does not follow that “in itself” designates a second external receptacle beyond the thing.
records.stage86_source_note: Two identified spans explaining nafs al-amr; intervening text not transcribed.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:62, physical combined PDF p.75
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: the many senses of the term
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله فصل في الماهية الخ)» · «إذا اعتبرت مع التحقق سميت ذاتا وحقيقة» · «وإذا اعتبرت مع التشخص سميت هوية» · «الوجود الخارجي».
records.english: On “Section: On quiddity.” The commentator cites the *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid* to explain that, when quiddity is considered with actuality, it may be called an essence (*ḏāt*) or reality (*ḥaqīqa*); when considered with individuation it is called a concrete identity (*huwiyya*). The term *identity* may also be applied to individuation itself or to external existence, and *essence* can designate the essence insofar as it is predicable of individuals. These are different **respects under which one quiddity is contemplated**, not automatically different objects in external existence.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: can quiddity be made up of all its accidents?
records.arabic_anchors: «الماهية تعتبر جميع عوارضها لازمة أو مفارقة» · «الأمور العامة باطل» · «الأحوال والعوارض».
records.english: The gloss contests a proposed way of gathering all concomitants into the definition of quiddity. If quiddity were understood as the totality of its necessary and separable accidents, every predicate would become constitutive of what the thing is, and the distinction between essence and what is predicated of the essence would collapse. That cannot be the meaning of the standard definition. The author examines what is necessary to the thing, what belongs to it by accident, and what can be set aside without destroying what is answered to the question “What is it?”
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: what is signified by the word 'what'
records.arabic_anchors: «الماهية ما صدقاتها» · «المفهوم الصادق» · «ما هو ذي ماهية» · «(قوله عن السؤال بما هو الخ)».
records.english: The expression *mā* in “What is it?” directs attention to an answer indicating an essence rather than to a bare occurrence of the word *thing*. But one must beware of construing the answer as nothing more than a name for the existing individual; an individual may bear many descriptions, none of which individually supplies the definition demanded. The question seeks the content by which the thing is what it is. The gloss therefore distinguishes what a general expression signifies, the instances of which it is true, and the essence that is intended by the definitional answer.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: definition, the intelligible, and signification
records.arabic_anchors: «هو حد الشيء» · «ما يؤخذ منه الموصوفة» · «المقصود بالإشارة» · «هذا المحدد».
records.english: The commentator further considers whether “quiddity” is being used for a complete definition, for the intelligible meaning delivered by such a definition, or for the thing to which it points. These may coincide in the act of successful definition, but must not be confused when disputing a definition's wording. In particular, the *meaning* intended by the question may be the same whether the corresponding thing happens to be externally present or not. The concluding transition leads to the different ways in which a quiddity can be taken or considered.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the subject of the chapter
records.arabic: فصل في الماهية
records.arabic_anchors: «فصل في الماهية» · «آخر مباحث ما بحث الوجود والعدم» · «لأن البحث عنهما من حيث إنهما صفتان للماهية معروضتان لها».
records.english: “Section: On Quiddity.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: **Section: On Quiddity.** It is placed after the discussions of existence and nonexistence, because inquiry into the latter two is an inquiry into them as descriptions attributed to quiddity, the thing of which those descriptions are predicated. To discuss existence and nonexistence in that manner presupposes an explanation of what is intended by the quiddity receiving the two descriptions.
records.stage86_source_note: Section heading only; subsequent arguments require literal translation.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:63, physical combined PDF p.76
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: what 'what is it?' asks for
records.arabic: ماهية الشيء ما يجاب به عن السؤال ما هو
records.arabic_anchors: «لفظة ما مأخوذة عن ما هو» · «ماهية الشيء ما يجاب به عن السؤال بما هو».
records.english: “The quiddity of a thing is what answers the question ‘What is it?’”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The word *māhiyya* (“quiddity”) is derived from the question *mā huwa* (“What is it?”). **The quiddity of a thing is what is given in reply to the question, “What is it?”** The requested answer identifies what the thing is rather than supplying a merely accidental circumstance associated with it. [The last phrase proceeds into I:64.]
records.stage86_source_note: Definition only; grammatical and philosophical comments remain.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:63, physical combined PDF p.76
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: whether the same quiddity is also 'the agent'
records.arabic_anchors: «ليس بمحل الفاعل كما صرح به في شرح المقاصد» · «يجعل الفاعل ما به يكون الفاعل» · «بها يكون الشيء هو هو».
records.english: The commentator remarks that what is at issue is the quiddity itself, not an arbitrary attribution of agency or action to it. A definition of *agent* appeals to what makes an agent an agent; the definition of *quiddity* appeals to what makes the thing the thing it is. It does not follow that a quiddity, simply because it is a quiddity, is its own producer. Confusion can arise if the particle “by which” is given one and the same causal force wherever it occurs.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: the 'whatness' of the essence cannot be identified with all its descriptions
records.arabic_anchors: «وأقول ذلك ممنوع على هذا التقدير أيضا» · «الماهية ما به الشيء هو هو» · «المعروض للعوارض» · «تغاير المفهوم».
records.english: “I say: that is denied even on this interpretation.” The proposed account still threatens to identify the subject described with its accidents or with the meaning of a phrase predicated of it. The question *what is it?* is not answered by supplying any description that happens to be true. Rather, the definitional content must be distinguished from subsequent concomitants, even when the same actual subject supports them all. This is why a verbal change in the proposed definition does not automatically resolve the difficulty.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: generic, specific, and differential descriptions
records.arabic_anchors: «الجزء» · «الضرر واللزوم» · «الضربين من الضمير» · «خبر الذي» · «الماء ماء».
records.english: The gloss then tests the account against the familiar parts of definition: what is predicated by a genus, what is added as a differentia, and what belongs only as a property or accident. The expressions may refer to the same subject and differ in their meanings, yet still not be interchangeable in an answer to *what is it?* Repetition of an identical noun (“water is water”) supplies no new conception, whereas a suitable definition does; an accidental description, even if informative, may not answer the question in the requisite way. The last lines introduce an objection concerning the **quiddity considered without an accompanying condition**, continued on I:65.
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: a separate objection to describing the division as a real partition
records.arabic: (قوله قد تؤخذ إلخ) وإنما لم يقل «تنقسم الماهية إلى كذا» لأنه يرد عليه أن المقسم يجب أن يكون واحداً من تلك الأقسام، فيلزم تقسيم الشيء إلى نفسه وإلى غيره، بخلاف «قد تؤخذ»، فإنه بيان لاعتبارات الماهية لا أجزائها. اه منه.
records.arabic_anchors: «(قوله قد تؤخذ الخ)» · «إنما لم يقل تنقسم الماهية إلى كذا» · «المقسم يجب أن يكون واحدا» · «هذه الاعتبارات للماهية الواحدة».
records.english: On “it may be taken, etc.”: He did not say “quiddity is divided into such-and-such,” because that would invite the objection that what is divided must be one of the divisions, so that the thing would be divided into itself and something other than itself. Saying “it may be taken” instead expresses different ways of considering quiddity, not parts into which it is divided. [End of the printed ruled note.]
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On “It may be taken ...”: The expression is **not** simply “quiddity is divided into these species,” because the thing divided must be one in the relevant sense, whereas these are modes of taking or considering the same quiddity. A partition into different sorts of real things would be misleading: one does not first have three externally distinct quiddities which are subsequently labelled by their conditions. One rather makes different conceptual qualifications of what is one as a subject of consideration.

records.title: the three considerations
records.arabic: قد تؤخذ بشرط شيء … تسمى المخلوطة
records.arabic_anchors: «قد تؤخذ بشرط شيء» · «أي المقارنة للعوارض» · «تسمى المخلوطة» · «تخلطها مع العوارض» · «ولاحقا في وجودها».
records.english: “[Quiddity] may be considered on condition of something … [and] is called the mixed [quiddity].”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: Quiddity may be considered **on the condition of something** (*bi-šarṭ šayʾ*), namely with the accompanying accidents. In that respect it is called a **mixed quiddity** (*al-māhiyya al-maḫlūṭa*), because it has been taken together with accidents that accompany it in existence. The example begins with human existence among external individuals, in which a quiddity is not encountered bereft of all determinations.
records.stage86_source_note: Two source clauses; the examples of concomitant accidents remain.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:64, physical combined PDF p.77

records.title: external individuals and the relation of their accidents
records.arabic_anchors: «فإن وجود الأشخاص في الخارج» · «بين كرم وعرض من أفراد الإنسان».
records.english: The existence of individuals externally always occurs with particular qualifications and accidents—one individual may possess generosity, another some other attribute. Such differences are genuinely associated with existing persons, but they do not all enter the definition by which each is human. The discussion is not asserting that every accident is essential merely because no particular exists without accidents.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemmas and Sanandaji sharh
notes: Original Arabic must be consulted; the English condenses some longer marginal syntax.

records.title: The question of actuality and mental occurrence, unassigned lower commentary
records.arabic_anchors: «المركب منها الذي اشتهر أن الفرد»؛ «ليس من التشخص كذلك»؛ «الوجود والاختصاص»؛ «قولـه لتجردها عنها»؛ «تسمى الماهية بشرط لا أيضا».
records.english: The individual is often described as a composite of the quiddity and its individuation, but this composite must not simply be confused with an entity in which individuation subsists apart from what is individuated. What is claimed to be excluded under the abstracting consideration needs care: an act of abstraction neither abolishes the thing's quiddity nor proves the existence of a bare quiddity outside. The lower writer calls attention to the language of particular existence, qualification, and individuation. In discussing “because it is abstracted from them,” he insists that abstraction *from concomitants* is an intellectual operation, not the appearance of a new concrete component corresponding to the abstracted aspect. The alleged absence of accidents is precisely the consideration under which the quiddity receives the technical label “taken on condition of no thing.”
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: The kinds of accident, separate short note
records.arabic: قسموا العارض للشيء قسمين: أحدهما عارض الوجود والآخر عارض الماهية
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله لأن الوجود الخ»؛ «قسموا العارض للشيء قسمين»؛ «عارض الوجود»؛ «عارض الماهية»؛ «الوجود الخارجي»؛ «الوجود الذهني»؛ «كالكلية والجزئية».
records.english: “They divided what supervenes on a thing into two: an accident of existence and an accident of quiddity.”
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: On “Because existence ...”: scholars have divided what supervenes on a thing into accidents of existence and accidents of quiddity. They further distinguish accidents associated with external existence, such as sensible characteristics, from accidents associated with mental existence, such as universality and particularity. What is being excluded by abstraction must therefore be specified: exclusion of independently external accidents is not identical to exclusion of anything attaching to a nature in the act of thinking. The accompanying note cautions against using the term “unconditioned” as though it meant a condition of exclusion. [The printed note's final short reference to the three conditions requires a more literal second reading.]
records.stage86_source_note: One initial portion of the separately ruled gloss, not the entire ruled register.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:65, physical combined PDF p.78

records.title: The quiddity taken on condition of abstraction
records.arabic: تؤخذ بشرط لا شيء أي الخلو عن العوارض واللواحق وسميت المجردة
records.arabic_anchors: «تؤخذ بشرط لا شيء»؛ «أي الخلو عن العوارض واللواحق»؛ «وسميت المجردة»؛ «ولا توجد في الأذهان فضلا عن الأعيان»؛ «لأن الوجود في الذهن ... من العوارض».
records.english: “It is taken on condition of no thing—that is, free of accidents and concomitants—and called the abstracted [quiddity].”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: A quiddity may be taken “on condition of no thing,” that is, conditioned by being free of concomitants and accidents. It is therefore called the **abstracted** quiddity, because of the abstraction of all such things from it. So understood, “it does not exist in minds, still less in external things.” For existence in the mind is itself an accident of the apprehended thing. This holds whether the accidents being excluded are all accidents without qualification or only those taken to be external, since mental existence also supplies a determination to what is conceived. The explanation turns on distinguishing the nature in itself from the features attaching to the nature *as apprehended*. The phrase continues onto I:66.
records.stage86_source_note: Bounded opening of printed I:65; remaining discussion of mind/external existence still open.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:65, physical combined PDF p.78

records.title: Mental abstraction, external accidents, and the apparent inconsistency
records.arabic_anchors: «قيد العوارض بالخارجية جوز وجود المجردة في الذهن»؛ «المعروض الخارجية بهذا المعنى»؛ «سواء ...»؛ «فالماهية المجردة لا توجد من حيث هي مجردة»؛ «قولـه وأما الحكم عليها باستحالة وجودها».
records.english: Restricting the excluded accidents to *external* accidents appears to allow an abstracted nature to exist mentally, since the mentally present nature need not bear the external accompaniments of its external instances. But the classification is not so straightforward: the mental determination itself is an accident for one purpose, and no such external accident for another. The note compares the manner in which intellects count or consider objects with the kinds of qualification inherited from external things. If all mental determinations are excluded as well, then the supposedly abstracted quiddity cannot have mental existence *under that restrictive consideration*. Yet the intellect may still grasp the meaning to which that condition is appended; otherwise it could not form the judgement that such an abstraction is impossible. This last point is the bridge to the next leaf.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: What the expression “an accident” excludes
records.arabic: (قوله بأن يتصوره عارضاً) وليس المراد من هذا أن هذا العارض ليس عارضاً له أصلاً، وإنما هو محض اعتبار الذهن له واعتبار عروضه لذلك الشيء، بل المراد […]
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله بأن تعتبر له عارضا»؛ «ليس المراد من هذا أن هذا العارض ليس عارضا له أصلا»؛ «وإنما هو محض اعتبار الذهن له»؛ «من يحصل في الذهن أن ذلك العارض عارض له».
records.english: On “by conceiving it as an accident”: What is meant is not that the accident is in no way predicated of it, and that its being so is merely the mind’s consideration of it and of its inherence in that thing. Rather, what is intended is […]
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage92_prior_working_overview: On “that you consider it as having an accident”: the author's intention is not that the supposed accident is in no sense an accident of the object. Rather, the question is whether the intellect merely *considers* it as added, or whether it belongs to the way the object occurs in the mind and so cannot be omitted by an arbitrary stipulation. Conceiving a nature and then noticing its mentally supervening attributes are distinguishable acts, but the mental existence underlying the latter is not thereby eliminated. [Several pronouns and the note's final phrase need a second literal proof.]

records.title: Does mental conception itself violate the abstraction?
records.arabic: الذي تفرضه موجودا في الذهن عرض له في نفس الأمر كونه في الذهن
records.arabic_anchors: «الذهن»؛ «فإن الشيء الذي تفرضه موجودا في الذهن»؛ «يعرض له بنفس الوجود في الذهن»؛ «من غير أن يعتبر الذهن عارضا له»؛ «وأما الحكم عليها باستحالة وجودها فلا الحكم على الشيء إلا بعد تصوره».
records.english: “That which you suppose to exist in the mind has, in the thing itself, the determination of being in the mind.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The mental attribute under discussion does not have to be separately *attached* by an act of consideration: something posited as existing in thought acquires that determination through its very existence in thought, even without the intellect subsequently predicating it as an accident. But if it is said that the abstracted quiddity cannot exist, how can one make a judgement concerning it at all? A judgement about a thing presupposes some conception of the thing. It is not sufficient to declare the quiddity absolutely inconceivable; one must distinguish conceiving the nature and conceiving the nature *with the stipulated absence of every concomitant*. The argument continues in the ruled and lower comments.
records.stage86_source_note: Source-facing excerpt; remainder of the dispute about mental accidents is not transcribed.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:66, physical combined PDF p.79

records.title: Why there need not be a contradiction in conceiving what is judged impossible
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله من حيث ذاتها»؛ «فلا تناقض»؛ «الماهية المجردة»؛ «الوجود في الذهن»؛ «الاستحالة».
records.english: The gloss objects that the apparent resolution still risks a contradiction. If the intellect judges a quiddity to be impossible *as abstracted*, it must apprehend what the expression designates. If its mental apprehension makes it mixed, what exactly is the subject of the impossibility judgement? The reply depends on whether a judgement of possibility is made about the nature considered absolutely, or about a nature under a condition of excluding all concomitants. Merely knowing a meaning does not establish that the precise *condition* added to it is instantiated in the same act of knowing. The writer explains that the two considerations can be distinguished, but warns that a switch from one to the other must not occur without notice.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: The act of predication and the object of predication
records.arabic_anchors: «المحكوم عليه»؛ «جواز الوجود»؛ «التجرد في الذهن»؛ «الوجود في الخارج»؛ «إذا كانا متحدين من وجه ...».
records.english: The subject of a proposition about possibility can be an intellectually signified nature, not an abstracted entity already realised in the mind in every respect specified in the proposition. It follows that saying “the abstracted quiddity is impossible” need not assert that the quiddity possesses no intelligible meaning; rather, the predicative subject is distinguished from the restriction about which the judgement is made. The marginal discussion considers different senses of “abstracted” and “mixed,” and argues that the answer must fix which sense is intended before claims about conceptual identity, external being or impossibility can be tested. [The last printed lines join the next leaf and include a difficult example that is not securely resolved here.]
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: The judgement “impossible” is made under a different consideration
records.arabic: وقد تؤخذ لا بشرط شيء من مقارنة العوارض والتجرد عنها
records.arabic_anchors: «كانت من حيث ذاتها مجردة مقارنة للمخلوطة»؛ «ومن حيث وجودها في الذهن قسما من المخلوطة»؛ «فيصح الحكم عليها باستحالة الوجود من حيث ذاتها»؛ «وقد تؤخذ لا بشرط شيء من مقارنة العوارض والتجرد عنها»؛ «وهي أعم من المخلوطة».
records.english: “It may also be considered without stipulating anything concerning accompanying accidents or abstraction from them.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: A quiddity may be abstracted when considered in itself and yet, insofar as it is present in the mind, belong to what is mixed with determining features. We can therefore judge its existence impossible **under the consideration of sheer abstraction**, without denying that it can be apprehended under another consideration. It may further be taken “without the stipulation of anything”—neither stipulating the accompanying accidents nor stipulating abstraction from them. The nature so considered is more general than what is taken with accompanying accidents, because the latter is only one of the possible instantiations admitted by the former. The comparison continues on I:68.
records.stage86_source_note: Bounded opening of the unrestricted-quiddity discussion.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:67, physical combined PDF p.80

records.title: What is being denied by “not a part of it”?
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله لصدقها عليهما»؛ «مفهومه غير ذلك المفهوم»؛ «قوله لا جزءا منها»؛ «الماهية المخلوطة»؛ «الفرد»؛ «المطلقة».
records.english: The gloss first examines how the unrestricted nature applies both to what is accompanied and to what is abstracted, noting that a sameness of external subject does not imply the same mental meaning. It then objects to the statement that the nature is “not a part” of the composite. If the individual is made up of a quiddity and individuating features, one may describe quiddity as a constituent of the individual; but whether it is an independent part with its own external existence is another question. The use of “mixed” sometimes refers to the whole individual and sometimes to the quiddity qualified by concomitants. These cannot be interchanged without explaining how predication relates the part and whole.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: The difference between predication and conceptual inclusion
records.arabic_anchors: «الوجود في الخارج»؛ «مطلق إنسان»؛ «زيد»؛ «ماهية من العوارض»؛ «القول».
records.english: It is not necessary that an unrestricted human nature exist alongside Zayd as a second external entity before “human” can truly be predicated of Zayd. Conversely, the mere possibility of forming an unrestricted human concept does not prove that this concept, considered with its mental universal qualification, itself exists externally. The question is instead whether a nature predicated of an individual is the very nature in that individual, or merely one of its constituents. The marginal writer explores the alternative senses of “individual,” “absolute,” and “mixed,” which opens the more elaborate set of objections on I:69–70. [The final clause crosses I:68/I:69 and requires a second precise transcription pass.]
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Unrestricted nature is not an externally separate part
records.arabic: وصدق المطلق على المقيد
records.arabic_anchors: «وهي أعم من المجردة لصدقها على ما ...»؛ «وصدق المطلق على المقيد»؛ «فتوجد الماهية لا بشرط في الخارج لكونها نفسها ... أي نفس المخلوطة في الخارج»؛ «لا جزءا منها»؛ «إذ ليس الموجود من الإنسان إلا زيد وعمرو»؛ «فلا يصدق عليه المطلق لامتناع صدق الجزء الخارجي ...».
records.english: “And the unrestricted is truly predicated of the restricted.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: The nature taken without a condition is more general than the abstracted nature, since it can apply both when there are accompanying features and when such features are abstracted. This is the sense in which an unrestricted concept can be predicated of a restricted instance. The quiddity taken without stipulating anything “exists externally,” because it is the very quiddity found with its individuating concomitants—**not merely a part of that external composite**. Only particular humans, such as Zayd and ʿAmr, occur outside the intellect, but it would be wrong to infer that unconditioned humanity is a separately existing part in them. Rather, the nature under this conceptual consideration is predicated of individuals. If it were an externally detached constituent, predication of it as the whole could not straightforwardly be made. The argument continues on I:69.
records.stage86_source_note: Short principle; the long external-individual example is not fully transcribed.
records.stage86_copytext: Būlāq 1318 AH, printed Volume I:68, physical combined PDF p.81
records.stage86_attribution_policy: Upper, ruled and lower voices retained separately; no unassigned note is attributed to Wasīm

records.title: Long marginal discussion, unassigned author: unrestricted and restricted
records.arabic_anchors: «وحينئذ يتم القول بأن المطلقة نفس المخلوطة في الخارج لا جزؤها»؛ «وإنما التغاير في العقل»؛ «قوله دون الخارج ... أي بحسب المصدوق»؛ «وإنما التغاير بين المطلق والمقيد».
records.english: On this basis the assertion is completed that the unrestricted nature is the very mixed nature externally, rather than a part of it: that is because the unrestricted nature does not need a separate external determination to distinguish it from the mixed nature. The distinction lies in thought. The words “not externally” may be read with reference to what the two concepts apply to, rather than as a denial that their *meanings* differ. The commentator had explained “mixed” in one sense, while an objector took it otherwise; the objection therefore risks shifting between the mixed quiddity as an entire compound and the unrestricted nature as considered without its qualification. As for the unrestricted human being and one restricted by some particular specification, one cannot simply infer that the unrestricted human subsists as an external item distinct from the restricted human. [The precise syntax of the initial reference to the author and commentator requires a clearer reading.]
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: The mixed nature as whole, or the nature as a part
records.arabic_anchors: «لو كانت المخلوطة جزءا للفرد في الخارج»؛ «المطلقة ... لم يصح ما يأتي»؛ «المخلوطة هي الأفراد في الخارج»؛ «لا يصح حمل نحو الإنسان على زيد مثلا»؛ «بأن يقال الفرد قد يطلق ويراد به المجموع».
records.english: If one were to say that the mixed quiddity is only a *part* of an individual existing externally, the unrestricted quiddity, insofar as it coincides with that mixed quiddity, would likewise become a mere part; the subsequent predication would then fail. Moreover, the claim that the mixed quiddity just *is* the external individuals must be carefully distinguished from saying that all the parts of a complex individual are each identical to the entire individual. Otherwise it would be impossible to predicate “human” of Zayd, when such predication is plainly accepted. One answer is that the word “individual” may denote the entire composite, while in another use it may denote the quiddity together with the specifying accidents. The author warns that distinctions in conceptual consideration must not be turned into unsupported distinctions between independently existing external objects.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Reply to the remark about the nature “taken without a condition”
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله ثم إذا اعتبرت المأخوذة لا بشرط»؛ «إن المأخوذ لا بشرط يمتنع أن يوجد في الخارج لأنه كلي طبيعي»؛ «لأن الوجود فيه يستلزم التشخص المنافي للكلية»؛ «وتنافي اللوازم دليل ...».
records.english:
On “Then if the thing taken without a condition is considered ...”: it can be objected that what is taken without a condition cannot exist externally if its being a natural universal is understood as requiring universality itself, since every external existent must be individuated, and individuation conflicts with the mental universal taken as universal. The implication of the conflicting consequences is itself evidence that the respective premises cannot all be maintained together. This objection is continued, with its answer, at the start of I:70.

## I:70 — The quiddity exists externally, but the mental accident of universality does not
*Physical combined PDF page 83.*

records.title: Upper, Taftāzānī lemma embedded in Sanandajī's commentary
records.arabic: وإنما ذلك التغاير بين المطلق والمقيد في العقل دون الخارج
records.arabic_anchors: «الوجود الكلي عليه»؛ «وإنما ذلك التغاير بين المطلق والمقيد في العقل دون الخارج»؛ «ثم إذا اعتبرت المأخوذة لا بشرط شيء معروضة للكلي المنطقي»؛ «فهو ... الكلي الطبيعي»؛ «وإنما يوجد منه المعروض دون الكلي العارض»؛ «مجردا عن العوارض ... من الكلية والجنسية والنوعية».
records.english: “That distinction between what is unrestricted and what is restricted exists in the intellect, not externally.”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: —the universal's existence [or its predication] of it. “That,” namely the distinction between what is unrestricted and what is restricted, obtains **in the intellect**, not externally. “Then if” the quiddity “taken without stipulating anything” is considered as something to which the logical universal is predicated, it is—the quiddity under that consideration—the **natural universal**. What exists externally of it is “that which receives the predicate,” that is, the quiddity of which universality is predicated, “not the universal that is predicated of it.” This last item is the abstract attribute of universality, not an additional external thing. One might object that the quiddity too should have no external existence, since the predicated universality excludes it. But the quiddity is not present externally *stripped of all accidents*: universality, genus-character and species-character, and similar attributes are mental accidents which, considered as such, preclude external existence. This clarifies the celebrated saying that the natural universal has existence outside: its externally present subject is not the external instantiation of the *mental predicate* of universality. The sentence continues on I:70.

records.title: The objection and answer to I:69, unassigned margin
records.arabic_anchors: «تنافي الملزومات»؛ «مجرد المأخوذ لا بشرط ليس كليا طبيعيا بل مع اعتبار كونه معروضا للكلي المنطقي»؛ «والوجود هو مجرد ذلك من غير اعتبار الكلية»؛ «وأما المأخوذ مع عارض الكلية فلا وجود له في الخارج».
records.english: —the incompatibility of the necessary consequences establishes incompatibility in the things that entail them. The answer, in summary, is that the thing *merely* taken without a condition is not thereby a natural universal; rather, it becomes one when considered as the subject of the logical universal. External existence belongs to the subject as such, without including the mental universality among its constitutive features, and that existence is realised when individuating accidents arise. What is taken together with universality as an accident has no external existence. This is the intended sense of the familiar statement that the natural universal exists externally. Consider it carefully: the explanation would not permit an unrestricted quiddity to float free of its external instantiations.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Mixed quiddity is not unambiguously an external composite
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله فالوجود حقيقة هي المخلوطة وهي الأفراد»؛ «لا يجوز أن تكون عبارة عن المقيدة المقترنة بالعوارض لا المجموع»؛ «كان الأول معتبرا مطلقا والآخر مقيدا»؛ «أجزاء الكل موجودة بوجود واحد»؛ «فلا محيص إلا بأن يقال أن المخلوطة هي المجموع المذكور كالفرد».
records.english: On “What truly exists is the mixed quiddity—that is, the individuals”: this is correct if the mixed quiddity is taken to mean the composite whole. It must not simply be made identical with the nature qualified by accidents while excluding the whole, since such usage allows the nature, in thought, to be a constituent of a compound without therefore being a separate constituent existing in reality. Were one part unrestricted and another restricted by something else, one could speak of them as different conceptual parts; yet externally the parts of a whole need not possess a separately multiplied existence. One may instead say that the quiddity and its accompanying accidents subsist together with one external existence; or that several existences are attributed to constituents. The claim “mixed” thus requires an explicit account of what sort of composition is meant, and whether “individual” stands for the whole or for the qualified nature. The author's language is examined on both possible readings, rather than assuming a conclusion.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Transition to Ibn Sīnā, unassigned margin
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله والقائل ابن سينا»؛ «الماهية قد تؤخذ بشرط لا شيء بأن يتصور معناها بشرط أن يكون ذلك المعنى وحده».

records.title: Upper commentary: existence of the externally individuated nature
records.arabic: ووجوده فيه إنما هو عند عروض التشخص … فالوجود حقيقة هي المخلوطة وهي الأفراد
records.arabic_anchors: «أما صدقه هو عليه وهو المأخوذ لا بشرط شيء فموجود فيه»؛ «ووجوده فيه إنما هو عند عروض التشخص»؛ «فالوجود حقيقة هي المخلوطة»؛ «وهي الأفراد»؛ «وأما المأخوذ مع عارض الكلية فلا توجد»؛ «الكلي العقلي».

records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh

records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: As for its being truly predicated of that subject, the thing taken without stipulating anything does exist in it. Its existence there, however, only obtains when individuation supervenes. Accordingly, the actually existent quiddity is the **mixed** quiddity, namely the individuals. The feminine pronoun may be explained through the grammatical predicate, or because its referent is the quiddity. But a quiddity considered along with the accident of universality does not exist externally; nor does the compound of quiddity and that mental accident, namely the **intellectual universal** (*al-kullī al-ʿaqlī*).

records.title: Does the material part precede the composite in both existences?
records.arabic_anchors: «ولا يكون المعنى الأول مقولا على المجموع مع حال المقارنة بل جزء منه مادة له»؛ «قوله مثلا الحيوان إذا أخذناه بشرط أن يكون معه الخ»؛ «هذا هو المذكور بقوله وقد يقال الماهية الخ».
records.english: The first meaning is not predicated of the composite while the accompanying feature is present. It is instead its part and serves as matter for it. The passage concerning animal taken with a further condition is an exposition of the alternative account introduced by “It has also been said concerning the quiddity ...”. Yet this depends on taking the example exactly as specified, not on treating every use of “animal” as denoting the same concept in the same respect.

records.title: Objection: a composite is not necessarily an exterior part plus an interior part
records.arabic_anchors: «ومعناه على ما سبق آنفا»؛ «حيث لو اقترن به النطق كان النطق زائدا عليه وصار المجموع مركبا من الحيوان والناطق»؛ «فلا تكون الحيوان مقولا على ذلك المجموع بل كان جزءا ومادة له»؛ «ما هو زائد عليه متناقضا».
records.english: If rationality is associated with animality, then on the restricted reading rationality is an addition to it and the whole is a composite of animal and rational. Animality so construed cannot be predicated of the whole; it is a constituent and its matter. But if “animal” is instead treated simply as that which can have something accompanying it, whether the concomitant is an accident or something else, the conclusion cannot be transferred without argument. At issue is whether the addition is part of the thing's definition, or only a condition under which the thing is apprehended; confusing the two makes the assertion “animal is the whole” contradict “animal is its part.”

notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Objection concerning genus, species and differentia
records.arabic_anchors: «قوله كان نوعا»؛ «واعترض عليه بأن النوع مجموع الجنس والفصل»؛ «فكيف جعل عبارة عن المأخوذ بشرط شيء»؛ «وأجيب بأنه تسامح مبني على أن الجنس والنوع والفصل واحد بالذات لكن ...».
records.english:
On “it is a species”: an objection is raised that the species is the combination of genus and differentia. How, then, can species be identified with the genus taken under the stipulation that the differentia accompany it? One reply describes this as a permissible looseness of expression, founded on the claim that genus, species and differentia are one in their external subject, while intellectually distinguished. The marginal writer stresses, however, that their unity in subject does not make their *conceptual definitions* interchangeable. The discussion passes into the next page.

records.title: Upper commentary: a nature taken with a stipulation of separateness
records.arabic: لا شيء بمعنى أن يفرض عليها كل ما يقارنها
records.arabic_anchors: «لا شيء بمعنى أن يفرض عليها كل ما يقارنها»؛ «فتكون مادة للشخص»؛ «متقدمة عليه في الوجودين»؛ «فالمراد من التقدم هو التقدم بالطبع»؛ «ولا يصح حملها على الشخص لانتفاء شرط الحمل وهو الاتحاد في الوجود».
records.english: “‘No thing’: in the sense that everything accompanying it is supposed [to be an additional qualification].”
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.
records.stage86_prior_english_analytic_draft: —“no thing,” in the sense that whatever accompanies the quiddity is assumed to be additional to it, and the quiddity is considered apart from those accompanying features. “It then becomes matter” and a constituent “of the individual,” understood as the composite of the nature and what accompanies it, “prior to it in both kinds of existence,” external and mental, since a whole cannot be realised without its constituent. The priority intended is **priority by nature**, not temporal priority. Nor may it be predicated of the individual under that consideration, because the condition of predication—unity in existence—does not obtain.

records.title: Upper commentary: the example of animal and rational
records.arabic_anchors: «الحيوان إذا أخذناه بشرط أن لا يكون معه الناطق»؛ «كان جزءا ومادة للمجموع المركب من الحيوان والناطق ولا يحمل عليه»؛ «وإذا أخذناه بشرط أن يكون معه الناطق كان نوعا»؛ «وإذا أخذناه لا بشرط أن يكون معه شيء كان له جهتان».
records.english: Thus, when we take *animal* on condition that the rational does not accompany it, it is a part and a material constituent of the composite of animal and rational, and is not predicated of that composite. When we take animal on condition that rationality accompanies it, it becomes a **species**. When we take it without stipulating whether anything accompanies it, it admits two aspects: we can consider the difference between it and what accompanies it, or consider their unity. The first animal is thus a part of the human being, preceding it in both modes of existence, and cannot be predicated of it. The contrast between the second and third cases closes in I:72.
records.attribution: mixed Taftazani lemma and Sanandaji sharh
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: The proposed resolution and the commentator's disagreement
records.arabic_anchors: «فيه تأمل والتحقيق ما ذكر»؛ «قوله والثالث جنس له محمول الخ»؛ «حقيقة الكلام أن المأخوذ لا بشرط شيء إذا اعتبر بحسب أنحاء ...»؛ «هذا يخالف ما في الشرح نوع مخالفة فتأمله».
records.english: There is room for reflection here, and the correct resolution requires further precision. On “The third is a genus predicated of it”: it has been said that the real account is as follows. If the nature taken without stipulating anything is considered with respect both to its difference from an accompaniment and to its unity with it, it can be an essential constituent capable of predication. Considered under sheer unity, it may be taken as a species. I say, however, that this differs in a certain respect from the account given in the commentary. Consider that difference carefully. The comparison must therefore not be presented as an unqualified agreement between Ibn Sīnā and the later terminology.

records.title: What precisely is meant by 'without stipulating'?
records.arabic_anchors: «لا يشترط أن يكون ذلك المعنى وحده ولا وحده مع تجويز أن يقارنه غيره وأن لا يقارنه»؛ «ويكون المعنى الأول مقولا على المجموع حال المقارنة»؛ «قد يكون غير متحصل بنفسه»؛ «بل يكون مبهما محتملا للمقولية على أشياء مختلفة الحقائق».
records.english: A meaning taken without a condition does **not** stipulate that it be alone, nor that it be alone with the additional requirement that some other thing may or may not accompany it. Rather, both accompaniment and non-accompaniment are left open. Under this consideration the first meaning may be predicated of a composite when an accompaniment is present; it need not be independently complete by itself. It can remain indeterminate and open to predication of things with different essential realities. Its further completion arises from what is conjoined to it, enabling it to be specified and become, in some instances, one of several genuinely distinct natures.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Animal as genus, and the source of the problem
records.arabic_anchors: «كما في الأنواع الداخلة تحت الجنس وهو نوع مثلا إذا أخذ الحيوان بشرط أن لا يكون معه شيء»؛ «وإن اقترن به ناطق صار المجموع مركبا من الحيوان والناطق»؛ «وإذا أخذ بشرط أن لا يكون معه الناطق مختصا ومتحصلا به كان نوعا»؛ «وإذا أخذ لا بشرط أن يكون معه شيء».
records.english: This may be illustrated by the species falling under a genus. If we consider “animal” under the condition of not including any further thing, then, when rationality accompanies it, a composite of animal and rational results; animal in that respect is its material component rather than something predicated of the completed whole. If it is taken together with rationality as specifying and completing it, it is the species. If it is taken without stipulating what may accompany it, the relation to completion remains open. The controversy is about whether “animal” in each of these examples stands for the same conceived nature or for a nature taken under an additional condition. The latter would make apparently simple claims of identity or priority equivocal.

notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Matter, priority, and conceptual versus external order
records.arabic_anchors: «الأول جزء الإنسان مقدم عليه في الوجودين والثاني نفس الإنسان والثالث جنس محمول عليه»؛ «لا يكون جزءا لأن الجزء لا يحمل على الكل بالمواطأة»؛ «الفصل أنه جزء من النوع»؛ «أنه لا بد للعقل من ملاحظتهما في تحصيل صورة مطابقة للنوع»؛ «فيكون متقدما على النوع في العقل»؛ «وأما بحسب الخارج فيكون متأخرا لأنه ما لم يوجد الإنسان في الخارج لم يعقل له شيء يعمه وغيره».
records.english: Thus the first [animal] is a constituent of the human being and prior to it in the two modes of existence, the second is the human being itself, and the third is a genus predicated of it. Nevertheless, a constituent, precisely insofar as it is a constituent, cannot be predicated of the whole *univocally* as though it were identical with the whole. The genus and differentia must be distinguished in their role in an intellectual definition: each must be considered in order to form a concept adequate to the species, and in that respect the constituent is prior to the species in understanding. In the external order, however, the nature as an abstract genus is not found prior to concrete humans; the argument therefore cannot simply infer an independent external genus from its conceptual priority. The last lines connect to I:73, which is a full leaf of continuing marginal discussion, not a new principal-text page.
records.attribution: unassigned printed marginal or ruled annotation
notes: DO NOT CLAIM full all-register literal translation, second-pass certification or independent witness collation.

records.title: Three different senses of quiddity “taken with a condition”
records.english: —Abū ʿAlī [Ibn Sīnā] [discussed it] in the Shifāʾ, and the investigator summarized it in his commentary on the Ishārāt. End [of the citation]. The author, may God have mercy on him, then mentioned that it presents points for discussion; we have already indicated some of them earlier, so refer back to that passage. Once this is understood, know that the distinctions given at the beginning of the chapter are the customary ways in which later scholars consider quiddity. Yet the Chief Master's reported words may suggest ways of considering it other than those that have become customary. In his usage, quiddity taken on condition of nothing is the meaning conceived in isolation: were something to accompany it, that accompanying thing would be reckoned external to the meaning and not included in it. Accordingly, when they are conjoined the meaning is not predicated of the resulting composite as a whole, but is a constituent part of it—its matter.
records.arabic: أبو علي في الشفاء ولخصه المحقق في شرح الإشارات انتهى ثم ذكر المصنف رحمه الله أن فيه مواضع بحث وإنا قد أشرنا إلى بعضها فيما سبق فلينظر إذا تقرر هذا فاعلم أن ما سبق أوائل الفصل هي الاعتبارات المشهورة للماهية بين المتأخرين وأما الشيخ الرئيس فقد يستفاد من كلامه المنقول اعتبارات غير ما اشتهر وهي أن الماهية المأخوذة بشرط لا شيء هي ما يتصور معناها وحده بحيث لو قارنها شيء اعتبر ذلك الذي قارنها خارجا عنه غير داخل فيه فلا يكون ذلك المعنى مقولا على المجموع المركب حال المقارنة بل جزءا منه ومادته

records.prior_english_stage77: —[This account is attributed to] Abū ʿAlī [Ibn Sīnā] in the *Shifāʾ*, and [the investigator] summed it up in his commentary on the *Ishārāt*. End of citation. The author, may God have mercy on him, then said that there are points in it admitting discussion. We have already indicated some of them; consult what precedes. With that established, know that the considerations stated at the beginning of the chapter are the **familiar classifications of quiddity among later scholars**. But one may infer from the Chief Master's quoted wording considerations other than those conventionally reported. In one sense, *quiddity taken on condition of nothing* (*bi-sharṭ lā shayʾ*) is the meaning conceived **by itself alone**. If something accompanies it, the accompanying thing is regarded as external to it, not included within it. The meaning under this consideration cannot be predicated of the composite whole once another thing has been conjoined to it; rather, it will be a **part** or **material element** of that whole.
